en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Pañcaka-nipāta (The Book of Fives) in the Aṅguttara Nikāya.
1. The First Fifty [Discourses] 1.
The Chapter on the Powers of a Trainee 1.
Commentary on the Short Discourse (Saṃkhittasutta)
1. In the first [chapter] of the *Pañcakanipāta*, "the powers of the seven trainees" refers to the powers of one in training (*sekha*).

Among the powers of faith and so forth: it does not waver in the face of lack of faith, thus it is the power of faith; it does not waver in the face of shamelessness, thus it is the power of moral shame (*hirī*); it does not waver in the face of lack of dread, thus it is the power of moral dread (*ottappa*);
it does not waver in the face of laziness, thus it is the power of energy (*vīriya*); it does not waver in the face of ignorance, thus it is the power of wisdom (*paññā*).
Therefore, because these are the powers of the seven trainees, therefore [it is said].
2. Commentary on the Vitthata Sutta. 2.

In the second [sutta], regarding the phrases "by bodily misconduct" and so forth, the instrumental case is used in the sense of the accusative; that is, bodily misconduct and the rest are things for which one should feel shame (*hirīyitabbāni*).
"Hirīyati" means "he feels shame"; this is the meaning. In the description of *ottappa* (fear of wrongdoing), the instrumental case is used in the sense of the causal ablative;

the meaning is that he feels *ottappa*, that is, he fears, because of bodily misconduct and so forth, which serve as the causes for *ottappa*. "Āraddhavīriyo" means one whose energy is exerted, one whose mind is not despondent. "Pahānāya" means for the purpose of abandoning. "Upasampadāya" means...
For the sake of attainment. "Possessed of fortitude" means endowed with the power of energy (*vīriya*). "Firm in exertion" means having steadfast perseverance.
"One who has not laid down the burden regarding wholesome states" means one who has not set aside the burden nor slackened his effort regarding wholesome states.
"Leading to arising and passing away" means [the path] leading to the arising and the passing away of the five aggregates, in order to penetrate both their arising and their passing away.
"Capable. "Endowed with wisdom" means one who possesses both the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*) and the wisdom of the path (*magga-paññā*).
"Noble" means that which stands far removed from the defilements by way of suppression and by way of eradication, and is thus purified.
"Penetrative": it is called penetrative because it pierces through; the meaning is that he is endowed with that [wisdom].

In this context, path-wisdom is "penetrative" because it penetrates and shatters the mass of greed, the mass of hatred, and the mass of delusion—things never before pierced through or shattered—by way of total eradication. Insight-wisdom is penetrative by way of partial eradication;
and since that insight leads to the attainment of path-wisdom, it is appropriate to call that insight "penetrative" as well.

Regarding the phrase "leading rightly to the destruction of suffering": here too, path-wisdom is called "leading rightly to the destruction of suffering" because it proceeds by means of a correct cause and method, exhausting both the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*) and the suffering of the defilements (*kilesadukkha*).

Insight-wisdom (*vipassanāpaññā*), on the other hand, is "leading to the destruction of suffering" because it proceeds by way of its specific factor (*tadaṅgavasena*), exhausting both the suffering of the round of existence and the suffering of the defilements.
Or, it should be understood as "leading to the destruction of suffering" because it conduces to the acquisition of the path-wisdom that leads to the destruction of suffering.
Thus, in this sutta, the five powers are spoken of as mixed together; likewise in the fifth [sutta].
6. Commentary on the *Samāpatti-sutta*.

6. In the sixth [case], "the attainment of the unwholesome" (*akusalassa samāpatti*) means the entering into an unwholesome state (*akusaladhamma*); the meaning is that one possesses it along with that [state]. "Abides having become obsessed" (*pariyuṭṭhāya tiṭṭhati*) means he abides having become enveloped. 7. Commentary on the Seventh Sutta:

"Sporting among sensual pleasures" (*kāmesu laḷitā*) means sporting in and delighting in both sensual objects (*vatthukāma*) and the defilements of sensual pleasure (*kilesakāma*). "A sword-blade for eating" (*asitabyābhaṅgi*)...
"Both the grass-mat and the grass-carrying pole. A "son of good family" (*kulaputta*) is one who is well-born by virtue of his conduct.
"Having abandoned" (*ohāya*) means having relinquished. "Worthy of being spoken" (*alaṃ vacanāya*) means fit to be said. "Obtainable" (*labbhā*) means easily obtained; it is possible to acquire.

"Low desires" (*hīnā kāmā*) are the sensual pleasures of the five low-born classes. "Middle desires" (*majjhimā kāmā*) are the sensual pleasures of middle-class beings. "Exquisite desires" (*paṇītā kāmā*) are those of kings and great ministers.

Sensual pleasures (*kāmā*). They are reckoned as "sensual pleasures" because they are themselves sensual and because they are to be indulged in as sensual; thus, by way of being sensual and by way of being objects of sensual indulgence, they are reckoned simply as "sensual pleasures.
"He is grown old" means he is aged. "Possessed of sufficient wisdom" means possessed of appropriate wisdom.
"Self-guarded" means guarded and protected by himself, or capable of guarding and protecting himself. "Not fit for negligence" means not inclined toward it.
To neglect. "It was not done out of faith" means that whatever ought to be done toward wholesome states by way of faith has not been done.

The same method applies to the remaining phrases as well. "Bhikkhus, I have no regard for that bhikkhu"—this is said after one has established that person in the fruit of stream-entry by having them perform what ought to be done through faith and the other qualities.
He shows: "I am without longing. In this sutta, the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*) is explained.
8. Commentary on the *Cavana-sutta*:

In the eighth [sutta], "in the true Dhamma" means in the true Dhamma of the Dispensation (*sāsana*). "Lacking faith" refers to both the faith of conviction (*okappanasaddhā*) and the faith of leaping forward (*pakkhandanasaddhā*).

"Devoid of both kinds of faith" means he lacks both types of confidence. "He falls away and does not find a footing" means that within this teaching he falls away from its virtues and is unable to establish himself.
Thus, in this sutta, both non-establishment and establishment are discussed.
9. Commentary on the First Sutta on Lack of Respect.

9. In the ninth [sutta], "he has no respect" means he is disrespectful (*agārava*). "He has no deference" means he is undeferential (*appatisso*), one who does not acknowledge the eldest or act with humility.
The rest here is exactly like the previous [sutta]. 10. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Disrespect:

In the tenth [sutta], "incapable" means unfit as a vessel (*abhājana*). "Growth" (*vuddhi*) means increase. "Increase" (*virūḷhi*) means a state of being immovable due to having deep roots. "Expansion" (*vepulla*) means a state of greatness. The rest is clear in every respect.
The First Chapter on the Powers of a Trainee.
2. The Chapter on Powers. 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on What Has Not Been Heard.

11. Regarding the first [statement] of the second [discourse], "Bhikkhus, formerly regarding things unheard of" means, bhikkhus, formerly regarding the four truths, which are the Dhamma unheard of by me.

"I claim to have reached the perfection of finality through direct knowledge" means that, having directly known the sixteenfold function regarding the four truths by means of the four paths, I have reached the perfection of finality.

"I declare that I have reached the further shore, having accomplished the state of one who has done what was to be done because all duties are completed"—thus, on the Great Enlightenment Seat (Mahābodhipallaṅka), he demonstrates his own qualities to be attained.
"Of the Tathāgata" means [endowed] with eight reasons for being a Tathāgata. "The powers of a Tathāgata" refers to the powers of knowledge that have proceeded exactly as they ought to proceed.
"The place of the bull" (āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ) means the preeminent position.
“Lion’s roar” means a roar of fearlessness. “The Brahma-wheel” means the supreme wheel. “He sets it in motion” means he proclaims it. 2.

Commentary on the Kūṭasutta In the second [sutta], “the powers of the trainee” means the powers of knowledge belonging to those in training (*sekha*). “Supreme” means the highest. It is “comprehensive” because it gathers together the remaining powers as beams support a roof-peak. It is “unifying” because it brings those very powers into a unified whole.
3. Commentary on the Short Discourse (Saṃkhittasutta).

13. Regarding the third [discourse]: "It does not waver there in forgetfulness" refers to the power of mindfulness (*satibala*). "It does not waver in restlessness" refers to the power of concentration (*samādhibala*).
4. Commentary on the Detailed Discourse (Vitthatasutta).

14. Regarding the phrase "with mindfulness and discernment" (*satinepakkena*) in the fourth [sutta]: here, *nepakka* refers to wisdom (*paññā*), which is included because it serves as an aid to mindfulness.
5. Commentary on the Daṭṭhabba Sutta: 15.
In the fifth [sutta], in order to speak specifically regarding mundane and supramundane phenomena within their own respective domains, [the Blessed One asks]: "And where, monks..."
He said, "The power of faith (saddhābala) is to be seen," and so forth.

For example, when four sons of merchants—along with a king as their fifth companion—descend onto a street thinking, "We shall enjoy a festival," and while they have gone to the house of one merchant's son, the other four sit in silence;
the owner of that house [says], "Give these people hard and soft food."

“Give them perfumes, garlands, ornaments, and so forth,” he would direct within the house. When the second, third, and fourth had entered the house, the other four sat in silence, while the master of the house himself directed within the house, saying, “Give these people solid food and soft food;
give them perfumes, garlands, ornaments, and so forth. Then, when they had all entered the king’s house last of all—
Just as a king, though he is the master everywhere, at this particular time directs his affairs only within his own palace,
saying, "Give these people hard food and soft food; give them perfumes, garlands, ornaments, and so forth," even so,
when the five powers— faith being the fifth— arise with a single object, as if those friends were descending together into one street, [it is like that].
In the first man’s house, the other four sit in silence while the master of the house alone deliberates;
likewise, having attained the factors of stream-entry, the power of faith—characterized by resolution—is the eldest and the precursor, while the remaining factors follow in its wake.
Just as in the second man’s house, the other four sit in silence while the master of the house alone deliberates.
Thus, having reached the right efforts (*sammappadhāna*), the power of energy (*vīriyabala*) alone— characterized by exertion— is the foremost and the precursor, while the others follow in its wake.
Just as in the third house the other four sit in silence while the master of the house alone deliberates,
so too, having reached the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), the power of mindfulness (*satibala*) alone— characterized by establishing— is the foremost.

The first is the precursor, and the others follow in its wake. Just as in the fourth house the other four sit in silence while the master of the house alone deliberates, so too, having attained the jhānas and liberations, the power of concentration—characterized by non-distraction—is the eldest and the precursor, while the others follow in its wake.
This is last of all, at the time when they have gone to the king’s house.

However, just as when the other four sit in silence while the king alone conducts affairs in the palace, even so, having reached the Noble Truths, the power of wisdom—characterized by understanding—is the foremost and the leader, while the remaining powers follow after it;
thus, in this context, the five powers are described as being mixed together. The sixth [power] has its meaning already explained. Thus...
In the previous section and here in these eight suttas, only the powers of the trainee (*sekhabala*) are discussed. However, the Elder Mahādatta, who dwelt at Karaṇḍakola, said:
"In the four suttas below, the powers of the trainee are discussed; in the four above, the powers of the adept (*asekhabala*).
7. Commentary on the First Discourse on What is Beneficial (*Paṭhamahitasutta*)

17. In the seventh [sutta], virtue and the other factors are explained as being mixed. "Liberation" (*vimutti*) refers specifically to the liberation of the fruit of Arhatship. "Knowledge and vision of liberation" (*vimuttiñāṇadassana*) is the knowledge of retrospection (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*), which is purely mundane (*lokiya*).
8–10. Commentary on the Second *Hita-sutta* and following: 18–20.
In the eighth [sutta], one who is immoral but learned is described; in the ninth, one who is immoral and unlearned; and in the tenth, one who is learned and whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).
The Second Chapter on Strength.
3. The Chapter on the Five Factors. 1.
Explanation of the First Discourse on Lack of Respect.
21. Regarding the first [section] of the third [chapter]: "One of dissimilar conduct" means one who possesses a dissimilar, that is, distinct, mode of livelihood.

"The Dhamma of proper conduct" refers to the virtue prescribed by way of formal observance (*vatta*), which constitutes the highest standard of conduct. "The Dhamma of the trainee" refers to the virtue prescribed for those in training (*sekha*).
"Virtues" refers to the four great virtues (*mahāsīla*). "Right view" refers to the right view of insight (*vipassanā-sammādiṭṭhi*).
"Right concentration" refers to both path-concentration and fruition-concentration. In this sutta, the aggregates beginning with virtue are explained as being mixed together.
2. Commentary on the Second Sutta on Lack of Respect (Agārava-sutta) 22.

In the second [sutta], "the aggregate of virtue" means a mass of virtue. The same method applies to the other two as well. However, these three aggregates are indeed explained here as being mixed together.
3. Commentary on the Discourse on Corruptions (Upakkilesasutta) 23.
In the third [verse]: "It does not shine" means it does not possess radiance. "Dissolving" means having the nature of breaking apart.
"Iron" refers to black iron. "Metal" refers to metal other than the four types mentioned here. "Copper" [is as follows].
Silver. "Of the mind" means of the wholesome consciousness belonging to the four planes. Let it be that there are defilements for the [consciousness] of the three planes;
but how can they exist for the supramundane? By way of not allowing it to arise.
For to the extent that they do not allow it to arise, to that same extent they are called defilements of both the mundane and the supramundane. And "fragile" refers to the object.
It has the nature of breaking apart by undergoing a state of being pulverized and crushed.

"It is rightly concentrated for the destruction of the taints" means it is concentrated by means of the cause or reason for the sake of arahantship, which is designated as the destruction of the taints.
Up to this point, he shows the mind purified and established in arahantship, with the taints exhausted. Now, his penetration of direct knowledge—
He said, "Showing whatever [it may be]," and so forth. That has an obvious meaning. 4.
Commentary on the Dussīla Sutta (The Discourse on the Immoral). 24.

In the fourth [verse], "one whose proximate cause is destroyed" (*hatūpanisa*) means one whose supporting condition (*upanissaya*) is destroyed, one whose cause is destroyed. "Knowledge and vision according to reality" (*yathābhūtañāṇadassana*) is the knowledge that discerns name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Beginning with "young insight" (*taruṇavipassanā*). "Disenchantment and dispassion" (*nibbidā-virāga*) refers to both disenchantment and dispassion.

Therein, disenchantment is powerful insight, while dispassion is the path. "Knowledge and vision of liberation" (*vimutti-ñāṇadassana*) refers to both the liberation of the fruit and the knowledge of reviewing.
5. Commentary on the *Anuggahita Sutta* (The Untended)
25. In the fifth [case], "right view" refers to the right view of insight (*vipassanā-sammādiṭṭhi*). Regarding the phrases "fruits of liberation of mind" and so forth:

"liberation of mind" (*cetovimutti*) refers to the concentration of the path and its fruits (*maggaphala-samādhi*). "Liberation by wisdom" (*paññāvimutti*) refers to the knowledge of the fruit (*phala-ñāṇa*).

"Supported by virtue" means supported and protected by virtue. "Supported by learning" means supported by great erudition (*bāhusacca*). "Supported by discussion" means supported by discussion on the Dhamma (*dhamma-sākacchā*).
"Supported by serenity" means supported by one-pointedness of mind.

To clarify this meaning: suppose one were to plant a sweet mango seed, construct a boundary around it on all sides, water it from time to time, clear away the roots [of competing plants] from time to time, and remove the insects that have fallen [into it] from time to time...
A man who, from time to time, brings back a spider’s web, strips it away, and tends to the mango tree should be shown.
For that man’s planting of the sweet mango seed is to be regarded as right view accompanied by insight;
his securing the boundary fence is to be regarded as support through virtue; his watering with water is to be regarded as support through learning; and the clearing of the roots...

Supporting through conversation is like watering; supporting serenity (*samatha*) by way of clearing away obstacles to *jhāna* and insight (*vipassanā*) is like removing pests; and supporting powerful insight is like pulling out a spider’s web.
Just as a tree thus supported grows quickly and yields fruit, so too does the root of right view (*mūla-sammā-diṭṭhi*), when supported by these factors such as virtue (*sīla*).
It should be understood that by increasing [the practice] quickly through the path, one bestows the fruits of liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom.
6. Commentary on the *Vimuttāyatana Sutta*. 26.
Regarding the sixth [sutta], "bases of liberation" (*vimuttāyatanāni*) means causes for being liberated. "In which" (*yattha*) means in those bases of liberation. The Teacher...
"He teaches the Dhamma" means he teaches the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. "Experiencing the meaning" refers to one who knows the meaning of the text (*pāḷi*).
"Experiencing the Dhamma" refers to one who knows the text itself. "Gladness" (*pāmojja*) is tender joy (*taruṇa-pīti*). "Rapture" (*pīti*) is powerful joy in the form of satisfaction.
"Body" (*kāya*) refers to the mental body (*nāmakāya*). "Becomes tranquil" means it subsides. "Experiences happiness" means happiness...
He attains it. "The mind becomes concentrated" means it becomes concentrated by means of the concentration of the fruit of Arahatship.
For while hearing that Dhamma, he understands the jhānas, insight, the path, and the fruits in every place he goes;
as he understands thus, rapture arises. Not allowing that rapture to falter in the interim, he becomes one who practices the preliminary stage of meditation (upacārakammaṭṭhāna).
Having increased insight, he reaches Arahantship. It is with reference to this that it is said: "The mind becomes concentrated.
The same method applies to the remaining cases as well. However, this is the distinction:

"the sign of concentration" means that among the thirty-eight objects of meditation, any one of them—concentration itself—is the sign of concentration. Regarding the phrases "it is well grasped," and so forth, [it refers to] the meditation subject in the presence of the teacher...
"By one who learns it, it is well grasped, well attended to, and well scrutinized.
"Thoroughly penetrated by wisdom" means it has been made directly evident by wisdom. "In that Dhamma" refers to that Dhamma of the scriptural text on the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
Thus, in this sutta, all five bases for liberation are explained as leading to Arahantship.
7. Commentary on the Samādhi Sutta 27.
Seventh: "The immeasurable" (*appamāṇa*) refers to the supramundane (*lokuttara*), which is devoid of qualities that create a measure.

"Clever and mindful" (*nipakā patissatā*) means being endowed with both cleverness (*nepakka*) and mindfulness (*sati*). "Five knowledges" (*pañca ñāṇāni*) refers to the five kinds of reviewing knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*). "Each for themselves" (*paccattaṃ yeva*)...
"They arise" means they arise within oneself. In such passages as "this concentration is pleasant in the present," etc., it is the concentration of the fruit of Arahatship that is intended;
some also call it the "concentration of the Path. For that is "pleasant in the present" because it is pleasant at every moment of absorption;
it is "a result of happiness in the future" because each preceding moment serves as a condition for the subsequent moment of the bliss of concentration.

It is "noble" (ariya) because it is remote from the defilements (kilesa); it is "unworldly" (nirāmisa) due to the absence of the bait of sensual desire, the bait of material goods, and the bait of worldly honors;
it is "not practiced by base men" (akāpurisasevita) because it is practiced by Great Beings such as the Buddhas;

it is "peaceful" (santa) because of the peace of its factors, the peace of its object, and the peace of all the distress of the defilements; it is "sublime" (paṇīta) in the sense of being unassailable; and it possesses the state of the subsiding of defilements because it has been attained through the subsiding of defilements.

Or, it is "attained through subsiding" (paṭippassaddhaladdha) because it is attained by one for whom [the defilements] have subsided. For "subsided" (paṭippassaddha) and "subsiding" (paṭippassaddhi) are identical in meaning.
Or, it is "attained through subsiding" because it is attained by an Arahant whose defilements have subsided;

or, it is "attained to unification" (ekodibhāvādhigata) because it is reached through the state of being unified (ekodibhāva), or because it is reached precisely by means of the state of being unified. This refers to weak, mundane concentration (appaguṇasāsavasamādhi).

Because he has not yet attained [the higher stages], he is not one who has "restrained and barred by effort" (sasaṅkhāra-niggayha-vārita-gata), even though he restrains opposing states and wards off defilements with a mind that involves volitional effort and application.

When entering that concentration or emerging from it, because he has reached a fullness of mindfulness, he enters mindful and emerges mindful; or else, he enters mindful according to the time limit previously determined.

One emerges mindful. Therefore, when one reflects upon this thus: "This concentration is pleasant in the present and has a pleasant result in the future," the knowledge that arises within oneself, independent of another, is one kind of knowledge.
The same method applies to the remaining [concentrations]. Thus, these five kinds of knowledge arise within oneself alone.
8. Commentary on the Discourse on the Five Factors (Pañcaṅgikasutta) 28.
In the eighth [discourse], “of the noble one” (*ariyassa*) means of one who stands far removed from the defilements abandoned by way of suppression.

“I shall teach the development” (*bhāvanaṃ desessāmi*) means I shall make manifest its cultivation and increase. “This very body” (*imaṃ eva kāyaṃ*) refers to this body composed of the four primary elements. “It moistens” (*abhisandeti*)...
"It refreshes" means it produces the happiness of joy as it occurs everywhere. "It cools" means it flows all around.
"It fills" means it fills [the body] like a bellows with air. "It pervades" means it touches everywhere.
"Of the entire body" means, in whatever place the continuity of the clung-to [aggregates] proceeds, in that entire body of this bhikkhu—
There is not even a minute spot following upon the skin, flesh, and blood that is not pervaded by the bliss of the first jhāna.
*Dakkho* means one who is clever, capable, and skilled in preparing, mixing, and kneading bath-powders.
*Kaṃsathāle* means in a vessel made of any kind of metal; however, a clay vessel is not durable for one who is kneading.
It breaks apart; therefore, he did not show it. "Sprinkling repeatedly" means having sprinkled again and again.

"He should knead" means that, taking a bronze bowl with his left hand and sprinkling a suitable amount of water with his right hand again and again, he should form a lump while rubbing it. "Followed by moisture" means followed by the moisture of water.

"Smeared with moisture" means embraced by the moisture of water. "Internally and externally" means together with the internal region and the external region; the meaning is that it is entirely pervaded by the moisture of water.
"And not trickling" means that the water does not drip drop by drop, and it is possible to grasp it even with the hand or with two fingers.
The meaning is that one may also do it with the elbow.
In the simile for the bliss of the second jhāna, *ubbhidodaka* means water that has burst forth;

it does not mean water that rises up after bursting from below, but rather water that arises right within [the vessel], such is the meaning. *Āyamukha* means the path of arrival. *Deva* means a cloud. At the proper time...
"At times" means from time to time; the meaning is "every half-month or every ten days. "Streams" refers to rain. "Should not pour down" means should not enter [the lake];
the meaning is "should not rain. "Cold streams of water welling up" means cold streams of water, filling that lake, welling up.
For it is the water rising from below that, having emerged, breaks through [to the surface].
It agitates: it agitates the water entering from the four directions with old leaves, grass, sticks, poles, and so forth.

It agitates the rainwater with the drops falling from the clouds and the bubbles; however, there is no such thing as water that, having remained still, arises like a creation by psychic power (iddhinimmita) and pervades this area while not pervading that. Therefore, there is no place untouched by it.
There is no name for it. In this context, the body born of kamma is like the lake, and the bliss of the second jhāna is like the water;
the rest should be understood in the same manner as before.
Regarding the simile for the bliss of the third jhāna: because there are lotuses (*uppala*) here, it is called *uppalinī*. The same applies to the other two terms.

This is the method. And herein, among the white, red, and blue [lotuses], anything that is indeed a *uppala* (blue lotus); the *puṇḍarīka* has fewer than a hundred petals, while the *paduma* has a hundred petals.
Alternatively, even without this restriction on the number of petals, the white is the *paduma* and the red is the *puṇḍarīka*;
such is the analysis here. "Not emerged from the water" means they have not risen out of the water. "Nourished submerged within" means they are indeed submerged inside the surface of the water.
"Having offered, they nourish and increase"—this is the meaning. The remainder should be understood in the same manner as before.
In the simile for the fourth jhāna, regarding the phrase "with a mind that is purified and cleansed":

here, it should be understood as "purified" in the sense of being free from defilements (*nirupakkilesa*), and "cleansed" in the sense of being luminous (*pabhassara*). "With a white cloth" is said for the purpose of illustrating its pervasiveness due to the weather.
It has been said. For when a cloth is soiled, there is no pervasion by heat; when it is washed and purified at that very moment, the pervasion by heat becomes powerful.
In this simile, the physical body is like the cloth, and the bliss of the fourth jhāna is like the pervasion by heat.
Therefore, just as for a well-washed man sitting with a purified cloth draped over his head—
The bodily heat pervades the entire cloth; there is no part of the cloth that is not touched by it.
In the same way, no part of the bhikkhu’s material body remains untouched by the bliss of the fourth jhāna—this is how the meaning here should be understood.
Alternatively, the mind of the fourth jhāna itself is like the cloth, and the matter originated by it is like the pervading heat. For just as in some places or other...
Just as even when a white cloth does not actually touch the body, the entire body is permeated by the temperature originating from it,
so too the monk’s entire body is permeated by the subtle material form (rūpa) produced by the fourth jhāna;
this is how the meaning should be understood here.

The "sign of reviewing" (*paccavekkhaṇanimitta*) is simply the knowledge of reviewing itself. "It is well grasped" means that just as the jhānas, insight, and the path have been properly grasped by him, so too the sign of reviewing is properly grasped by successive signs of reviewing.
"One [is] another" means one person [is] another; for even to oneself, one's own self is not manifest.
"Standing or sitting": for one who is standing, the sitting person is clearly visible; therefore it is stated thus. The same method applies to the remaining cases as well.
"A water-jar" (udakamaṇika) is a water-vessel with a rim. "Level to the brim" means filled evenly.
"Drinkable by a crow" means that it can be drunk by a crow sitting on the rim of the mouth without having to stretch its neck.

“On level ground” means on even ground. In the passage, “One should plant seeds in a good field on level ground where stumps have been cleared away,” it is the well-prepared soil (*maṇḍabhūmi*) that is referred to as “level ground.
“At the crossroads of the four great highways” means at the place where two great roads intersect.
“A chariot with thoroughbred horses” means a chariot drawn by well-trained horses. “With a downward-pointing goad” means as if one were mounted upon the chariot.
When standing still, it is possible to seize [the horse]; likewise, one relies on the object of focus as a goad placed across [its path].
A trainer of horses (*yoggācariya*) is a horse-teacher. He himself guides the horses to be tamed, thus he is a charioteer of horses to be tamed (*assadammasārathi*).

"Wherever he wishes" means whichever path he desires. "In whatever direction he wishes" means whichever destination he desires. "He should drive forward" means he should send it straight ahead. "He should drive back" means he should turn it back.
Having thus explained the preparation for attainment with the five lower factors and shown the benefits of mastery in attainment through these three similes,
he now says, "If he should wish," etc., in order to show the sequence of direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) for one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).
That [passage] has its meaning already explained.
9. Commentary on the Caṅkamasutta 29.
In the ninth [verse], "enduring the journey" means that while traveling a long distance along a road, one endures it;

one is able to tolerate it. "Enduring exertion" means enduring diligence (*vīriya*). "Concentration attained through walking" refers to the concentration achieved by one who is intent upon the walking meditation (*caṅkama*).
He has attained a concentration belonging to one of the eight meditative attainments. "It remains for a long time" means it persists for a long duration.
For a sign grasped while standing may be lost when sitting; a sign grasped while sitting may be lost when lying down.
However, for one who resolves upon walking meditation, the sign grasped at the moving object remains even when standing or sitting.
"Even for one who is lying down, it shall not be lost.
10. Commentary on the Nāgita Sutta: 30.
In the tenth [verse], they are called "those with loud noises and great noises" because their sound is high due to rising upward and because of its massiveness.
For when those eminent Kshatriya householders, eminent Brahmin householders, and others had arrived after receiving great honors and were shouting, "Give space for so-and-so!
Give space for so-and-so!", there arose the sound of them speaking to one another: "We arrived first; we arrived before you; there is no space!"

It was both loud and great. "As if fishermen were hauling in fish"—it was like the scene when fishermen have caught their haul of fish and are at the place of sale, where a great crowd of people crying out, "Give me some! Give me some!
makes such a noise. "The pleasure of filth" means the pleasure of impurity. "The pleasure of sloth" means...
The pleasure of sleep. "The pleasure of gain, honor, and renown" refers to the pleasure arisen by depending upon both material gain and honor, as well as the chanting of one's praises.
"They will go only toward that" means they will go to that very place where the Blessed One has gone; it is said that they will simply follow after him.
"For such, Bhante, is the Blessed One’s virtue and wisdom," because such is your [virtue and wisdom], Venerable Sir.

The meaning is: "virtue and knowledge. "And let there be no glory for me" means: "let there be no association with glory together with me. "Of those dear ones" means: "of dear people. "This is its outflow" means:
this is the result of that state of being dear. "Devotion to the sign of the foul" means: devotion to the meditation subject of the foul (*asubha-kammaṭṭhāna*).
"In the sign of the beautiful" means: in a desirable object that is a basis for lust. "This is its outflow" means: [this is the result of that].
This is the accomplishment of that practice of the sign of foulness. Thus, in this sutta, it is insight alone that is taught in these five places.
The Third Chapter on the Five Factors.
4. Sumanavagga 1.
Sumanasuttavaṇṇanā 31.
Regarding the first [sutta] of the fourth [chapter]: "The princess Sumanā"—having made a great offering and having made an aspiration.

Thus was the name given to the princess. During the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Vipassī, when the city-dwellers—resolving that "even by waging war, we shall capture the Teacher"—had secured the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha with the help of their general and begun to perform meritorious deeds in succession, it was the general’s turn on the very first day. In that [day]...
On that day, the general prepared a great almsgiving and stationed men all around, saying, "Protect it today so that no one else gives even a single monk a portion.

On that same day, the merchant’s wife, having returned from playing with five hundred young girls while weeping, said to her daughter who had come back: "If, my dear, your father were alive, today I would first—"
“...should feed the One Possessed of the Ten Powers. She said to her, “Mother, do not worry;
I shall act in such a way that the Saṅgha, headed by the Buddha, will eat our first alms-food.

Then, having filled a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand [pieces] with rice-porridge without water, and having prepared it with ghee, honey, sugar, and other ingredients, she gave it to another woman.

Having closed the lid of the casket and surrounded it with clusters of *sumana* flowers, making it resemble a flower bouquet, she herself lifted it up at the time the Blessed One was entering the village and went out from her house surrounded by a group of female kinswomen.
Along the way, the supporters of the general said, "Mother, do not come this way. For those of great merit are indeed...
Their conversation was pleasant, and it was not possible to refuse them as they spoke again and again.
She said, "Little father, great father, uncle, why do you not let me go?
The general replied, "We have been told by the commander, 'Do not give any hard or soft food to anyone else,' mother. She asked, "But what about my hand?"
"Do you see the hard food and soft food? "We see bouquets of flowers. "Does your general not allow you even to perform flower-worship?
"He does, ma'am. "In that case, go on," she said. She approached the Blessed One and said, "Blessed One, please accept these bouquets of flowers.
The Blessed One looked at one of the general's attendants and had him take the bouquets of flowers.
Having paid homage to the Blessed One, she made this aspiration: "May there be no life of anxiety for me as long as I am reborn in various states of existence;
may I be dear wherever I am born, just like this jasmine garland, and may my name be 'Sumanā' alone.
Then, having been told by the Teacher, "May you be happy," she paid homage, circumambulated him, and departed.
The Blessed One also went to the general’s house and sat down on the prepared seat. The general approached carrying rice porridge, but the Teacher covered the bowl with his hand.
"Venerable sir, the community of monks is seated," he said. "Did we receive any almsfood along the way?
[The general] removed the garland and saw the almsfood. The junior attendant said, "Master, this is a garland."
“Having spoken thus, the woman has deceived me. The milk-rice was sufficient for all the bhikkhus, beginning with the Blessed One.
The general gave his own offerings. After the Teacher had finished his meal and pronounced a blessing, he departed.
The general asked, “Who was that woman who gave the alms-food? “It was the daughter of the treasurer, sir,” they replied. “She is a wise woman,” [the general thought].
Thinking, "For one who lives with such a woman in the home, it is not difficult for a man to attain the excellence of heaven," he brought her and established her in the position of his eldest wife.
She took wealth from both her father’s house and the general’s house, and throughout her entire life, she gave alms to the Tathāgata and performed meritorious deeds.
When she passed away from there, she was reborn in the world of the gods of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara). At the very moment of her rebirth, [she appeared] knee-high...
By her supernormal power, she caused a rain of *sumana* flowers to fall, filling the entire realm of the gods.
The deities, thinking, "She has come taking her own name for herself," gave her the name "Sumanā, daughter of the gods.
As she wandered through the realms of gods and humans for ninety-one aeons, never failing to produce a rain of *sumana* flowers wherever she was reborn, she was known as "Sumanā."
She was indeed named Sumanā. At that time, however, she took rebirth in the womb of the chief queen of the King of Kosala.
Those five hundred maidens also took rebirth on that very same day in various families, and on one and the same day, they all emerged from their mothers' wombs.
At that very moment, by a flood reaching up to their knees...

A rain of *sumana* flowers fell. Seeing this, the king thought, "She must have made a resolution in the past," and with a joyful heart, he said, "My daughter has come having taken her own name for herself. He gave her the name Sumanā.
Thinking, "My daughter will not be born alone," he had the city searched, and it was found that five hundred girls had been born.
Having heard this, she supported them all herself. She said, "Every month, when it arrives, bring them here and show them to my daughter.
Thus, having performed great honors and made her aspiration, she should be understood as one who obtained such a name.
When she was seven years old, after Anāthapiṇḍika had completed the monastery and dispatched messengers to the Tathāgata—
The Teacher, accompanied by the community of monks, arrived at Sāvatthī. Anāthapiṇḍika went and said to the king:
"Great King, the Teacher’s arrival here is an auspicious occasion for us as well as for you.
Let the princess Sumana take five hundred maidens along with full water-jars, perfumes, garlands, and other offerings."
“Send a welcoming party for the One Possessing the Ten Powers. The king said, “Very well, Great Merchant,” and did so.
She too, having gone according to the manner instructed by the king, paid homage to the Teacher, honored him with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, and stood to one side.
The Teacher taught her the Dhamma; together with five hundred young women, she was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
Furthermore, at that very moment, five hundred other girls, five hundred women, and five hundred lay followers attained the fruit of stream-entry.
Thus, on that day, two thousand stream-enterers were born even while on the way.
As for the phrase "he approached the Blessed One," why did he approach him? It was because he desired to ask a question. During the time of the Samma-sambuddha Kassapa—

It is said that there were two monks who were companions. Of them, one fulfilled the duty of endearing conduct (*sāraṇīya-dhamma*), while the other observed the proper etiquette regarding the meal hall (*bhattagga-vatta*).
The one who fulfilled the duty of endearing conduct said to the other: "Friend, there is no such thing as the fruit of what has not been given;
it is proper to eat after giving to others what one has received oneself. But the other replied: "Friend, you do not understand; the gift to be given..."
"It is not permissible to cause [the alms] to fall; however, it is permissible for one who takes only what is sufficient for his own maintenance to fulfill the duties regarding the meal-hall.
Not even one among them was able to bring the other into compliance with their own advice.

Both, having fulfilled their respective practices, passed away from there and were reborn in the world of the gods of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*). There, the one who fulfilled the qualities conducive to conciliation (*sāraṇīya-dhamma*) [instructed] the other...
He accepted [them] by means of five qualities.
Thus, wandering through existence among gods and humans, having spent one interval between Buddhas, they were reborn at this time in Sāvatthī.
He who fulfilled the qualities of endearment was conceived in the womb of the chief queen of the King of Kosala.
One took rebirth, while the other took rebirth in the womb of that very same woman who had been his attendant.
Both of them were born on the very same day. On the day their names were given, they were bathed and laid upon couches in the inner chamber, while their two mothers arranged honors outside.
Among them, he who was full of the qualities of endearment opened his eyes and—
Seeing the great white parasol, the well-prepared couch of glory, and the decorated and ready residence, he realized, "I have been reborn in a royal family.

Reflecting, "What deed did I perform to be reborn here? and knowing it was "through the outflow of the *sāraṇīya-dhamma* (the qualities that create bonds)," he wondered, "Where has my friend been reborn?"
Reflecting thus, and seeing him lying on a low bed, he thought, "He did not heed my words, saying, 'I am fulfilling the duties of the refectory.
It is now appropriate to reprimand him for this. He said, "Friend, you did not do as I told you.
[The other asked: "What has happened? [He replied: "Behold my prosperity; I am reclining upon a magnificent couch beneath a white parasol."
"You are lying on a low couch with merely a stiff covering. "But what pride do you take in this?
Is it not all merely the earth element, made from bamboo strips and wrapped in rags?
Having heard their words, Sumanā thought, "There is no one in the presence of my brothers," and she went toward them.
Standing by the door, she heard the word "relics" (dhātu). Thinking, "This word 'relics' does not exist outside;
these must be my brothers, the sons of the ascetic devas," she reflected:
"If I tell my parents that they are speaking thus, they will have them driven out as 'non-human beings' (amanussa). Without telling this matter to anyone else—"
“I shall ask my father, the Great Gotama, the Ten-Powered One, the cutter of doubt and the royal treasurer of men,” he thought.
Having finished his breakfast, he approached the king and said, “I am going to attend upon the One of Ten Powers.
The king had five hundred chariots prepared. For indeed, among the daughters of kings in the land of Jambudīpa, there were only three such as these princesses.
Five hundred chariots were obtained: Cundī, the princess and daughter of King Bimbisāra;
Visākhā, the daughter of the merchant Dhanañjaya; and this Sumanā, the princess.
Taking perfumes and garlands, standing in her chariot and accompanied by a retinue of five hundred chariots, she approached the Blessed One with the thought, "I shall ask this question."
*Idhassu* means "they might exist here. *Eko dāyako* means one who, having given from what he himself has obtained, enjoys [the merit] by fulfilling the *sāraṇīya-dhamma*.
*Eko adāyako* means one who, without giving to another from what he himself has obtained, enjoys it by fulfilling the duties of the dining hall (*bhattagga-vatta*).
*Devabhūtānaṃ pana nesaṃ* means "of these when they have become devas. *Adhigaṇhāti* means...
Having overcome, he grasps, overspreads, and surpasses. "By way of predominance" means by way of being the primary cause.
"By these five grounds" means that, like Sakka the king of the gods over the other devas, he grasps [others] by means of these five reasons.
Regarding the phrases beginning with "by human [factors]," [he excels] by life-span, as did the Elder Mahākassapa, the Elder Bākula, and the Elder Ānanda.
Furthermore, he is preeminent as the eldest for five reasons: by appearance, like the Elder Mahāgatimba-Abhaya or the treasurer-minister;
by happiness, like the noble son Raṭṭhapāla, the merchant’s son Soṇa, and the youth Yasa; by fame, like Dhammāsoka; and likewise by sovereignty.
Thus, through these five causes, he is the most excellent elder.

"Only when requested, for the most part": like the Elder Bākula, the Elder Sīvali, the Elder Ānanda, and others, he uses robes and other requisites only when requested; for these reasons, he is "superior" and "foremost.

Regarding the phrase "the liberation of one [is] liberation by means of the liberation of the other," this refers to the distinction that must be stated concerning the liberation of one person in relation to the liberation of another.

"If it were so, I would not say that"—this is the meaning. Whether it be a seven-year-old boy who penetrates liberation, or a hundred-year-old elder monk, or a nun, or a lay follower (upāsaka), or a lay follower (upāsikā), or a deva, or Māra, or Brahmā—once the supramundane path has been penetrated, there is no distinction whatsoever.
"It is indeed sufficient" means it is entirely appropriate. "Yatra hi nāma" means "those which indeed."
"Gacchaṃ ākāsadhātuyā" means traveling through the space-element, that is, moving by way of the sky. "Saddho" means one who has faith in the qualities of the Triple Gem.
"Thanayan" means thundering. "Vijjumālī" means endowed with lightning flashes that move across the face of the cloud like garlands.
"Satakkaku" means having a hundred peaks; the meaning is that it is possessed of a hundred cloud-crests rising here and there.
"One endowed with vision" means a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*). "Surrounded by wealth" means surrounded by wealth being given away through the practice of giving, as if by a flood of water;
the meaning is that he has been brought to the world of the gods. "Having passed away" means in the next world.
"Rejoices in heaven" means that in whichever heaven he is reborn, there alone he rejoices.
2. Commentary on the Cundīsutta 32.

Regarding "with five hundred chariots" in the second [verse]: the meaning is that, having sent [her] to her father after he had finished his morning meal, she was surrounded by five hundred chariots that had been harnessed.
"She approached" refers to the exchange of questions carried out together with her brother.
Thinking, "I shall ask him," he approached, taking with him perfumes, garlands, powders, and other such items.
"Yadeva so hotī" means "at whatever time he is," or alternatively, "whoever he may be. "Ariyakantāni sīlāni" refers to the virtues associated with the paths and fruits.
For these are beloved by the Noble Ones (ariya), and they do not abandon them even in another existence. The rest [is explained] in the Catukkanipāta.
It should be understood according to the same method as stated in the *Aggappasāda Sutta*.
3. Commentary on the *Uggaha Sutta* 33.
In the third [sutta], "at Bhaddiya" means in the city of Bhaddiya. "In the Jātiyavana" means in the self-grown, uncultivated [grove] by the Himalayas.
"In a grove of trees joined together" means that he dwelt in that forest in dependence upon that city.
"With himself as the fourth" means with himself as the fourth person. But why did he invite the Blessed One specifically as his fourth?
It is said that there was a great festival in his house, and many people would gather there with grand preparations.
Thinking, "If they were to attend upon the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, they would be difficult to manage," he invited only himself as the fourth.

Furthermore, it occurred to him: "If young girls were to sit in the midst of the great Saṅgha of bhikkhus while the Teacher was giving exhortation, they might become distracted and unable to receive the instruction. For this reason as well, he invited only himself as the fourth.
"May he instruct them, venerable sir," means: "Venerable Blessed One, may he instruct these women; may he give them instruction.
This is the genitive case used in the sense of the accusative. "Whatever [instruction] for them" refers to whatever counsel and exhortation is for them.
Having spoken thus, that merchant, thinking, "These women might feel ashamed receiving instruction in my presence," paid homage to the Blessed One and departed.
"Bhattūti" means for the husband. "Out of compassion" (anukampaṃ upādāya) means out of sympathy.
"Rising early" (pubbuṭṭhāyinīyo) means those whose nature it is to rise first of all. "Going to bed late" (pacchānipātinīyo) means those whose nature it is to lie down last of all.
For it is not proper for a woman to go to bed and lie down after eating before [her husband]; rather, she should feed all the household members first.

Having arranged the household utensils and implements, and having ascertained which cattle and other livestock have arrived or are yet to arrive, one should deliberate on the tasks to be performed for the day.
Taking the keys and seal in hand, if there is food, one may eat;
if not, one should have something else cooked and satisfy everyone before retiring to bed. Even when lying down, it is permissible to sleep until sunrise.

It is not permissible [to delegate everything]. However, it is permissible for her to rise first of all, summon the slaves and laborers, assign the work by saying, "Perform this and that task," supervise the work, have the cows milked, and personally oversee every duty to be done in the household.
It is with reference to this matter that it is said: "They rise before [others] and lie down after."
He said: "Those who respond with 'What shall we do? are those whose habit is to wander about looking at one's face, asking, 'What shall we do? What shall we do?
Those who act agreeably are those whose habit is to perform only pleasing deeds. Those who speak kindly are those whose habit is to utter only pleasant words.
'We shall honor' means we shall honor with the four requisites."
"Abbhāgate" means those who have come into one's presence. "Āsanodakena paṭipūjessāma" means we shall honor them with both a seat and water for washing the feet.
In this regard, daily hospitality should be rendered to one's mother and father;
furthermore, when ascetics and brahmins have arrived, a seat should be given, water for washing the feet should be offered, and hospitality should be performed.

“Wool” means sheep’s wool. “We shall be skilled therein” means we shall be expert in such tasks as disentangling, washing, dyeing, and carding the sheep’s wool, as well as spinning, pounding, beating, and cutting cotton.
“By means of the requisite methods for that” means by means of the methods employed in the preparation of that wool and cotton, thinking: “At this time, it is proper to do this. Thus...

"Endowed with active inquiry" means they will be both fit and capable of performing the task themselves or having it performed by others, thinking, "We shall be able to do it and arrange it. Furthermore,
they will know what has been done as "done" and what has not been done as "not done," having performed this specific work throughout the entire day.
We shall know that for those who have arrived, for those who have returned after performing such-and-such work for half a day,
and for those who sit at home without work, it is proper to give this and to do this; and we shall know the strength and weakness of those who are ill,
for if, when they are sick, one does not provide them with medicine, food, and so forth, and thus fails to relieve their illness— “these...”
"When we are healthy, they make us do whatever they wish; when we are ill, they do not even recognize our existence.
Thus, becoming disenchanted, they later refuse to perform their duties or commit misdeeds.

Therefore, [the Buddha] shows that you should train yourselves thus: "Having understood their strength and weakness, we shall know what is to be given and what is to be done. [Regarding] solid food (khādanīya):
"And his soft food and hard food" means: his soft food and hard food for his own family. "By way of a portion" means: by way of a share to be received;
the meaning is, according to the respective portions each is entitled to receive. "We shall share" means: we shall give.
"We shall provide" means: we shall procure.

*Adhuttī* means unchaste women, in the sense of being unchaste through being unchaste toward men or unchaste toward liquor. *Athenī* means non-thieves, those who do not steal. *Asoṇḍī* means those who are not addicted to drink, in the sense of not being addicted to liquor and so forth.
Having thus concluded the prose discourse (*suttanta*), he now provides the summary verse (*gāthā*) beginning with “He who supports her in every way,” thereby capturing the essential point (*kūṭa*).
Therein, *bharati* means he nourishes or looks after her. *Sabbakāmaharaṃ* means the giver of all desires. *Sotthī* means well-being.
"It proceeds thus" means it proceeds after fulfilling this much of the duty (*vatta*). "Those gods are called 'delightful'" refers to the *Nimmānarati* gods.
For they are called both "Nimmānarati" (Delighting in Creations) and "Manāpa" (Delightful) because they take delight by creating whatever form they desire.
4. Commentary on the *Sīhasenāpati-sutta* (The Discourse to General Sīha)
34. In the fourth [verse], "visible" (*sandiṭṭhika*) means that which is to be seen for oneself. "A giver" (*dāyaka*) is a hero of generosity.

The meaning is that he does not remain merely with faith, but is also capable of relinquishing. "A master of giving" (*dānapati*) means that he gives as the master of whatever gift he bestows, not as a slave or a mere companion.
For one who enjoys sweet things himself but gives what is not sweet to others—
One who gives as a slave to the gift-object known as "giving" gives only that which he himself eats;
such a one gives as a friend. But one who maintains himself by whatever means possible and gives what is sweet to others gives as a husband, an elder, and a master.
It is with reference to such a person that it is said: "a lord of giving."
"Unfaltering" means not being devoid of luster. "Confident" means having attained the joy of knowledge.

"Gone to companionship" means gone to a state of association or oneness. "Having made an opportunity" means that because they have performed the action by which an opportunity exists there, they have made an opportunity;
and since that [action] is exclusively wholesome, it is said "having performed what is wholesome. "In the delightful" means they rejoice.
They rejoice. "Of one who does not eat" (asitassa) means of the Tathāgata, who is independent. "Such a one" (tādi) means one who has attained the characteristic of suchness.
5. Commentary on the Discourse on the Benefits of Giving (Dānānisaṃsasutta).
In the fifth [verse], "he does not depart from the duties of a householder" means he possesses the five precepts unbroken. They follow the Dhamma of the virtuous.
Following the Dhamma of true persons, great beings. "The virtuous resort to him" means that true persons—namely Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Tathāgata—resort to this [Dhamma].
6. Commentary on the Sutta of Timely Giving (Kāladānasutta) 36.
In the sixth [verse], "timely gifts" (kāladānāni) means appropriate gifts, gifts given at the right moment, or suitable gifts. "New crops" (navasassāni) means...
"First fruits": "new fruits" refers to the first-fruits produced at the monastery.
"He establishes them first among those possessed of virtue" means that he gives them first to those who possess virtue and afterwards partakes of them himself.
"Generous" (vadaññū) means one who understands what has been spoken. "Given at the proper time" means given at the appropriate and fitting time. "Rejoice" means standing to one side.
They rejoice. "Service" means they perform manual labor with their bodies. "With an unopposing mind" means with a mind free from weariness.
"Where what is given bears great fruit": one should give in whatever place a gift becomes of great fruit.
7. Commentary on the Discourse on Food (Bhojana-sutta)

37. "He gives life" means he gives the gift of life (*āyudāna*). "Beauty" refers to the beauty of the body. "Happiness" refers to physical and mental happiness. "Strength" refers to bodily vigor. "Intelligence" refers to appropriate and excellent eloquence. 8. Commentary on the Saddha Sutta 38.
In the eighth [verse], "having compassion" means they favor [others]. "Like a great tree with a trunk" means a great tree endowed with a trunk.
"Delightful abodes" means in a charming place for gathering. "Those seeking shade go to the shade" means that those who have need of shade indeed approach the shade.
"Humble conduct" means lowly behavior. "Free from stubbornness" means devoid of the rigidity of anger and pride.
"Gentle" means endowed with amiability and pure virtue. "Affable" means friendly and welcoming.
9. Commentary on the *Puttasutta* (Sutta 39).

Regarding the ninth verse, "He has supported us, or he will support us": "Supported" means that we were nurtured and cared for by him through such acts as suckling us with breast milk and massaging our hands and feet;
"will support us" means that when we have grown old, he will support us by washing and bathing our hands and feet, and by giving us rice-gruel, food, and so forth.
"‘He will perform our duties’ means that, setting aside his own work, he will go and perform whatever tasks have arisen for our royal family and so forth.
‘The lineage will endure for a long time’ means that by protecting our fields, lands, gold, silver, and so on, without letting them perish, our sons will ensure the lineage lasts long;
or else, the *salākabhatta* (ticket-food) and other offerings instituted by us [will continue]."
"He will cause it to continue without interruption; thus our family lineage will endure for a long time.
"He will take up his inheritance" means that by making himself worthy of the inheritance through conduct befitting the family lineage, he will take up the inheritance belonging to us.
"He will provide for the offering" means that after making a gift of merit, from the third day onward...
"He will bestow gifts.
In this context, "peaceful and true persons" (santo sappurisā) should be understood as those who practice rightly toward their mother and father.
"Recalling what was done in the past" means recalling the virtues previously performed by their mother and father. "One who acts upon advice" (ovādakārī).
One who carries out the advice given by one's mother and father. A "supporter of those who supported him" means one who maintains those by whom he was supported.
"Praiseworthy" means one who is to be praised by the great multitude even in this very life.
10. Commentary on the Mahāsālaputtasutta.
40. "Great sal trees" (*mahāsālā*) refers to large trees. "Growing with branches, leaves, and foliage" means they grow with small branches and with foliage in the form of leaves.
"In the forest" (*araññasmiṃ*) means in a place devoid of villages.
"In a vast forest" (*brahāvaṇe*) means in a great forest, a wilderness (*aṭavī*). The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
The Fourth Chapter: The Chapter on Sumanā.

Commentary on the Ādicca Sutta.

"Clarified oil" (*nibbattatela*) means oil that has been refined. This is not...
Regarding the phrase "it is allowable for the Blessed One," it is stated that even what is allowable is not allowable when compared to what is unallowable.

It was one and a half ratanas in length, but because it was made of the finest and most excellent materials, it was very costly.

"In those who have become straight" means in those who are upright in body, speech, and mind. "With longing" means with affection. In the phrases beginning with "gave away," it refers to the sense of relinquishment.

"A certain mind-made [body]" (*aññataraṃ manomayaṃ*): a class of deities produced by means of a particular jhāna in the Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsa*). "According to one's intention" (*yathādhippāyo*):...
"According to his inclination. What does he ask by this? It is said that while he was a human being, his inclination was toward attaining arahantship;

"Wherever he is reborn, there he will be long-lived and famous.

The same method applies to the remaining phrases as well. "It would not please" (*nacchādeyya*) means it would not be agreeable. "He drew out" (*abbuhi*) means he extracted.
*Yato*: at which time. *Āpadasu*: in calamities or misfortunes. *Na vedhati*: does not tremble, does not grieve. *Atthavinicchayaññū*:

"By the giving of a hundred or a thousand. "By family tradition" (*paveṇiyā*) means by way of the lineage of one's clan;

50. "Absorbed" (*ajjhomucchito*) means being completely infatuated;

The Chapter on Hindrances.
1. Commentary on the Āvaraṇa Sutta 51.
In the first [section] of the second [chapter], they are "obstructions" (āvaraṇā) by way of being obstructions; they are "hindrances" (nīvaraṇā) by way of being hindrances.

They "ascend upon the mind" (ceto ajjhāruhanti), thus they are "ascenders upon the mind" (cetaso ajjhāruhā). They are weak in the sense of obstructing the arising of both insight-wisdom (vipassanā-paññā) and path-wisdom (magga-paññā).
"They cause [wisdom] to become weak" means they weaken wisdom by means of their own weakness. Alternatively, when wisdom arises mixed with these [hindrances], they cause that wisdom to become weak;
thus they are called "weakening wisdom. "Powerless" means devoid of strength because it is enveloped by the five hindrances.
"The distinction of noble knowledge and vision superior to human states" refers to what is comprised by the ten courses of wholesome action.
A distinction of knowledge and vision capable of producing a noble state beyond the human condition.
"Carrying away what should be carried away" means capable of carrying away that which ought to be removed. "Plough-mouths" refers to the openings of the furrows;
for they are called plough-mouths because they resemble ploughs and because they are dug up by ploughs.
"Even so" (*evameva kho*): here, insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) should be regarded as being like the stream;
the time when the opening between the two plow-muzzles is wide open is like the time when restraint at the six doors has been abandoned;

and the time when the water is dispersed, scattered, and spread out after a dam has been made with straw, grass, and clay by pounding [the bank] at the foot of a tree in the middle of the river is like [the state of the mind].

The time when one is shrouded by the five hindrances should be understood as being like the time when water, its force having been checked by such obstructions, is unable to drag along grass, straw, and so forth to reach the ocean;
likewise, it is the time when, after all unwholesome states have been destroyed by insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*), one is unable to reach the ocean of Nibbāna.
For the bright side (*sukkapakkha*), the application is by way of the opposites of what was stated above.
[These things] should be practiced. In this sutta, the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) and its cessation (vivaṭṭa) are explained.
The second [sutta] is of obvious meaning. 3. Commentary on the Padhāniyaṅga Sutta: 53.
Regarding "the factors of striving" (*padhāniyaṅgāni*): "striving" (*padhāna*) refers to the state of exerting effort; that which possesses such striving is called "one who strives."
"Exertion" (*padhāniya*) means the factors for a monk who is exerting himself; thus, they are called "factors of exertion. "Faithful" (*saddho*) means endowed with faith.

This faith is fourfold: faith through tradition (*āgama-saddhā*), faith through realization (*adhigama-saddhā*), faith through conviction (*okappana-saddhā*), and faith through serene confidence (*pasāda-saddhā*).
Among these, the faith of the omniscient Bodhisattvas is called "faith through tradition," because it has come down from the very moment of their initial resolve (*abhinīhāra*).
The faith of realization (*adhigama-saddhā*) is so called because it is attained through the penetration of the Noble Disciples (*ariya-sāvaka*).

The firm conviction (*okappanā*) characterized by immovability when the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha are mentioned is called the faith of conviction (*okappana-saddhā*). The arising of serene confidence is called the faith of serenity (*pasāda-saddhā*).
Here, the faith of conviction is intended. "Enlightenment" (*bodhi*) refers to the knowledge of the four paths. That has been well-penetrated by the Tathāgata.
"He has faith. This is merely a summary of the teaching; however, by this factor, faith in all three Jewels is intended.
For one who possesses strong confidence in the Buddha and the others, his energy for striving succeeds.
"Free from illness" means healthy. "Free from affliction" means free from suffering. "With a well-digested [stomach]" means with a balanced digestion. "Of the stomach" (gahaṇiyā) means...
Of the fire element born of karma. "Neither too cold nor too hot" means that one who perceives extreme cold is afraid of cold, while one who perceives extreme heat is afraid of heat;
for them, striving does not succeed, but it succeeds for one who perceives the moderate.
Therefore he said: "Moderate, capable of enduring striving. "To reveal oneself as one really is" means as it truly is...
One who reveals one's own lack of virtue. "Leading to arising and passing away" means capable of reaching—that is, discerning—both arising and passing away;
by this, the knowledge of rise and fall (*udayabbaya-ñāṇa*), which grasps the characteristics of the five aggregates, is stated. "Noble" means pure.
"Penetrative" means capable of penetrating those masses of greed and so forth that have not been penetrated before. "Leading rightly to the destruction of suffering."
Because the defilements have been abandoned by means of those very factors, it leads to the destruction of whatever suffering is destroyed.
Thus, by all these terms, it is specifically insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*) that is spoken of; for the striving of one who is lacking wisdom does not succeed.

"Having seen [this], zeal arose in me, thinking: 'I shall behold Nibbāna. As I was beholding Nibbāna, effort arose in me.

In the eighth [sutta], "strung bows" means bows with strings that have been drawn. "They saw" means they beheld. They will be...

Commentary on the Sājīva Sutta (Discourse on Livelihood)
66. In the sixth [verse], "one who lives by means of" (*alaṃsājīvo*) means one who is engaged with "living together" (*sājīvā*).

"Living together" refers both to the posing of questions and the answering of questions.
