(8) 3. The Chapter on the Warrior.
1. Commentary on the First Discourse on the Fruit of Liberation of Mind (Paṭhamacetovimuttiphalasutta-vaṇṇanā) 71.

Regarding the first [discourse] of the third [chapter]: "Bhikkhus, when... This was begun for the purpose of praising the monk who has now attained Arahantship after having increased his insight (*vipassanā*) in the manner explained below.
In this context, "when" (*yato*)— [The remainder of the text follows the same structural pattern.]
When he stands with the crossbar lifted: having lifted up and removed the crossbar of ignorance (*avijjā-paligha*).
With the moat filled in: having filled in and destroyed the moat of *saṃsāra*. With the pillar pulled out: having pulled out and uprooted the pillar-post known as craving (*taṇhā*).
Without bolts: having thrown open the door-panel of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). With the banner lowered...
"One who has laid down the burden" means one who stands having cast down and lowered both the banner of conceit and the burden of the aggregates, volitional formations, and defilements.
"Dissociated" means dissociated from the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*). The remainder should be understood according to the method of the text (*pāḷinaya*).

At this point, the Blessed One, having exhausted the defilements by means of the Path and having attained the excellent bed of cessation, enters the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) which has Nibbāna as its object.
The time for one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) who dwells having attained [this state] is shown.
For it is as if there were two cities: one a city of thieves, the other a secure city.
Then, a great warrior might think: "As long as this city of thieves remains standing, so long will the secure city not be freed from fear."
Thinking, “I shall turn this city of thieves into a non-city,” he donned his armor, took up his sword, and approached the city of thieves. There,
having cut down the pillar-staff raised at the city gate with his sword, broken the door-panel along with the door-posts,
lifted the crossbar, breached the wall, and filled in the moat, [he proceeded] for the sake of the city’s beauty.
Having lowered his banner, set fire to the city, and entered the secure city, he would ascend the palace and, surrounded by his circle of kinsmen, eat delicious food.
In this way, the city of the thief is like *sakkāya* (the basis for personal existence); the secure city is like *nibbāna*;
and the great warrior is like the practitioner (*yogāvacara*). It occurs to him: "As long as the cycle of *sakkāya* continues..."
“Until then, there is no liberation from the thirty-two tortures, the ninety-eight diseases, and the twenty-five great fears.
Thus, that great warrior, having donned the armor of virtue as if it were his own mail, took up the sword of wisdom;

and with that sword, like pulling out a wooden stake with a blade, he extracted the stake of craving by means of the path of Arhatship. That warrior [then stood] like the city gate with its two door-panels.
Having torn asunder the five lower fetters (*pañcorambhāgiya-saṃyojana*), that warrior, like one tossing aside a crossbar, has cast up the crossbar of ignorance;
like one breaking down a wall, he has shattered the formative forces of karma (*kamma-abhisaṅkhāra*) and scattered the moat of the cycle of birth and rebirth;
like a warrior raising a banner for the glory of the city, he has raised the banner of pride.

Having cast down the city of *sakkāya* (personality-belief) and burned it, that warrior—like one enjoying a fine meal in an upper palace within the city of security (*khemanagara*)—enters the city of the final extinction of defilements (*kilesaparinibbāna*).
There, experiencing the bliss of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) which has the deathless cessation (*nirodha*) as its object, he passes his time.
2. Commentary on the Second Discourse on the Fruit of Liberation of Mind (*Dutiyacetovimuttiphalasutta-vaṇṇanā*)

72. Second, the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*) is the perception that arises taking the five aggregates as its object and regarding them as impermanent by way of their mode of non-existence.
The perception of suffering in the impermanent (*anicce dukkhasaññā*) is the perception that arises regarding whatever is impermanent as suffering by way of its mode of oppression.
The perception of non-self in what is suffering (*dukkhe anattasaññā*) is the perception that arises regarding whatever is suffering as non-self by way of its mode of lack of mastery.
The remainder is exactly as explained below. In these two suttas, however, what is called the "fruit of insight" (*vipassanā-phala*) is discussed.
3. Commentary on the First *Dhammavihārī-sutta* (73):
"In the third [sutta], 'he passes the day' means he lets the day elapse. 'He neglects seclusion' means he neglects solitude."
He expounds. "Teaches" means he speaks and proclaims. "By way of the designation of the Dhamma" means for the purpose of making the Dhamma known.
"He masters the Dhamma" means he masters, employs, and speaks the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths by way of the ninefold division.
"He does not neglect seclusion" means he does not abandon solitude. "He devotes himself to internal mental tranquility."
One cultivates and develops concentration of mind regarding one’s own internal states; one is devoted to the practice of the meditation subject of serenity (*samatha*).
"Seeking welfare" means seeking what is beneficial. "Compassionate" means feeling compassion. "Out of compassion" means having embraced compassion with the mind;
it is also said to mean "on account of. "That has been done for you by me"—that [work] has been performed by me for these five...
The Teacher who desires to benefit you has fulfilled his duty by teaching the Dhamma without error; for this alone is the task of a compassionate Teacher.
Beyond this, however, the task belongs to the disciples, namely, the practice of the path.
Therefore he said: "These are the roots of trees, O bhikkhu... [etc. ...this is our instruction. And herein, by the phrase "roots of trees," he refers to the lodging at the foot of a tree.
He shows this. By the phrase "empty huts," he indicates a place secluded from people. With both [of these], he describes a dwelling suitable for yoga and hands over his inheritance.

"Meditate" means: meditate upon the thirty-eight objects by way of object-contemplation (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*), and meditate upon the aggregates, bases, and so forth, as impermanent and so on, by way of characteristic-contemplation (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*); that is, develop both serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).

This is what is meant. "Do not be negligent" means: do not be heedless. "Lest you be full of regret later" refers to those who, in the past—during their youth, during the time of health, during the time of possessing the seven requisites such as suitable food, and while in the presence of the Teacher—were devoid of wise attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*), spent their days and nights eating like crows, and were devoted to the pleasure of sleep and the pleasure of sloth.

They are negligent; later, at the time of old age, the time of illness, the time of death, the time of misfortune, and at the time of the Teacher’s parinibbāna, they will remember that former state of negligence and, perceiving the gravity of their untimely death with rebirth still pending, they will be filled with remorse.
To show you that you must not become like them, he said: "Do not..."
"You will come to regret it later. This is our instruction for you; this is our instruction and exhortation to you from us, saying: "Meditate; do not be negligent. 4.
Commentary on the Second Dhammavihārīsutta (Discourse on Those Who Dwell in the Dhamma)

74. In the fourth [case], "and he does not understand the meaning beyond that by means of wisdom" means that beyond the mere textual study (*pariyatti*), he does not understand the meaning of that Dhamma by means of the path-wisdom accompanied by insight (*vipassanā*); the sense is that he does not see or penetrate the Four Truths.
This same method applies to the remaining sections as well. Thus, in these two suttas, the bhikkhu who is learned...

It should be understood that six types of persons—the one practicing insight (vipassanākammika), the stream-enterer (sotāpanna), the once-returner (sakadāgāmī), the non-returner (anāgāmī), and the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava)—are called "dwellers in the Dhamma" (dhammavihārino).
5. Commentary on the First Discourse on the Warrior (Yodhājīvasutta) 75.

In the fifth [discourse], "warriors" (yodhājīvā) refers to those who live by war. "Dust-clouds" (raja-ggaṃ) refers to the dust raised when the ground is broken up by the trampling of the feet of elephants, horses, and so forth.
A column of dust raised from the ground. "It does not stiffen" means it is unable to stand still.
"It endures the dust" means that even upon seeing a cloud of dust, it remains patient.
"The tip of a banner" refers to the top of banners raised on the backs of elephants and horses, or on chariots. "The shouting" refers to the elephants, horses, chariots, and the army itself.
And there was a great clamor and a loud noise. "He strikes" means he strikes even when [the opponent] has merely approached;
"he is struck" means he is afflicted, he falls into distress. "He is injured" means he falls into misfortune, he abandons his natural state.

"He endures the striking" means that even after receiving two or three blows, he endures them, he bears them. "That very front of the battle" means that very place where the victorious army is stationed.
"He dwells" means he dwells having overcome [the enemy] for a period of seven days. For what reason?

For the purpose of tending to those who have received wounds, for the purpose of granting higher positions to those who have performed meritorious deeds once their excellence is known, and for the purpose of enjoying the pleasures of sovereignty.
Now, since there is no need for the Teacher’s warriors, yet in this Dispensation there are five such [warriors]:
This simile was brought forward in order to show types of persons. Therefore, showing those persons, he said:
"In the same way," and so forth. Therein, "sinks" means he sinks into or enters into wrong thought.
"He is not able to sustain the holy life" means he is not able to protect the dwelling in the holy life so that it remains uninterrupted. [This refers to] weakness in training.
"By revealing" means by making manifest the weakness of the training.
"What is his 'dust-storm'? means he asks: "What indeed is called the dust-storm of that person? "Beautiful" means possessing beauty. "Pleasant to behold" means worthy of being seen.
"Inspiring confidence" means that by the mere sight of her, she brings about clarity of mind. "Supreme" means most excellent. "By the excellence of her complexion" means by the color of her body.
And by means of bodily posture as well. *Ūhasati* means she laughs at [him]. *Ullapati* means she speaks.
*Ujjhagghati* means she laughs with a loud laugh after clapping her hands. *Uppaṇḍeti* means she tells mocking talk.
*Abhinisīdati* means she sits down nearby or on the same seat, having overcome [him]. The same method applies to the second word as well. *Ajjhottharati* means...
"He covers over. "Having unfastened and released" means having both unloosened her hand from the place where it was grasped and having set it free.
The rest here is of plain meaning. In this sutta, the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*) are explained.
6. Commentary on the Second Yodhājīva Sutta.
76. "In the sixth [case], 'having taken sword and shield' means having taken both a sword and a shield.
'Having fastened bow and quiver' means having fastened both a bow and a quiver of arrows. 'Arrayed' means standing in the formation for battle.
'Enters the battle' means he enters into a great war. 'Exerts himself' or 'strives' means he makes effort and exertion. 'Slay' means..."
They kill. "They cause to perish" means they bring to ruin. "They lick" means they pierce. "They carry off" means they take their own property and depart.
"Having carried it off, they lead it to their kinsmen" means having taken their own property, they then lead it into the presence of their kinsmen.
"Being led away" means being led to one's own home or to the presence of other kinsmen. "They attend upon" means they serve.
They tend and protect [the wound] by performing such acts as cleaning the blow and dressing the sore.
"With an unprotected body" means with an unprotected door of the body. "With unprotected speech" means with an unprotected door of speech.
"With an unprotected mind" means with an unprotected door of the mind. "With unestablished mindfulness" means...
Without having established mindfulness well. "With the faculties unrestrained" means with the six faculties, including the mind, being unguarded and unprotected.
"Lust assails the mind" means that as lust arises, it destroys the mind of serenity and insight;
it hurls it far away. "I am overwhelmed by lust, friend, I am possessed by lust" means: "Friend, I am colored by lust, I am pursued by lust."
Regarding the similes beginning with "like a skeleton": it is like a skeleton in the sense of providing little gratification; like a piece of meat in the sense of being common to many;

like a grass torch in the sense of burning up; like a pit of embers in the sense of great torment; like a dream in the sense of appearing only for a short time; like a borrowed article in the sense of being temporary;
and like the fruit of a tree in the sense of crushing all one's limbs and members.
They are like swords in the sense of cutting; they are like spears and spikes in the sense of piercing; they are like the heads of snakes in the sense of being dangerous and fearful.
"I will exert" means I will make an effort. "I will maintain" means I will maintain the state of a recluse.
"I will delight" means I will generate delight and not become weary. The rest here is of plain meaning. In this sutta...
"The cycle of existence and its cessation have been explained.
7. Commentary on the First Discourse on Future Perils (Paṭhama-anāgata-bhaya-sutta-vaṇṇanā) 77.

In the seventh [discourse], "by one who dwells in the forest" means by one who lives in the wilderness. "Of that which has not been attained" refers to the various states consisting of jhāna, insight, the path, and the fruit, which have not yet been reached.
"For the sake of attaining distinction. The same method applies to the remaining phrases as well.

"It would be an obstacle for me" means it would be an obstacle to my life and an obstacle to the holy life (*brahmacariya*); for one who dies as an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), it would be an obstacle to heaven and an obstacle to the Path.
"Handā" is a particle used in the sense of encouragement. "I shall exert energy" refers to both kinds of energy.
I do. "Sword-like winds" means winds that cut the joints and ligaments like a sword. "By wild men" means by those who are cruel. "By youths" means by thieves.

Regarding the phrase "those who have committed the deed or those who have not committed the deed": here, those who have gone out after committing a theft are called "those who have committed the deed";
those who are going to commit a theft are called "those who have not committed the deed. Among them, as for those who have committed the deed, regarding the deed...
Because beings have been brought to fruition, they take the blood from the throat and perform an offering for the deities;
those who have not yet performed their work do so even earlier, thinking, "In this way our work will be accomplished. It was with reference to this that it was said, "They would deprive me of life.
"Fierce non-humans" refers to cruel and wicked non-humans such as *yakkhas* and others.
8. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Future Perils (Dutiya-anāgata-bhaya-sutta) 78.
Regarding the eighth [peril]: "Before that state comes to me" means: "As long as that state has not yet approached me, I shall exert effort even earlier.
"Become like milk and water" means: become like milk and water [mixed together].
They have attained a state of oneness. "With loving eyes" means with eyes of loving-kindness (*mettā*). 9.
Commentary on the Third Discourse on Future Dangers (Tatiya-anāgata-bhaya-sutta). 79.
Regarding the ninth [point], "from corruption of the Dhamma comes corruption of the Vinaya": through the corruption of the Dhamma, there occurs the corruption of the Vinaya. How so?

But when the Dhamma is corrupted, is it not said that the Vinaya is corrupted? When the factors of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) do not take conception, the fivefold Vinaya does not exist;
thus, when the Dhamma is corrupted, the Vinaya is corrupted. Furthermore, for one who is immoral, there is no so-called "Vinaya of restraint";
in its absence, serenity and insight do not take conception. Thus, through the corruption of the Vinaya as well—
The corruption of the Dhamma is to be understood. A discourse on the Abhidhamma is a discourse on the supreme Dhamma, such as virtue and so forth.

A Vedalla discourse is a discourse connected with the Vedas, mixed with knowledge. "Falling into dark states" means falling into black (evil) states by way of seeking out faults and searching for grounds for reproach.
Furthermore, even those who provoke a person with a corrupt mind fall into that dark state.
Even those who burn themselves, or speak for the sake of gain and honor, still fall into dark states.
"Profound" means profound in their textual expression (*pāḷi*). "Profound in meaning" means profound in their sense. "Supramundane" means elucidating supramundane phenomena.
"Connected with emptiness" means connected with the aggregates, elements, bases, and the principle of dependent origination. No other [thought] arises in the mind.
“They will not establish their minds for the purpose of knowing” means they will not apply their attention to it.

“To be learned and mastered” refers to both what is to be acquired and what is to be employed. “Poetry” (*kavitā*) refers to works composed by poets through the composition of *śloka* verses and so forth.

“Verses” (*kāveyya*) is a synonym for that same thing. “External” (*bāhiraka*) means those existing outside the Teaching (*sāsana*). “Spoken by disciples” (*sāvakabhāsita*) means [those spoken] by external disciples.
It has been spoken. The rest here is easy to understand because it follows the method explained below and its meaning is plain.
10. Commentary on the Tenth Discourse, *The Future Perils*. 80.

In the tenth [discourse], "those who desire what is lovely" (*kalyāṇakāmā*) means those who desire what is beautiful. "Exquisite flavors" (*rasaggānī*) means the most excellent flavors. "They will dwell in association" (*saṃsaṭṭhā viharissantīti*).
They will dwell associated by five kinds of association. "Enjoyment of what has been stored up" means the enjoyment of that which has been kept in reserve.
"Even a coarse sign": here, even one who digs the earth or commands another to dig it creates a coarse sign in the earth.
Even one who cuts grass, wood, branches, or foliage [creates a sign] when saying, "Cut!"...
Even one who causes [grass] to be cut creates a coarse sign at the tips of the green blades.
For one who, for the sake of livelihood, has leaves, fodder, and so forth brought, or who plucks fruits himself or has them plucked, there is simply nothing that can be said [by way of blame].
In these four suttas, the Teacher has spoken of growth and decline within the Dispensation.
The Third Chapter: On Warriors.
(9) 4. The Chapter on Elders. 1.
Explanation of the Discourse on the Alluring.

81. In the first [section] of the fourth [sutta], "in regard to things provocative of lust" (*rajaniyesu*) means in regard to objects that serve as conditions for greed (*rāga*). The same method applies to the remaining [terms] as well. 2.
Commentary on the *Vītarāga-sutta* (Discourse on One Free from Lust) 82.

In the second [sutta], "one who is censorious" (*makkhī*) means one who censures virtues. "One who is spiteful" (*paḷāsī*) means one who is possessed of spite (*paḷāsa*), which is characterized by grasping at opposition.
3. Commentary on the Kuhaka Sutta (83).
In the third [verse], "a deceiver" (*kuhaka*) is one who is endowed with the three bases of deception (*kuhanavatthu*). "A flatterer" (*lapaka*) is one who is endowed with speech based upon gain.
"One who hints" (*nemittika*) is one who performs acts of hinting. "An extortionist" (*nippesika*) is one who is endowed with the practice of extorting.

"One who seeks gain through gain" means one who desires to acquire further gain by means of a previous gain. The "white side" (the virtuous alternative) should be understood by way of the reversal of what has been stated.
The fourth [case] is self-evident.
5. Commentary on the *Akkhamasutta* (The Discourse on Intolerance).

85. “He is not patient with forms” means he does not endure forms as objects; he is overcome by lust and other defilements that have those forms as their object. This same method applies everywhere. 6.
Commentary on the *Paṭisambhidāppatta Sutta* 86.

“One who has attained the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*)” means one who has attained the knowledge that has reached the distinctions among the five kinds of meanings. “One who has attained the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*)” means...

He has attained knowledge that has reached differentiation regarding the fourfold Dhamma. "One who has attained the analytical knowledge of language" (niruttipaṭisambhidāppatta) means one who has attained knowledge that has reached differentiation regarding the linguistic expressions of the Dhamma.

"One who has attained the analytical knowledge of perspicuity" (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidāppatta) means one who has attained knowledge that has reached differentiation regarding those three types of knowledge.
However, he knows only those three knowledges themselves; he does not perform their function. "High and low" means...
"Great and small": "duties to be performed" means those things that ought to be done.
7. Commentary on the Sīlavanta Sutta (Discourse on the Virtuous).

87. The seventh [sutta] has a meaning that is self-evident. However, here "virtue" refers specifically to the virtue of one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), and "great learning" also refers specifically to the great learning of one whose taints are destroyed.

It should be understood that even the speech of one whose taints are exhausted is exclusively wholesome speech, and likewise, his meditative absorptions (jhānas) are said to be only functional absorptions (kriyā-jhāna).
8. Commentary on the Discourse to the Elder (Therasutta-vannanā): 88.
In the eighth [discourse], "the elder" (thera) refers to one who has attained stability. "Long-standing" (rattaññū) refers to those days that have passed since the day of his going forth (pabbajjā).
"Known for many nights. "Known" means recognized or well-publicized. "Famous" means dependent on fame. "Holding wrong view" means holding a view that is not according to reality.
"Having turned away from the true Dhamma" means having turned away from the Dhamma of the ten courses of wholesome action.
"He establishes in the non-true Dhamma" means he establishes them in the courses of unwholesome action.
9. Commentary on the First Discourse on the Trainee (Paṭhamasekhasutta) 89.

Regarding the ninth [discourse], "of a trainee" (*sekha*) means of one who is still in training and has duties yet to be performed. "For the sake of decline" (*parihānāya*) means for the purpose of falling away from higher qualities.
"Delight in work" (*kammārāmatā*) is the state of taking pleasure in new building projects. "Delight in talk" (*bhassārāmatā*) is the state of taking pleasure in conversation and discourse.
"Delighting in sleep" means the state of finding pleasure in sleeping. "Delighting in company" means the state of finding pleasure in socializing with a crowd.

"He does not review his mind as it has been liberated" means that he does not review the mind as it has been liberated, nor the faults that have been abandoned, nor the qualities that have been attained;
the meaning is that he does not exert effort for the sake of attaining further qualities.
Thus, in this sutta, the causes of decline and the causes of growth regarding the higher qualities of the seven trainees (*sekha*) are explained.
Furthermore, whatever is a cause of decline for a trainee, that very thing occurs first for an ordinary person (*puthujjana*).
10. Commentary on the Second Sutta on the Trainee (*Dutiyasekhasuttavaṇṇanā*)
90. "Skilled" (*viyatta*) means experienced and clever. "In what is to be done" (*kiṃkaraṇīyesu*) refers to those things that ought to be performed.
"Tranquility of mind" (*cetosamatha*) is the meditation subject of concentration (*samādhi*). "By the non-conforming" (*ananulomika*) means by that which is unsuitable for the Teaching.

"At too early a time" (*atikālena*) means too soon. "At too late a time" (*atidivā*): "day" (*divā*) here refers to midday; having passed beyond that. "Leading to effacement" (*ābhisallekhikā*) means exceedingly conducive to the wearing away of the defilements.
"Conducive to the opening of the mind" means conducive to serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), which are known as the opening of the mind.
"Discourse on fewness of desires" is discourse that says, "Be one of few desires. "Discourse on contentment" is discourse that says, "Be content with the four requisites.
"Discourse on seclusion" is discourse that says, "Be secluded by means of the three kinds of seclusion. "Discourse on non-association" is...
"Be unassociated with the five kinds of association"—this is talk about conversation.
"Talk on the arousal of energy" is talk about the two kinds of energy, saying, "Arouse energy. Regarding "talk on virtue" and so forth: talk concerning virtue is "talk on virtue";
talk concerning concentration, talk concerning wisdom, talk concerning the fivefold liberation, and talk concerning the nineteen kinds of reflection—
The discourse concerning the knowledge and vision of liberation is the *vimuttiñāṇadassanakathā*.
In phrases such as "not obtaining at will," the meaning is: not obtaining what one desires, obtaining with difficulty, and not obtaining in abundance. The rest is of plain meaning.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, the Chapter on Elders (*Theravagga*).
(10) 5. The Chapter on the Hump (Kakudhavagga). 1–2. Commentary on the Two Discourses on Accomplishments (Sampadāsuttadvaya). 91–92.
In the first [discourse] of the fifth [chapter], five accomplishments are taught as being mixed. In the second, the first four are mixed, while the fifth is purely mundane.
3. Commentary on the Byākaraṇa Sutta 93.

In the third [sutta], "declarations of final knowledge" (*aññā-byākaraṇāni*) refers to declarations of *arahantship*. "Through dullness" (*mandattā*) means through the state of being dull, that is, through ignorance.

"Through delusion" (*momūhattā*) means through the state of being excessively bewildered. "He declares final knowledge" (*aññaṃ byākaroti*) means he says, "I have attained *arahantship*. "Overpowered by desire" (*icchāpakato*).
"Overcome by desire. "By overweening pride" means by the pride of having attained [what one has not]. "Just as it truly is" means by way of cause, method, and reason.
4–5. Commentary on the *Phāsuvihāra-sutta* and others, §§94–95.
In the fourth [sutta], "comfortable dwellings" (*phāsuvihāra*) means pleasant dwellings. In the fifth, "the unshakable" (*akuppa*) refers to Arahantship.

6. Commentary on the *Sutadharasutta* 96. In the sixth [verse]: "One with few duties" (*appaṭṭha*) means one with little exertion (*appasamārambha*). "One with few tasks" (*appakicca*) means one with little to be done (*appakaraṇīya*). "Easy to support" (*subhara*) means one who can be maintained easily or well-nourished.
"Easy to satisfy" (*susantosa*) means one who is thoroughly contented by the three kinds of contentment. "Regarding the requisites of life" (*jīvitaparikkhāresu*)...
Regarding the requisites for life: "one who eats little" means one whose food is meager. "Not gluttonous" means one who is not devoted to a state of gluttony or a nature of great greed.
"Not given to sleep" means one who does not sleep much. The seventh and eighth [factors] have their meanings obvious.
9. Commentary on the Sīha Sutta (The Lion Sutta)
99. In the ninth [case], he gives with respect and not without respect; that is, he gives without contempt and without neglecting [the recipient], not with contempt or by neglecting him.
"May my skillful way not be lost" means: "May the skillful way established by me not be lost to me;
let there not be those who would say, 'A certain lion, having risen and attacking a cat, missed his blow.'"
The meaning is as follows: regarding the phrase "to the food-bearers and hunters," here "food" (anna) refers to barley-rice; those for whom this is a burden are the "food-bearers.
This is a name for beggars. "Hunters" (nesāda) refers to fowlers. Thus, even to these—the lowest of the low among beggars and hunters—he teaches with full attention.
10. Commentary on the Kakudha Thera Sutta 100.
In the tenth [sutta], "attainment of a personal existence" (*attabhāvapaṭilābha*) means the attainment of a body. Regarding the phrase "two or three Magadhan village-fields":
here, a Magadhan village-field may be small, medium, or large. The small one—
A small village field is forty ox-lengths from this side and forty ox-lengths from that side; a medium one is one *gāvuta* from this side and one *gāvuta* from that side, which makes half a *yojana*;
a large one is one and a half *gāvutas* from this side and one and a half *gāvutas* from that side, which makes three *gāvutas*.
Among these, with a small village field there are three [rods], and with a small or medium one there are two.
The villages and fields are his very self; for his body extends for three *gāvutas*. "I will look after it" means I will tend to it and protect it.
"Guard this" means you must guard this. "Foolish man" means an empty man. "It would not belong to him" means it would not be his.
"We would address [him]" means we would speak to him. "He honors" means he performs an act of respect. That which...
"Whatever he shall do, by that alone will he be known"—whatever this person shall do, by that very action he will become manifest.
The remainder is clear in meaning throughout.
The fifth chapter, the Kakudha-vagga, is concluded.
The Second Fifty is finished.
3. The Third Fifty (11) 1.
The Chapter on Comfortable Living (Phāsuvihāravagga)
1. Commentary on the Sārajja Sutta (101).

In the first [verse] of the third [chapter], "producing fearlessness" means bringing about a state of confidence (*visārada*). "There is timidity" (*sārajjaṃ hoti*) means there is mental distress (*domanassa*).
2. Commentary on the Ussaṅkita Sutta.
102. "In the second [case], 'suspected and doubted' means both suspected and doubted.
'Even though he is of an unshakable nature' means that even though he is one whose taints are destroyed and is of an unshakable nature, he is still suspected and doubted by other wicked bhikkhus;

this is the meaning. Regarding 'one who frequents prostitutes' and so forth: 'prostitutes' refers to those who live by their beauty; one for whom they are the resort (*gocara*) is 'one who frequents prostitutes.'"
The meaning is that she goes frequently to their houses. The same principle applies to the remaining terms as well. In this context, however, "widow" means one whose husband has died;
"mature maiden" means older girls. 3. Commentary on the Mahācora Sutta (The Discourse on the Great Thief)

103. In the third [case], "I will provide hospitality from this wealth" means: "Having taken wealth from my own property here, I will provide hospitality with that, and I will bridge the gap between him and me.
"Seizures" (*gahaṇāni*) means the seizing of goods belonging to others.
"Secret counsels" (*guhyamantrāḥ*) means counsels that ought to be kept secret. "Those who grasp at extremes" (*antagrāhikāya*) refers to [the view of] eternalism (*sassata*).
...or for one who stands having grasped at annihilation. The rest here is of plain meaning. In the fourth [discourse], everything is according to the method already stated below.
5. Commentary on the Phāsuvihāra Sutta (Discourse on Comfortable Living). 105.
In the fifth, "loving bodily action" means bodily action performed with a mind of loving-kindness. Both openly and in private...

"And so forth" means both in the presence and in the absence [of others]. The same method applies to the other cases as well. "Those virtues," and so forth, is stated by way of the fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*).

"Conducive to concentration" (*samādhisaṃvattanikāni*) means those which produce the concentration of the path and the concentration of the fruit. "One who has attained the commonality of virtue" (*sīlasāmaññagato*) means having reached a state of shared virtue;
the meaning is that one has become of identical and similar virtue. "Of the one who does it" (*takkarassa*) means of him who performs it.
Thus, in this sutta, virtue is spoken of as mixed; "view" refers to right view as insight (*vipassanā-sammādiṭṭhi*).
6. Commentary on the Ānanda Sutta: 106.
Regarding the sixth [case], "but he does not engage others in higher virtue," it means he does not reproach others for their state of virtue.
He does not revile. "One who observes oneself" means one who observes oneself by way of knowing what has been done and what has not been done by oneself.
"Not observing others" means being unoccupied with what has been done or not done by another. "Unknown" means unmanifest and of little merit.
"By way of being unknown" means by way of being unmanifest and of dull merit. "He does not tremble" means he does not fall into a state of fear.
Thus, in this sutta, only one whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava) is described.
7–8. Commentary on the Sīla-sutta and others: 107–108.
In the seventh [sutta], virtue, concentration, and wisdom are mentioned together; liberation is the fruit of arahantship, and the knowledge and vision of liberation is [the final stage].
Knowledge of reviewing is purely mundane. The same method applies to the eighth [knowledge] as well.
However, in this context, it is called "of the Asekha" because it occurs in one who is an Asekha (one beyond training).
9–10. Commentary on the Cātuddisa Sutta, etc.

109–110. “In the ninth [sutta], ‘one who moves unimpeded in the four directions’ (*cātuddisa*) means one whose movement is unobstructed in the four quarters. In this sutta as well, only one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*) is described. In the tenth, ‘it is fitting (*alaṃ’),” he is so called.
Here too, only one whose taints are exhausted is described. The first chapter, “On Comfortable Dwelling,” is concluded. (12) 2. The Chapter on Andhakavinda.
1. Commentary on the Kulūpaka Sutta 111.
Regarding the first [verse] of the second [chapter]: *Asanthavavissāsī* means that one places trust in those with whom one has no intimacy, even though they do not place trust in oneself.
*Anissaravikappī* means that while being without authority, one says, "Give this to me," and so forth.
“Take this! he assigns [the task] like a lord. “One who associates with those who have been abandoned” means he associates with families that have been cast out for the purpose of reconciling them.
“One who whispers in the ear” means he receives counsel at the root of the ear. The white side (the virtuous alternative) is to be understood by reversing what has been stated.
2. Commentary on the *Pacchāsamaṇa-sutta* 112.
Regarding "he does not take what has fallen into the bowl": when the preceptor has turned back and stopped, he gives his own empty bowl and does not take the preceptor’s bowl;
or, he does not accept what is being offered from that [bowl]. "He does not prevent" refers to this statement.

He does not know what is meant by "speaking in transgression of an offense. Or, even if he knows, he does not restrain him, saying, "Venerable sir, it is not proper to speak in such a manner. How does he "entice"?
He breaks his own position and introduces his own position [into the other's]. "Dull" means stupid. "A fool" means one whose mouth is dripping with saliva. The third [section] is self-evident.

4. Commentary on the *Andhakavinda Sutta* 114. In the fourth [verse], "Be virtuous" (*sīlavā hotha*) means: be possessed of virtue. "Endowed with guarding mindfulness" (*ārakkhasati*) means: being endowed with mindfulness that guards the doors [of the senses].

"Possessed of watchful mindfulness" (*nipakkasati*) means: those whose mindfulness is endowed with the very same wisdom (*ñāṇa*) that guards the doors. "With mindfulness as a guard" (*satārakkhena*)...
“Endowed with a mind” means endowed with a mind protected by mindfulness. “Of little radiance” means one who speaks little.
“Possessing right view” means endowed with the fivefold right view by way of the contemplation on the ownership of kamma, insight, the path, and the fruit.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the knowledge of reviewing is also indeed right view.
5. Commentary on the Maccharinīsutta 115.
In the fifth [verse], "one who is stingy regarding her dwelling" (*āvāsamaccharinī*) means she is envious of her dwelling; she does not tolerate the residence of others there.
"One who is stingy regarding her family" (*kulamaccharinī*) means she is envious of the family that supports her; she does not tolerate others approaching them.
"Envious of gain" means she is envious of gain; she cannot bear others' obtaining it. "Envious of praise" means she is envious of virtue;
she cannot bear talk of others' virtues. "Envious of the Dhamma" means she is envious of the Dhamma as study;
she does not wish to give it to others.
6–7. Commentary on the *Vaṇṇanāsutta*, etc. (116–117).

In the sixth [verse], "she squanders what is given in faith" means that she does not take the best portion from the alms-food given by others out of faith, but gives it to another. In the seventh, "envious" means possessed of envy. The remainder is clear in every respect.
Thus ends the second chapter, the *Andhakavinda-vagga*.
(13) 3. Gilānavagga 4.
Commentary on the Second Upaṭṭhākasutta 124.

In the fourth [sutta] of the third [vagga], "not capable" means not endowed with either physical strength or the power of knowledge. "One who seeks material goods" means one who, for the sake of material gain, looks forward to robes and other requisites.
5–6. Commentary on the Two Discourses on the Shortness of Life (Anāyussasutta): 125–126.
In the fifth discourse, "shortness of life" (*anāyussa*) means the cutting off of life, not the increase of life. The same principle applies to the sixth as well. 7.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Clearing Away (Vapakāsasutta).
127. "He is not fit to be sent away from the Saṅgha" means that it is not proper for him to live alone after departing from the Saṅgha.
Granted, he is indeed unfit even to live in the midst of the Saṅgha because he does not adorn the Saṅgha;
however, in the primary sense, he is unfit to be sent away from the Saṅgha because he is independent of exhortation and instruction. "He is fit to be sent away from the Saṅgha."

Because he belongs to the Saṅgha of the four quarters, he is fit to live alone after departing from the Saṅgha; yet, because he is an ornament to the Saṅgha, he is also indeed fit to live within the Saṅgha.
The eighth [verse] has a self-evident meaning.
9. Commentary on the *Parikuppa-sutta*.

129. In the ninth [verse], "destined for the states of misery" (*āpāyika*) means those who go to the states of misery (*apāya*). "Destined for hell" (*nerayika*) means those who go to hell (*niraya*). "Inflamed" (*parikuppa*) means having a nature that is prone to inflammation, like an old wound. "Incurable" (*atekiccha*) means not fit for medical treatment. The tenth [verse] has its meaning already explained.
Thus ends the third chapter, the Chapter on the Sick (*Gilānavagga*). (14) 4. The Chapter on Kings (*Rājavagga*).
1. Commentary on the First Discourse on Turning the Wheel (Paṭhamacakkānuvattanasuttavaṇṇanā) 131.
In the first part of the fourth [discourse]: "By means of the Dhamma" means by means of the ten wholesome states (*dasakusaladhamma*).

"The wheel" refers to the wheel of authority (*āṇācakkam*). "One who knows the goal" means one who knows the purpose of sovereignty. "One who knows the Dhamma" means one who knows the traditional law (*paveṇidhamma*). "One who knows moderation" means [one who knows moderation] regarding punishment or military force.

Or he knows the proper measure. "One who knows the time" means he knows the time for experiencing the pleasures of sovereignty, the time for administering justice, and the time for wandering through the countryside.
"One who knows the assembly" means he knows, "This assembly is an assembly of kshatriyas; this is an assembly of brahmins, vaishyas, shudras, or shramanas. In the section concerning the Tathagata:
"One who knows the meaning" means he knows the five kinds of meanings. "One who knows the Dhamma" means he knows the four kinds of Dhammas. "One who knows moderation" means...

He knows the mere acceptance and enjoyment of the four requisites. "One who knows the right time" means he knows the time thus: "This is the time for seclusion; this is the time for meditative attainment; this is the time for teaching the Dhamma; this is the time for wandering through the countryside.
"One who knows the assembly" means he knows: "This assembly is an assembly of khattiyas... [and so on]... this is an assembly of ascetics. "Unsurpassed" means...
The unsurpassed Wheel of Dhamma by means of the nine supramundane states; it is the supreme wheel, the "Dhammacakka.
2. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Turning the Wheel:

In the second [discourse], the "wheel set in motion by the father" refers to the Wheel-Treasure (*cakkaratana*) when the Universal Monarch (*cakkavatti*) has either gone forth into homelessness or passed away.
Having remained for only seven days, it vanishes; how, then, can it be said that he "continues" it?

Even when one remains within his father’s lineage, fulfills the duties of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*), and exercises the sovereignty of a wheel-turner, it is still said that he "continues" precisely what was set in motion by his father.
3. Commentary on the *Dhammarājāsutta* (The Discourse on the Dharma-King)
133. The third [sutta] is exactly according to the method explained in the *Tikanipāta*. However, the distinction here lies solely in the final two pairs of terms:
among those to be cultivated and those not to be cultivated, right livelihood (*sammā-ājīva*) is to be cultivated, while wrong livelihood (*micchā-ājīva*) is not to be cultivated.
A suitable village or town is to be cultivated, while an unsuitable one is not to be cultivated.
4. Commentary on the *Yassādisasutta* 134.
In the fourth [verse], "from both sides" (*ubhato*) means from both parties. "From the mother’s side and from the father’s side" (*mātito ca pitito ca*):

for one whose mother is a Khattiya, whose mother’s mother is a Khattiya, and whose mother’s mother’s mother is also a Khattiya; and for one whose father is a Khattiya, whose father’s father is a Khattiya, and whose father’s father’s father is also a Khattiya.
His father was a kṣatriya. He was well-born on both sides, from his mother’s side and from his father’s side.

"Of pure descent" means he was endowed with a pure maternal womb. Regarding the phrase "of a womb that digests evenly," here the "womb" (*gahaṇī*) refers to the metabolic heat element born of karma (*kammaja-tejo-dhātu*).
"As far as the seventh generation of ancestors" means: the father’s father is the grandfather; [the lineage] of the grandfather...
"Yuga" means the grandfather’s generation (*pitāmahayuga*). "Generations" (*yugāni*) is a term used for the measure of a lifespan. This is merely a verbal expression;
in actual meaning, however, the grandfather himself is the "grandfather’s generation. Beyond that, all preceding ancestors are included by the very mention of the grandfather.
Thus, one who has maintained pure descent as far back as the seventh person is called "one of pure lineage," or alternatively, "one who is unblemished and irreproachable."
He shows this by means of the expression "by way of birth. "Not reviled" means not reviled or insulted in such a manner as, "Take this man away;
what is the use of him? "Not censured" means not previously subjected to reproach, abuse, or blame.
For what reason? By way of birth; the meaning is: by such speech as, "This person is of such-and-such a low birth."
Regarding the passage beginning with "wealthy" (*aḍḍha*): anyone who is wealthy by means of his own possessions is called "wealthy. However, here it does not mean merely wealthy;
rather, the meaning is that he possesses great wealth—that is, he is endowed with a vast, immeasurable amount of riches.

One who has great and noble enjoyments (*bhoga*) by way of the five strands of sensual pleasure is called "of great wealth" (*mahābhoga*). Regarding "with full treasuries and storehouses": a "treasury" (*kosa*) is said to be a storehouse (*bhaṇḍāgāra*).
The meaning is that his treasury is full because of the wealth deposited and stored therein, and his storehouses are full of grain.

Alternatively, the fourfold treasury consists of elephants, horses, chariots, and the kingdom; and the threefold storehouse consists of the storehouse for wealth, the storehouse for grain, and the storehouse for clothing.
Since all of these are full for him, he is one whose treasury and storehouses are full (*paripuṇṇakosakoṭṭhāgāro*).
"Obedient" (*assavā*): even when someone gives much wealth, if the army does not listen, it is called "disobedient" (*anassavā*).
When they listen even when someone gives nothing, this is called "obedient. "Following instructions" (*ovādapaṭikārā*):
those who carry out the instructions given, such as, "This is to be done by you; this is not to be done. "Wise" (*paṇḍito*): endowed with wisdom. "Clever" (*byatto*)...
“Endowed with discernment” means possessed of analytical wisdom (*paññā-veyyattiya*). “Wise” means endowed with the wisdom that arises on the spot (*ṭhānuppattika-paññā*).
“Capable” means competent. “To consider the meaning” means to consider it for the sake of prosperity. For he considers by way of present circumstances alone, thinking:
“In the past they were thus, and in the future they will be thus. “Of those who have conquered” means of those who have achieved victory; by means of greatness...
Or those endowed with victory. "With liberated minds" means those whose mentalities are liberated by the five kinds of liberation.
5–6. Commentary on the Two Suttas on Aspiration (Paṭṭhānasutta). 135–136.
In the fifth [sutta], "of the townspeople and countryfolk" refers to the people living in market towns (*nigama*) and those living in the kingdom (*raṭṭha*). By the words "in the elephant," etc.,...
The sixteen great crafts—namely, elephant-riding, horsemanship, charioteering, archery, swordsmanship, seal-engraving, and arithmetic—are demonstrated. "Anavayo" means capable and proficient.
The rest here should be understood according to the method already explained below. In the sixth [case], "oparajja" refers to the status of a viceroy.
7. Commentary on the Appassutīsutta (The Discourse on the One of Little Learning)
137. "With intentions directed toward men" means having intentions arisen toward men by way of unrighteousness (*assaddhamma*), that is, having a mental disposition toward men.
"With the intention of seizing" means having the intention of grasping, thinking, "I will be able to seize it now," or "I will be able to seize it now.
"With the intention of disjunction" means having a mental disposition toward Nibbāna, thinking, "I will now reach Nibbāna," or "I will now reach it."
8. Commentary on the Bhattādaka Sutta 138.
In the eighth [sutta], "bhattādaka" means one who eats food; the meaning is "one who consumes much food.
"Okāsapharaṇa" means one who occupies space by filling up a place and thereby causing obstruction for others; thus, he is "space-filling" by his standing there. Here and there, excrement...

He causes [the dung] to be spread out and cast away; thus, he is a "dung-spreader" (*laṇḍasāraṇa*). He takes up a tally-stick at the time of counting "so many elephants"; thus, he is a "tally-taker" (*salākaggāhī*).

He crushes the bed and chair by way of sitting and lying down; thus, he is a "bed-and-chair-crusher" (*mañcapīṭhamaddana*). He takes up a tally-stick at the time of counting the monks; thus, he is a "tally-taker" (*salākaggāhī*).
9. Commentary on the Akkhamasutta 139.
In the ninth [verse], "a herd of elephants" (*hatthikāya*) means a multitude of elephants. The same method applies to the remaining [terms] as well.
"Moving about in battle" (*saṅgāmāvacara*) means those who frequent the battlefield. "Insulted by a single gift of grass and water" means by a single offering of grass and water on one day.
"Insulted" means that for even a single day he has not obtained grass or water. The same principle applies hereafter as well.
"He is unable to concentrate the mind" means he is unable to properly establish the mind upon the object of meditation (*ārammaṇa*). The rest here is self-evident.
However, it should be understood that in this sutta, the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*) are explained.
10. Commentary on the Sotasutta 140.
In the tenth [verse], "of ill-spoken words" means of harsh speech that has proceeded by way of fault, not being well-spoken.
"Of ill-arrived" means having arrived at the door of the ear in a manner that produces suffering. "Of paths of speech" means of words.
"Dukkha" means painful. "Tibba" means intense or having the nature of burning. "Khara" means harsh. "Kaṭuka" means sharp. "Asāta" means not sweet.
"Amanāpa" means incapable of pleasing or increasing the mind. "Pāṇahara" means life-taking.
"Yā sā disā" refers to [the direction] by way of the stilling of all formations and so forth.
It should be understood that *nibbāna* is called *disā* because it is seen (*dissati*) and will be seen (*apadissati*).

Furthermore, because all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) reach their subsiding (*samatha*) by coming to it, it is therefore called "the subsiding of all conditioned phenomena. The rest is clear everywhere.
In this sutta, however, virtue, concentration, and wisdom are taught in combination.
The Fourth Chapter on Kings.
(15) 5. The Fifth Chapter on Tikaṇḍakī. 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on Disparaging.
141. Regarding the first [offense] of the fifth [category], "by living together" means by dwelling in one place. "A source of acceptance" (ādeyyamukha) means a source of receiving;
the meaning is a source of grasping. "Having given this to him, he despises him" means he treats him with contempt, thinking, "This person knows only how to accept what has been given.
"He despises him because of living together" means that having become angry over some trivial matter, he thinks, "I know you..."
He speaks such words as, "What have I done? For how long a time have I lived? Was I not merely examining what you yourself have done and left undone?
Then the other, thinking, "Surely there must be some fault of mine," is unable to offer any rebuttal; he quickly becomes convinced, whether that [criticism] be praise or blame, and immediately—
He has faith. In the sense of believing, this "entrance" (mukha) is called the "entrance of taking up" (*ādāna*) because of its act of grasping.

However, according to the Pāḷi, "entrance of the receptacle" (*ādheyya-mukha*) means "the entrance established by being placed. Just as a pit dug in a road is said to have an "established entrance" for receiving whatever water comes along—whether good or bad—in the same way, it is said to have an "established entrance" for accepting [teachings] through the mode of faith.

"Of little faith" means having meager faith. Regarding the phrases "he does not know wholesome and unwholesome states," etc., he does not know wholesome states as "these are wholesome," nor does he know unwholesome states as "these are unwholesome.
Likewise, he does not know blameworthy, faulty states as "these are blameworthy," nor blameless, faultless states as "these are blameless," nor inferior states as "inferior."
"Exquisite, exquisite. Regarding "having counterparts of black and white":

he does not know that "these are called 'having counterparts' because they stand having excluded the white [states], and these white ones are called 'having counterparts' because they stand having excluded the black [states].
2. Commentary on the Ārabhati-sutta.
142. "In the second case, he both initiates [the action] and feels remorse" means that by way of transgressing an offense, he both initiates it and, on account of that, feels remorse.
"Liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom" refers to the concentration of Arahantship and the knowledge of the fruit of Arahantship.
"He does not understand" means he does not know because it has not been attained. "He initiates but does not feel remorse."
"He falls into it" means he commits an offense; however, because he has emerged from it, he does not feel remorse.

"He does not undertake it, yet feels remorse" means that although he has committed an offense once and emerged from it, and subsequently does not commit another, he is nevertheless unable to dispel his remorse. "He neither undertakes it nor feels remorse" means that he neither commits an offense...
And he does not feel remorse. That liberation of mind... [as before] ...ceases; yet he has not attained Arahantship.
By the fifth method, the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) is described.
"Arising from exertion" means arising from the occurrence of transgressions. "Arising from remorse" means born from remorse. "Increasing" means...

They increase by arising again and again. "Having abandoned the taints born of exertion" means having abandoned those taints that can arise through transgression, either by confessing the offense or by emerging from it.
"Having dispelled them" means having removed them by reflecting on the state of standing within the pure fold.
"Let him develop the mind and wisdom" means let him develop the mind of insight (vipassanā-citta) and the wisdom associated with it.
The remainder should be understood by this same method.
3. Commentary on the Sāraṇada Sutta 143.

In the third [verse], "those intent upon sensual pleasures" refers to those who are intent upon both material objects of desire (*vatthukāma*) and the defilements of desire (*kilesakāma*). "One who practices in accordance with the Dhamma" means...
In this world, a person who has entered upon the preliminary practice together with the moral precepts for the sake of the nine supramundane states and who fulfills that practice is rare. 4.
Commentary on the Tikaṇḍakī Sutta.

144. In the fourth [meditation], regarding that which is not repulsive (*appaṭikūla*), with a non-repulsive object (*appaṭikūlārammaṇa*). "Perceiving it as repulsive" (*paṭikūlasaññī*) means perceiving it thus:

"It is repulsive. This same method applies everywhere. But how does he dwell in this way? He either pervades a desirable object with the meditation on the foul (*asubha*) or he contemplates it as impermanent (*anicca*). In this manner, first of all, he dwells perceiving the non-repulsive as repulsive.
Toward an undesirable object, he either pervades it with loving-kindness or analyzes it by way of the elements.
Thus he dwells perceiving the non-repulsive in the repulsive. However, the third and fourth sections are stated by way of both the former method and the latter method;
the fifth is by way of the sixfold equanimity. And this sixfold equanimity belongs to one whose taints are destroyed.
It is similar to equanimity, but it is not the equanimity of one whose taints are destroyed. Therein, "he should dwell equanimous" means he should dwell established in a state of neutrality.
"In any [circumstance]" (kvacana) means on any object. "In any place" (katthaci) means in any location.
"Any trifle" (kiñcana) means even the slightest thing. Thus, in this sutta, insight alone is taught in five places. One who has initiated insight...

A bhikkhu is able to do it; one who possesses knowledge, one who is preeminent in wisdom, and even a learned recluse are also able to do it. Stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners are indeed able to do it;
as for those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), there is no need even to mention it. The fifth [sutta] is self-evident.
6. Commentary on the *Mittasutta*.
146. “He causes business to be carried out” means he causes agricultural work such as field labor to be performed.
“He takes up legal issues” means he takes up the four types of legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*). “Among the prominent monks” means among the monks who are renowned throughout the various directions.
“He becomes opposed” means he becomes antagonistic due to holding opposing views. “Wandering without a fixed residence” means wandering without a settled abode.
7. Commentary on the Discourse on the Gift of a Worthy Person (Asappurisadānasutta) 147.
In the seventh [verse], "he gives without respect" means he does not give having honored [the recipient] or having purified [the gift].

"He gives without regard" means he gives without a sense of esteem, out of a lack of reverence. "He gives what is cast away" means he does not give continuously; or alternatively, it means he gives with the desire to discard it.
It appears as such. "He gives without a view of coming" means that he does not give without having produced the view of coming, thinking, "Surely there will be a fruit for what has been done.
On the side of the bright, "he gives with veneration" means that he gives having established veneration toward both the gift and those worthy of offerings.
In that regard, one who gives by making the gift excellent and full of nutritive essence establishes veneration toward the gift.
...is called "respect. One who gives after having discerned the person establishes respect toward those worthy of offerings (*dakṣiṇīya*).

"Giving with one's own hand" means not giving by command through another's hand, but rather thinking: "In this beginningless *saṃsāra*, there is no measure to the time my hands and feet have not been used;
I shall effect the release from the cycle and the escape from existence," and thus giving with one's own hand.
He gives. "One who holds the view of coming" means that he gives having placed faith in both karma and its result, thinking, "There will be a condition for future existence.
8. Commentary on the Sappurisadāna Sutta (The Discourse on the Gift of a True Person) 148.
In the eighth [verse], "with faith" means having faith in both the gift and the fruit of the gift. "At the right time" means at the appropriate and fitting time.
"Unattached in mind" means having a mind that is not grasping, being one who has relinquished all things.

"Without harming" means without injuring or defiling his virtues. "And his timely gains are abundant" means that as for his gains, they do not come when he is already in decline or old age, but rather they arrive precisely at the appropriate time—during his prime—and moreover, they are numerous.
9. Commentary on the First Discourse on Liberation at the Appropriate Time (Paṭhamasamayavimuttasutta-vaṇṇanā) 149.

Regarding the ninth [discourse], "one liberated at the appropriate time" (*samayavimutta*): this refers to one whose mind is liberated by means of mundane liberation known as "liberation at the appropriate time," because it is liberated from the defilements that have been suppressed at the very moment of absorption. The tenth [discourse] has its meaning already explained.
The Fifth Chapter, the Tikaṇḍakī Chapter, is concluded.
The Third Fifty is finished.
4. The Fourth Fifty (16) 1.
The Chapter on the True Dhamma (Saddhammavagga).
1. Commentary on the First Discourse on Entering into the Certainty of Rightness (Paṭhamasammattaniyāmasuttavaṇṇanā) 151.

Regarding the first part of the fourth [discourse]: "Unable to enter into the certainty of rightness (*niyāma*) among wholesome states" means that he is unable to enter into the certainty of the Path (*magganiyāma*), which constitutes rightness among wholesome states; he is an unfit vessel. How so?
Regarding such phrases as "he despises," etc.: when one says, "What kind of talk is this?", one is indeed despising the talk.
When one says, "What is he saying? What does he know?", one is indeed despising the speaker. When one says, "What do we know?
From where do we have the strength to hear this?", one is indeed despising oneself. The "white side" (the virtuous alternative) should be understood by reversing [these cases].
2. Commentary on the Second Discourse on the Certainty of Rightness (Dutiyasammattaniyāmasuttavaṇṇanā) 152.

In the second [discourse], "one who imagines they have known what is not known" means one who, regarding that which has not been understood at all, possesses such conceit as thinking, "This has been understood by me.
3. Commentary on the Third Discourse on the Certainty of Rightness (Tatiyasammattaniyāmasuttavaṇṇanā)

153. Regarding the third [verse], "one who is malicious hears the Dhamma": being malicious, one hears the Dhamma with a mind that conceals the virtues of others. "With a mind intent on finding fault" means having a mind set on imposing censure.
"Seeking out flaws" means searching for a flaw or a defect in their virtues.
154. Regarding the fourth, "they do not listen to the Dhamma respectfully": they do not listen with attentive ears or by acting as those who perform their duty well.
“They do not master it” means that even while they employ the Dhamma as they have heard it, they do not employ it with due care. The fifth [discourse] is self-evident. 6.
Commentary on the Third Discourse on the Disappearance of the True Dhamma (Tatiyasaddhammasammosasutta):

In the sixth [discourse], “without a resort” (*appaṭisaraṇo*) means without a foundation. For teachers are indeed the resort of the Suttanta; because of their absence, one is without a resort. The rest here is exactly according to the method explained below.
7. Commentary on the Dukkathā Sutta 157.

“With reference to a person” means having set down this or that person as a comparison; the meaning is, having made them a witness. “While it is being spoken” means while it is being recited. The rest here, as well as the eighth [sutta], is of plain meaning.
9. Commentary on the Udāyī Sutta.

159. On the ninth [occasion], having established the thought, "I shall speak a discourse on gradual succession," one should teach the Dhamma to others by means of a discourse on the sequence of the teaching— such as "after giving comes virtue, after virtue comes heaven"— or by speaking a discourse appropriate to whichever specific passage of a sutta or verse has been set forth.
"Pariyāyadassāvī" means showing the respective reasons for each respective meaning; for here, "pariyāya" is said to mean "reason.
"Anuddayataṃ paṭicca" means having recourse to compassion, thinking: "I shall release beings who have fallen into great distress from their distress.
"Na āmisantara" means not caused by material gain; the sense is that he does not expect the acquisition of the four requisites for himself.
"Without harming oneself or another" means: without harming oneself or another by way of the impairment of their virtues through self-exaltation, disparagement of others, and so forth.
10. Commentary on the *Duppaṭivinodayasutta* (The Discourse on What is Difficult to Dispel)

160. "Difficult to dispel in the tenth" means that when occasions arise for performing such acts as laughing and so forth, they are difficult to remove and difficult to suppress even before reaching their conclusion. "Inspiration" (paṭibhāna) refers to the desire to speak.
These five are difficult to dispel; they are not easily dispelled. By means of a skillful method...
However, it can be dispelled by means of appropriate reflections, instructions, and so forth.
The first chapter, on the True Dhamma, is concluded.
(17) 2. The Chapter on Resentment.
1. Commentary on the First Discourse on the Removal of Ill Will (Paṭhama-āghātapaṭivinaya-sutta-vaṇṇanā) 161.
Regarding the second [discourse], they "remove" (*paṭivinenti*) ill will and "pacify" (*vūpasamenti*) it; thus, they are called "removers of ill will" (*āghātapaṭivinayā*).
That object upon which a monk's arisen ill will must be removed in its entirety is the object where the monk’s ill will [arises].
The meaning is that whatever has arisen there must all be dispelled by these five [factors]. Loving-kindness (*mettā*) toward that person should be developed;
this means loving-kindness should be developed by way of the threefold and fourfold jhānas. The same method applies to compassion (*karuṇā*).

By means of hearing the Dhamma, one obtains rapture and gladness known as the opening and clarity of the mind; having attended to that, the extinguishing of the arising of the mind should be understood.

and the act of bathing, drinking, emerging, lying down in the shade of a tree, and departing as one pleases is like [the state] among those [beings].
At the doors [of the senses], one should understand the settling of the mind by taking whatever object one desires as the focal point.

165. "They despise" means they treat with contempt; "thinking 'I shall likewise despise them,' he asks for the sake of despising"—this is the meaning. "Desirous of knowing" means having become desirous of knowing. 6.

“Does Sāriputta know anything, that the bhikkhus should oppose his words right in his presence?”—in order to ward off such a misconception arising among fools, he did not accept those words and approached the Blessed One. The time has been specified, but not for the accuser. For one who wishes to accuse another, he must not do so in the midst of the assembly, at the conclusion of the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā ceremonies, or in places such as the assembly hall or dining hall.

Rather, when the person being accused is seated in his daytime resting place, he should first ask for permission by saying, "Venerable sir, please grant me the opportunity; I wish to speak to you," and only after having thus obtained leave should he proceed with the accusation. As for the individual...
Having investigated, if a fickle person, having spoken what is untrue, brings infamy upon the monks, he should be admonished even without a formal act of granting leave (*okāsakamma*).
"By what is true" means by that which is factual and according to its actual nature. "Gently" means smoothly and softly.

"Beneficial" means endowed with the desire for their welfare and the desire for their benefit. "Remorselessness should be induced" means that a state of being free from embarrassment should be brought about.
"It is enough for you to be without remorse" means it is fitting for you to be free from hesitation. The rest here is self-evident.

9. Commentary on the *Khippanisanti-sutta*.
169. One who listens quickly and reflects upon it is "one of quick comprehension" (*khippanisanti*). One who grasps what has been well-learned is "one who grasps well-learned" (*suggahitaggāhī*).

"Skilled in meaning" (*atthakusala*) means one who is proficient in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). "Skilled in the Dhamma" (*dhammakusala*) means one who is proficient in the canonical texts (*pāḷi*).

"Skilled in etymology" (*niruttikusala*) means one who is proficient in the words of etymological derivation. "Skilled in phrasing" (*byañjanakusala*) means one who is proficient in the distinctions between syllables. "Skilled in the sequence of before and after" (*pubbāparakusala*)...

He is skilled in these five kinds of sequence: the sequence of meaning (*attha-pubbāpara*), the sequence of the Dhamma (*dhamma-pubbāpara*), the sequence of syllables (*akkhara-pubbāpara*), the sequence of phonemes (*byañjana-pubbāpara*), and the sequence of connection (*anusandhi-pubbāpara*).

In that regard, one who is skilled in the sequence of meaning knows the subsequent meaning by means of the preceding meaning, and knows the preceding meaning by means of the subsequent meaning. How so? For he indeed [knows] the preceding meaning...
Setting aside the meaning stated above, one knows that "there is a meaning below. Setting aside the meaning above, even when the meaning is stated below, one knows that "there is a meaning above.
Setting aside both [above and below], when the meaning is stated in the middle, one knows that "there is a meaning on both sides.
Setting aside the meaning in the middle, when the meanings are stated on both sides... [there is a meaning in the middle].
He knows: "It exists. This same method applies to the sequence of phenomena (*dhamma-pubbāpara*) and so forth.

However, when a sutta is begun with virtue (*sīla*) as the starting point and concludes with the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) at its end, he knows: "The sutta has proceeded according to its connection (*anusandhi*) and according to its demarcation (*anupariccheda*).
Even when a sutta is begun from the perspective of views (*diṭṭhi*) and the truths (*sacca*) appear later on, [he knows it] by way of its connection.

He knows: "It has proceeded. Even when the subsequent *sāraṇīya-dhammas* (qualities conducive to amity) have been introduced by way of quarreling and brawling, or when the subsequent ten bases of talk have been introduced by way of the thirty-two kinds of frivolous talk, he knows: "It has proceeded according to the connection.

170. In the tenth [verse], the Eldest One stands having overcome through mastery (*abhibhūti*). "Unconquered" (*anabhibhūto*) means not overcome by others.

"Immediately": by way of immediate succession, Arahantship arises. "This is the foremost of existences":
this final personal identity is called the foremost of all existences. Alternatively, "of one who has come to be as such" refers to those aggregates (khandhas) at the moment of the Path.
"Of that which has come to be, of that which exists": immediately thereafter comes the destruction of the taints (*āsava*); this means that the fruit arises immediately after the path.
"This is the foremost of existences": at the moment of the path, this pentad of aggregates is called the foremost of existences.

10. Commentary on the Gavesī Sutta (180):
"In the tenth [verse], he manifested a smile" means that while traveling along the great highway, he looked toward that sāla grove and [thought], "There is..."

Remaining in that very spot, he performed the act of breaking into a smile; showing the tips of his teeth, he smiled with a gentle laugh.
For Buddhas do not laugh like worldly people, who laugh while slapping their bellies and crying out, "Where? Where?
Rather, the laughter of Buddhas is merely an expression of being joyful and delighted.
This so-called "smile" occurs with thirteen types of consciousness accompanied by joy (*somanassa*).

In this regard, ordinary worldly people smile with eight types of consciousness—four unwholesome and four sense-sphere wholesome; those in training (*sekkha*) smile with six types of consciousness, having removed the two associated with wrong view (*diṭṭhigata*);
and those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) smile with one [type of] functional consciousness accompanied by roots (*sahetuka-kiriya-citta*).

They laugh with five types of consciousness by means of rootless functional (kiriyā) consciousness. Among these, when a powerful object enters the range of perception, they laugh with two types of consciousness associated with knowledge;

when the object is weak, they laugh with three types of consciousness: the two types of double-rooted consciousness and the rootless consciousness. In this context, however, it is the rootless functional mind-consciousness element accompanied by joy (*somanassa-sahagata*) [that is intended].
It caused the Blessed One to manifest a smile that was merely a flash of radiant joy.
Yet even such a slight smile as this became evident to the Elder. How so?
For at such a time, lightning flashes converged from the mouth of the great cloud that rains over the four continents upon the four canine teeth of the Tathāgata.
Beams of light, shining like [the moon] and as large as the trunks of great *tāla* trees, rose up, circled the noble head three times from left to right,
and vanished back into the tips of his fangs. By this sign, the Venerable Ānanda, even though he was walking behind the Blessed One,
knew of the manifestation of the smile.

"Sprinkled with water" means sprinkled with water and relinquished; for in whichever family he has reached maturity...
There was a girl; having gone there, she stood at his door. When asked, "Why do you stand here?
she said, "I have practiced the celibate life of a youth for forty-eight years; I give all of that to you, so you must give me your daughter.
They brought the girl and, pouring water into his hand, gave her to him. He [accepted her] as one consecrated by that water.
Having taken a wife, he goes away. *Atimīḷhajoti*: one born amidst excessive filth, in a great heap of excrement; *tassa sāti tassa esā* means "she belongs to him.
*Na davatthā*: not for the sake of sport; *na ratatthā*: not for the sake of sensual pleasure. *Methunaṃ uppādetvā*:
having produced [an offspring], that is, having produced a daughter or a son, thinking, "Now the lineage shall be continued," he departs.
"He goes forth. By "a happy destination, a heavenly world," this refers specifically to the Brahma-world.
"He becomes equal to the gods" means that because he is endowed with divine abidings (*dibbavihāra*), he is called "equal to the gods.
"Desiring that very same joy in children" refers to the affection for a child that one feels upon seeing a daughter or a son born.

Delight in a son arises; longing for that, he desires it. "He dwells with a household" means that having established a household, he lives in the midst of the household. The rest here is self-evident.
3. Commentary on the Saṅgāravasutta.
193. "In the third [case], 'even before'" means precisely first. "Overwhelmed by sensual lust" means seized by sensual lust.

"Submerged in sensual lust" means followed by sensual lust. "The escape" refers to the threefold escape from sensual lust: the escape by suppression (*vikkhambhana-nissaraṇa*), the escape by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga-nissaraṇa*), and the escape by eradication (*samuccheda-nissaraṇa*).
Among these, the first jhāna regarding the foul (*asubha*) is the escape by suppression.
The meaning is that one does not understand these three kinds: insight is called "emergence by substitution," and the path of Arahantship is called "emergence by eradication.
Regarding the phrases "one's own welfare" (*attattha*) and so forth: one's own welfare, consisting of Arahantship, is called "one's own welfare";
the welfare of those who provide the requisites is called "the welfare of others" (*parattha*); and both of these two types together are called "the welfare of both" (*ubhayattha*).
The meaning should be understood in this manner for all sections.
However, there is this distinction: regarding "the escape from ill will" and so forth, there are only two kinds of escape—the escape by suppression and the escape by eradication.
Therein, first, the first jhāna through loving-kindness is the escape by suppression from ill will.
The path of non-returning is the escape through eradication; for sloth and torpor, the perception of light is the escape through suppression;
and the path of Arahantship is the escape through eradication. For restlessness and worry, any form of serenity is the escape through suppression;
however, in this context, the path of Arahantship is the escape through eradication for restlessness, while the path of non-returning is the escape through eradication for worry.
The defining of phenomena regarding doubt is the escape by suppression; the first path is the escape by eradication.
As for the similes spoken here, such as "just as, brahmin, a bowl of water mixed with lac," and so forth:
in those similes, "bowl" refers to a vessel filled with water. "Mixed" means mixed in the sense of causing a change in color.
*Ukkudhito*: agitated. *Ussadakajāto*: become heated. *Sevālapaṇakapariyonaddho*:
covered with moss (*sevāla*)—such as the various kinds beginning with *tilabījaka*—or with *paṇaka*, which arises covering the surface of the water and is the color of a blue frog’s back.
*Vāterito*: stirred by the wind, shaken. *Āvilō*: turbid, lacking clarity. *Luḷito*: churned, unsettled.
"Kalalībhūta" means turned into mud. "Placed in darkness" means set in a place devoid of light, such as the interior of a granary and so forth.
In this sutta, the Blessed One concluded the teaching by way of the three existences and brought it to a climax with the attainment of Arahatship;
however, the brahmin was established at the mere level of taking refuge.
4. Commentary on the Kāraṇapālī Sutta 194.
In the fourth [sutta], "Kāraṇapālī": *pāli* is his name; however, because he causes the royal households to carry out their work (*kamma*), he became known as Kāraṇapālī.
Regarding "he causes the work to be carried out": having risen early in the morning, he [supervises] the gates, watchtowers, and walls that have not yet been built.

He has [buildings] constructed and causes the aged to be cared for. "The brahmin Piṅgiyānī" refers to a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka) of that name who was established in the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala).

It is said that he would rise early in the morning, have perfumes, garlands, and other offerings brought, go into the presence of the Teacher, pay homage, honor him with those perfumes, garlands, and so forth, and then return to the city; this was the brahmin’s daily routine.
[The duties] proceed. Having performed that duty, he saw him returning. He said this: having reflected, "This brahmin is wise and supreme in knowledge;
where has he been going since early morning? and having gradually recognized him as he approached his presence, he spoke the words beginning with, "Well now, from where [have you come]? etc.
In this context, *divā divassa* means "even during the day," that is, at the time of midday;
this is the meaning. *Paṇḍito maññe* means: does the venerable Piṅgiyānī consider the ascetic Gotama to be wise, or does he not?
This is the sense here. *Ko cāhaṃ, bho* means: "O sir, who am I" in the matter of knowing the ascetic Gotama’s analytical wisdom? Who indeed [am I]?
"I shall know the clarity of wisdom of the ascetic Gotama"—how indeed shall I know the clarity of wisdom of the ascetic Gotama, and by what means shall I know it?
In this way, he demonstrates his own state of ignorance in every respect.
"He too must surely be like him" means that whoever might know the clarity of wisdom of the ascetic Gotama, he too would surely be such.
Only one who has fulfilled the ten perfections and attained omniscience would be such a Buddha.
