For indeed, one who wishes to measure Mount Sineru, or the earth, or space, must obtain a measuring rod or a rope of corresponding length;
likewise, even by one who knows the wisdom of the ascetic Gotama, it is necessary to obtain an omniscient knowledge identical to his own.
He illuminates [this]. However, the repetition (*āmeḍita*) here is made out of respect. "Exalted" means supreme or best.
"And who am I, sir? means: "Sir, who indeed am I in the praising of the ascetic Gotama? And who shall praise the ascetic Gotama?"—by what reason shall I praise him?
"Praised by the praised" means he is praised by his own qualities alone—qualities that transcend all virtues and are praised by the entire world; for him, there is no need for praise by others.
Just as a *campaka* flower, a blue lotus, a red lotus, or red sandalwood are both beautiful and fragrant through their own color, scent, and splendor, so too is he.
He has no need for the praise of adventitious colors and fragrances.

Just as a precious gem or the lunar orb shines by its own radiance and has no need for another to illuminate it, so too the ascetic Gotama is praised and lauded by his own virtues, which are extolled by the whole world; he has been led to the state of preeminence over all the world.
He has no need for praise by another.

Or, he is "praised by the praised" because he is praised by those who themselves are praised. Who, then, are called the praised? King Pasenadi of Kosala is praised by the inhabitants of Kāsi and Kosala;
Bimbisāra by the inhabitants of Aṅga and Magadha; and the Licchavis of Vesālī [are praised by their own people].
The Mallas of Pāvā were praised by the inhabitants of Vajji; the Mallas of Kosinārā and other various kṣatriyas were praised by their respective localities;
Caṅki and other brahmins were praised by the brahmin assemblies; Anāthapiṇḍika and other laymen (upāsakas) were praised by the assemblies of laymen;
Visākhā and other female lay devotees (upāsikās) were praised by many hundreds of female lay devotees; Sakuludāyin and others...
It was praised by many hundreds of wanderers with their hundreds of wanderers;
by the great female disciples, such as the Elder Uppalavaṇṇā, with many hundreds of bhikkhunīs; by the great elders, such as the Elder Sāriputta, with many hundreds of bhikkhus;
by Sakka and other deities with many thousands of gods; and by Mahābrahmā and other Brahmās with many thousands of Brahmās.
Since they all praise, extol, and laud the One Possessing the Ten Powers, the Blessed One is called "praised by those who are praised.
"Atthavasa" means the benefit or advantage.
Then, explaining the cause of his own confidence, he said: "Just as if, sir, a man... and so forth. In that regard:
"Completely satisfied with the finest flavors" means: among the flavors of food, rice porridge (*pāyāsa*); among the flavors of oily substances, cow’s ghee (*gosappi*);
among the flavors of astringent substances, pure small honey (*khuddakamadhu*); among the sweet flavors, sugar—these and others like them are called "finest flavors.

He stands having eaten to the full, until his throat is filled, being satisfied by whichever of these he has consumed. "Of others that are inferior" means: of other inferior flavors as compared to those finest flavors.

"Suttaso" means by way of the discourses (*sutta*), that is, by way of their nature as discourses. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. "Tato tato" means from each respective one among the discourses and so forth.
"Of the criticisms of other various recluses and brahmins" refers to those criticisms—counted as their respective tenets—held by other various recluses and brahmins.
"He does not long for" means he does not desire them; even when they are being spoken, he does not wish to hear them.
He desires it. "Overcome by the weakness of hunger" means followed by both hunger and a state of physical frailty.
"Honey-ball" (*madhupiṇḍika*) refers to a ball of bound sesamum paste made by grinding rice flour, mixing it with the four sweets, and binding it together; or it may simply mean a sweet cake.
"He might obtain" (*adhigaccheyya*) means he might receive it. "Irresistible" (*asecanaka*) means [so called] because no other flavor is needed to make it sweet.
It is unsullied, rich in nutritive essence, and of superior flavor.
"Of yellow sandalwood" means of sandalwood that is golden in color. "Of red sandalwood" means of sandalwood that is red in color.

"Fragrant scent" means sweet-smelling. "Distress and so forth" refers to the distress of the round of existence (*saṃsāra*), the fatigue of the round of existence, and the fever of the round of existence.
Thus he uttered an *udāna*, that is, he made an utterance. For just as oil that cannot be contained in a measure and flows over is called an "overflow" (*avaseka*),
and water that cannot be contained in a pond and flows over it is called a "flood" (*ogha*), even so, that word of joy which cannot be contained by the heart—
If it cannot remain inside but, becoming excessive, does not settle within and instead issues forth, that is called an *udāna*.
The meaning is that he uttered such a word consisting of rapture (*pīti*).
5. Commentary on the Piṅgiyānī Sutta.
195. Regarding the fifth [meditation subject], "blue": this is a comprehensive term. "Blue-colored," and so forth, is the demonstration of its specific divisions.
In that context, their natural color is not blue; rather, it is stated thus because they are smeared and anointed with blue ointment.
"Blue garments" means that even their cloths, fine linen, silk, and so on, are blue. "Blue ornaments" refers to blue gems and blue flowers.
Adorned: their hand-ornaments, horse-ornaments, chariot-ornaments, as well as their canopies and tunics—all these are entirely blue.
In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all instances.
"Like a lotus" means like the hundred-petaled red lotus; *kokanada* is a synonym for that very same flower. "At dawn" means...
How much more so at the time of sunrise! "Siyā" means it would be. "Avītagandhaṃ" means not devoid of fragrance. "Aṅgīrasaṃ":
rays stream forth from every limb and member of the Blessed One; therefore, he is called Aṅgīrasa.
"Tapantamādiccamivantalikkhe" means shining in the sky by way of providing light throughout the four great continents, which are surrounded by two thousand islands.
"Behold Aṅgīrasa, shining like the sun"—this he says either referring to himself or to the great multitude of people.
6. Commentary on the Discourse on the Great Dreams (Mahāsupinasutta). 196.
Regarding "the six great dreams": they are called "great" because they are to be seen by great men and because they serve as the signs for great matters.
The great dreams. "Appeared" means they became manifest. In that regard, one sees a dream for four reasons:
either from a disturbance of the elements (*dhātu*), or from what has been previously experienced, or from the influence of deities, or from a prior omen.
Therein, one whose elements are disturbed by the application of conditions that cause the disturbance of bile and so forth sees a dream from a disturbance of the elements.
He sees. And while seeing, he sees various kinds of dreams: as if falling down a mountain, as if traveling through the sky, and as if pursued by wild beasts, elephants, thieves, and so forth.

Seeing from what was previously experienced, he sees an object that has been experienced in the past. For one who sees due to the intervention of a deity, [the dream arises] because the deity desires his welfare or does not desire his welfare.
They bring forth various kinds of objects for the sake of either benefit or harm.

By the power of those deities, he sees those objects. Seeing them as a premonitory sign (*pubbanimitta*), he sees a dream that serves as a premonitory sign of the benefit or harm about to arise through the influence of merit or demerit, just like the mother of a Bodhisatta.
Just as the King of Kosala [saw] sixteen dreams for the sake of obtaining a son, so too did this very Blessed One, while still a bodhisatta,
see these five great dreams.
In that regard, whatever one sees in a dream due to a disturbance of the elements or from what has been previously experienced does not come true.
That which one sees through the intervention of a deity may be either true or false;
for when deities are angry and desire to destroy [something] by means of a stratagem, they may show even what is perverted. However, that which one sees as a premonitory sign is invariably true.
Furthermore, there is indeed a distinction among dreams based on the combination and differentiation of these four primary causes.
Now, these four kinds of dreams are seen only by trainees (*śaikṣa*) and worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), because they have not yet abandoned the perversions (*viparyāsa*);
those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) do not see them, because they have abandoned the perversions. But as for this seeing, does one see while asleep, or while awake, or neither asleep nor awake?
In this regard, if one sees while asleep, there is a contradiction with the Abhidhamma.
[He] incurs [an offense]. For one sleeps by means of the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*);
that [consciousness] does not have visible forms or signs as its object, nor is it associated with lust and so forth. And such types of consciousness arise for one seeing a dream.

Now, if one were to see [the dream] upon waking, it would incur a contradiction with the Vinaya. For whatever one sees upon waking, one sees that with a consciousness belonging to ordinary worldly activity (*sabbohārika-citta*).

There is no such thing as "no offense" when a transgression is committed with a mind characterized by habitual practice (*sabbohārika-citta*). However, even if a transgression is committed while dreaming, it is invariably no offense at all.

Now, if one sees neither while asleep nor while awake—that is, if one does not see at all—does this not lead to the conclusion that there is an absence of dreaming? It is not an absence. Why? Because [the person] is overcome by *kapimiddha* (monkey-sleep).
He sees. For this has been said: "One overcome by monkey-sleep, O Great King, sees a dream.

"Overcome by monkey-sleep" means possessed of the sleep of a monkey. Just as the sleep of a monkey is characterized by rapid shifting, so too is that sleep which, because it is interspersed again and again with wholesome and other states of consciousness, is characterized by rapid shifting; during the course of which—
There is a repeated crossing over from the life-continuum (bhavaṅga); one who is engaged in that sees a dream.

Therefore, this dream may be wholesome (kusala), unwholesome (akusala), or indeterminate (abyākata). In that regard, it is wholesome for one performing such acts as worshipping a shrine, listening to the Dhamma, or teaching the Dhamma while dreaming;
it is unwholesome for one performing such acts as taking life; and it is indeterminate when free from both extremes at the moments of adverting and having that as the object.
It should be understood as indeterminate (*abyākata*). Because the volition (*cetanā*) has a weak basis, it is incapable of drawing forth rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
However, during the course of existence (*pavatta*), being supported by other wholesome and unwholesome states, it yields a result (*vipāka*).
Even though it yields a result, nevertheless, because it arises in an improper sphere, the volition of dreaming is merely nominal. Furthermore, this dream depends upon time as well.
First of all, a dream seen during the day does not correspond [to reality]; likewise for those seen in the first watch, the middle watch, and the last watch of the night.

However, at the strong dawn, when what has been eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted has been properly digested, when the nutritive essence (*ojā*) is established in the body, and while the sun is rising, a dream seen then corresponds.
One who sees a dream with a desirable sign obtains what is desirable; one who sees a dream with an undesirable sign obtains what is undesirable.

Furthermore, these five great dreams are seen neither by the common people of the world, nor by the great kings, nor by the wheel-turning monarchs, nor by the chief disciples, nor by the paccekabuddhas, nor by the perfectly enlightened Buddhas; only a single omniscient Bodhisatta sees them.
But when did our Bodhisatta see these dreams? On the fourteenth day [of the lunar fortnight], thinking, "Tomorrow I shall become a Buddha."
He saw them at the time when the night was breaking in that fortnight; some even say it was on the thirteenth day.
Having seen these dreams, he rose, sat cross-legged upon his couch, and reflected:
"If these dreams had been seen by me in the city of Kapilavatthu, I would have told them to my father, the Great King. But if my mother were still living, I would tell them to her."
“I shall speak. Yet, in this matter, there is no one to receive these [teachings]; I alone shall receive them.
Then, having himself received the dream—recognizing, “This is the omen for him;

this is the omen for her”—and having partaken of the milk-rice given by Sujātā in the village of Uruvelā, he ascended the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), attained awakening, and proceeded in due order.
While dwelling at Jetavana, the Blessed One, wishing to explain in detail the five great dreams he had seen during his own time as a Bodhisatta, addressed the bhikkhus and began this teaching.
In that context, "the great earth" refers to the great earth situated filling the interior of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*). "There was a great bed" means...
It became the couch for the Blessed One. "Placed" means set down. However, it should be understood that it was not merely placed in the water;
rather, having traveled along the uppermost part of the eastern ocean, it was placed upon the summit of the eastern world-sphere (cakravāḷa).
The same principle applies to the phrases "in the western ocean" and "in the southern ocean. "Tiriya" refers to a species of grass.
It is called *dabbatiṇa*. Having risen from the navel and reaching up to touch the sky, it stood there;

that is to say, rising from the navel with a plough-handle as thick as a red [lotus stalk], even as one looked on, it rose further and further—by a span, a cubit, a fathom, a staff-length, a league, half a yojana, and a full yojana. Thus it rose higher and higher.
It stood reaching up to the sky for many thousands of yojanas. "Climbing up on his feet" means having ascended by means of his feet, starting from the tips of his toes.
"Of various colors" means one was blue-colored, one yellow-colored, one red-colored, and one the color of a withered leaf;
thus they were of various colors. "White" means pale and pure. "Of the great mountain of filth" means...
"Of the dung-mountain three yojanas high. "He walks upon it, higher and higher" means he walks from summit to summit.
However, long-lived Buddhas appear as if they have entered and are sitting within that three-yojana dung-mountain.
Having thus displayed the portents by means of this much space, [the text now describes] the attainment together with those portents.

To demonstrate this, he said, "Bhikkhus, when... and so forth. In that context, because it bestows all virtues, the path to arahantship for Buddhas is called "unsurpassed perfect enlightenment" (anuttarā sammāsambodhi).

Therefore, the fact that he saw the great earth of the world-system as his glorious couch was a premonitory sign of his future Buddhahood; likewise, that he saw the Himalaya, king of mountains, as his pillow [was another].

That he saw [the world] was the omen for the bolstering of his omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). That he saw his four hands and feet standing at the summit of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) was the omen for the unassailability of the Wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakka*).
That he saw himself lying on his back was the omen for the state of having faces turned upward by beings who had been face-downward within the three realms of existence (*bhava*).
That which was as if he were seeing with his eyes wide open was a preliminary sign of the attainment of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).

That which became a single light reaching as far as the peak of existence (*bhavagga*) was a preliminary sign of unobstructed knowledge (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*). The rest should be understood according to the text (*pāḷi*) itself.
7. Commentary on the *Vassasutta*.
197. "Sattame nemittā" means fortune-tellers. "The fire element agitates" means a great mass of fire arises.
"Having received the water with his hand" means having taken up with his hand the seasonally produced water that had arisen, extending over three hundred leagues.
"They become negligent" means they become negligent in their own play, their mindfulness being lost. For of them—
When the thought arises, “May we delight in our own pleasure,” it rains even out of season; in the absence of that thought, it does not rain.
It is with reference to this that it was said: “It does not rain at the [wrong] time. The eighth and ninth [suttas] are of obvious meaning. 10.
Commentary on the *Nissaraṇīya Sutta* (The Discourse on Escape)

200. "In the tenth [chapter], 'nissaṭā' means emerged or detached. 'Elements' (dhātu) refers to those whose intrinsic nature is empty of self. 'While attending to sensual desire' means while one is attending to sensual desire;

the meaning is that, having emerged from the jhāna on the foul (asubha), one directs the mind toward sensual desire for the sake of investigation, like one who, having taken an antidote, tests the poison. 'Does not leap forward' means it does not enter."
"It does not become serene" means it does not attain confidence (*pasāda*). "It does not settle" means it does not become established. "It is not liberated" means it does not resolve with conviction.

Just as a cock's feather or a tendon-slip when thrown into a fire shrinks back, recoils, rolls away, and does not spread out, so too it shrinks back and does not spread out. [This refers to] renunciation (*nekkhamma*).
"Furthermore," here "renunciation" refers to the first jhāna regarding the foul (aśubha); his mind leaps forward when he attends to that.
"His mind": his mind consisting of that jhāna on the foul. "Well-gone" means it has gone well because it has entered its proper domain (gocara).
"Well-developed" means it has been well-cultivated because it is conducive to non-decline. "Well-emerged" means [emerged] from sensual desire.
“Emergent. “Well-liberated” means completely liberated from sensual pleasures (*kāma*). The taints conditioned by sensual pleasures are the four taints rooted in sensual desire.
“Afflictions” means suffering. “Fevers” means the fever of sensual lust.

“He does not experience that feeling” means he does not experience that feeling of sensual pleasure, nor the feeling of affliction and fever. “This is declared to be the escape from sensual pleasures.”
This foulness-jhāna is declared to be the escape from sensual desires because it has emerged from them.
However, one who takes that jhāna as a basis, contemplates formations, reaches the third path, and having seen Nibbāna through the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), knows:
"There are no more such things as sensual desires. His mind is the ultimate escape itself. The same method applies to the remaining phrases as well.
But this is the distinction: in the second round, the jhānas of loving-kindness (mettā) are called the escape from ill-will (byāpāda).
In the third round, the jhānas of compassion (karuṇā) are called the escape from cruelty (vihiṃsā). In the fourth round, the formless jhānas (arūpajjhāna) are called the escape from forms (rūpa).
And here, the fruit of arahantship (arahattaphala) should be connected as the absolute escape. In the fifth round, "he attends to personality" (sakkāyaṃ manasikaroti).
This refers to one who has attained Arahantship by comprehending pure formations (*suddhasaṅkhāra*), a dry-insight practitioner (*sukkha-vipassaka*) who,
having emerged from the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), directs his mind toward the five aggregates of clinging for the purpose of investigation.
"This is declared to be the escape from identity" (*sakkāya-nissaraṇa*) refers to one who stands having seen Nibbāna through both the path of Arahantship and its fruition.
For a bhikkhu, the thought that has arisen—"There is no further personal existence (sakkāya)"—is declared to be the escape from personal existence, namely the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship.
Now, speaking in praise of the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) who stands having reached this cessation which is the escape from personal existence, the Blessed One said:
"Even delight in sensual pleasures does not underlie him," and so forth. In this context, "does not underlie" means it does not arise.
"Latent tendencies" refers to non-arising. The rest here is of obvious meaning.
The fifth chapter on Brahmins is concluded.
The fourth fiftieth section is finished.
5. The Fifth Fifty (21) 1.
The Chapter on Kimila 1.
The Commentary on the Kimila Sutta
201. In the first [chapter] of the fifth [book], it was in the city named Kimilā. "In the Nicula grove" means in the Mucalinda grove.

"He said this": it is said that this elder, having been the son of a merchant in that very city, went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Teacher and attained the knowledge of previous births (*pubbenivāsāñāṇa*).
Recalling the continuum of aggregates (*khandhasantāna*) in which he had dwelt, [he recalled his past life under] Kassapa, the One Possessed of the Ten Powers (*Dasabala*).

At a time when the Dispensation was being neglected, he went forth into homelessness. When the four assemblies were showing disrespect toward the Teaching, he constructed a ladder, climbed a mountain, and performed the duties of a recluse there.

Seeing his own dwelling place from that height, he thought, "I shall approach the Teacher and ask him about this matter," and thus he spoke these words beginning with, "Who indeed, venerable sir? and so forth.
"They dwell without reverence and without deference toward the Teacher" means they dwell without establishing respect and seniority toward the Teacher.
The same method applies to the other cases as well.

In this context, one who dwells without reverence toward the Teacher is one who, while on the shrine grounds and so forth, carries a sunshade, wears sandals, wanders about, and engages in various kinds of useless talk.
Furthermore, one who sits at the head of the assembly for hearing the Dhamma and either falls asleep or engages in various kinds of useless talk is said to dwell without respect for the Dhamma.

One who, in the midst of the Saṅgha, flaps their arms about and speaks diverse chatter, and shows no honor toward the elders, novices, and those of middle standing, is said to dwell without respect for the Saṅgha. [Regarding] the training...
One who does not fulfill the training is said to dwell without respect for it. Engaging in mutual quarreling, brawling, and so forth, one is said to dwell without respect for one another.
The second [section] has a meaning that is already evident.
3. Commentary on the *Assājānīya Sutta* (The Horse-Bred Sutta)
203–204. In the third [verse], *ajjava* means by way of uprightness, by way of being straight, by way of proceeding without crookedness.
*Java* means by way of speed of foot. *Maddava* means by way of softness of body. *Khanti* means by way of patience of endurance. *Soracca* means by way of purity of virtue.
In the section on the bhikkhu, *ajjava* is the straight-going of knowledge. *Java* is the state of the movement of knowledge having become courageous. *Maddava*...
Virtue and gentleness. Patience is indeed patience as endurance. Amiability is simply the state of pure virtue. In the fourth [chapter], the five powers are explained as being mixed. 5.
Commentary on the Cetokhila Sutta.
205. Regarding the five mental obstructions (*cetokhila*): they are states of rigidity, like refuse, or like stumps in the mind.
"He doubts the Teacher" means he doubts either the Teacher’s physical body or his qualities.

Doubting the body, he wonders, "Does a body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man exist, or does it not? Doubting the qualities, he wonders, "Is there the capacity to know the past, future, and present..."
He doubts, wondering: "Does omniscient knowledge exist, or does it not? To "doubt" (*vicikicchati*) means that while investigating, one is troubled;
one encounters suffering and is unable to reach a definitive conclusion. "Is not resolved" (*nādhimuccati*) means that one does not obtain the conviction that "it is exactly so.
"Does not have serene confidence" (*na sampasīdati*) means that, having entered into the [Buddha's] qualities, one is not turbid, owing to a state free from doubt.
He is unable to become [accomplished]. "For ardor" means for the purpose of exerting the energy that scorches the defilements.
"For application" means for repeated application. "For persistence" means for constant practice. "For striving" means for the purpose of exertion.
"This is the first mental barrenness" means this first state of rigidity of mind, consisting of doubt regarding the Teacher, remains unabandoned by this bhikkhu in this way.
"Dhamma" refers to both the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*) and the Dhamma of realization (*paṭivedha-dhamma*). One who has doubt regarding the Dhamma of the scriptures wonders:
"They say there are the word of the Buddha in the Three Baskets and eighty-four thousand divisions of Dhamma; does this actually exist, or does it not?
One who has doubt regarding the Dhamma of realization wonders: "Is there indeed such a thing as the Path which is the outflow of insight (*vipassanā-nissanda*), and the outflow of the Path..."
Regarding "fruit": they say that the relinquishing of all conditioned phenomena is called Nibbāna; he doubts whether that exists or not.

"He doubts the Saṅgha" means: by way of such phrases as "one who has entered upon the straight path," etc., [he doubts] whether there exists this kind of practice—the assembly consisting of the eight types of persons, namely the four established in the paths and the four established in the fruits.

He doubts whether the Saṅgha exists or not. Doubting the training, he doubts whether what they call the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom actually exist or not.
This is the fifth: this is the fifth state of rigidity, coarseness, and stumps-like stubbornness of the mind, consisting of anger toward one’s fellow practitioners of the holy life.
6. Commentary on the Vinibandha Sutta 206.
In the sixth [sutta], "mental bondages" (*cetasovinibandhā*) means that they bind the mind and seize it as if holding it in a fist;

thus they are called mental bondages. "Sensual pleasures" (*kāma*) refers to both objective sensual pleasures (*vatthukāma*) and defilement-sensual pleasures (*kilesakāma*). "In the body" (*kāye*) means in one's own body. "In forms" (*rūpe*) means in external forms.
"As much as required" means as much as one desires, that much. "Filling the belly" means filling the stomach;
for it is called "filling the belly" because it fills the belly. "The pleasure of lying down" refers to the comfort of beds and seats, or the comfort of the seasons.
"The pleasure of the side" refers to the comfort of the right or left side for one who lies down turning over.
"Thus there is pleasure arisen. "The pleasure of sloth" means the pleasure of sleep. "Devoted to" means he dwells engaged and intent upon it.
"Having made an aspiration" means having wished for it. Regarding the phrases beginning with "by virtue": "virtue" (*sīla*) refers to the fourfold purity of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*).

"Vow" (*vata*) refers to the undertaking of observances. "Austerity" (*tapo*) refers to the practice of asceticism. "The holy life" (*brahmacariya*) refers to abstaining from sexual intercourse. "I shall become a god" refers to a god of great power.
"Or I shall become one. "Devāññataro vā" means "or another among the gods of little power.
7–8. Commentary on the *Yāgu-sutta* and others (207–208).
In the seventh [sutta], "it conforms with the wind" (*vātaṃ anulometi*) means it carries [the food] by conforming to the wind. "It cleanses the bladder" (*vatthiṃ sodheti*) means the channels...
She makes it pure. "She cooks what remains raw": if there is anything remaining raw, she cooks that.
In the eighth [verse], "not for the eye" means not beneficial for the eyes; it does not purify the eye. 9.
Commentary on the Gītassara Sutta.
209. In the ninth [case], by "protracted" (*āyatakena*), it means by a long [breath]; that is, by proceeding while destroying the rhythm of the verses and the completeness of the words and syllables.
"Even for one desiring the sound of a lute" (*sarakuttim pi nikāmayamānassa*) means for one who aspires to the performance of a lute, thinking, "In this way the tone of the song should be made.
"There is a breaking of concentration" (*samādhissa bhaṅgo hoti*) means there is the destruction of the mind of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
10. Commentary on the Discourse on Lack of Mindfulness (Muṭṭhassatisutta) 210.
In the tenth [discourse], "he sleeps badly" means that seeing various kinds of dreams, he sleeps with distress.
"He wakes up badly" means that even when waking, he wakes up terrified, with his hair standing on end. In this discourse...
Mindfulness and clear comprehension have been explained as mixed.
The first chapter, the Kimila Chapter, is finished.
(22) 2. The Chapter on Abusers.
1. Commentary on the *Akkosaka-sutta* 211.
In the first [verse] of the second [sutta], "one who reviles and insults" means one who reviles by means of the ten grounds for reviling, and one who insults by seeing [the consequences as] fearful.
"One whose obstacles are severed" means one whose obstacles are severed because the obstacles to the supramundane have been cut away.
"Affliction by disease" (*rogātaṅka*): it is simply "disease" (*roga*) that is called "affliction by disease" because it brings about a miserable livelihood.
2. Commentary on the Discourse on the Quarrelsome One (Bhaṇḍanakārakasutta) 212.
"One who creates legal issues" (*adhikaraṇakāraka*): one who creates any one of the four types of legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*). "Not yet attained" (*anadhigata*): a distinction not previously reached.
3. Commentary on the Sīla Sutta 213.

In the third [verse], "one who is immoral" (*dussīlo*) means one who lacks virtue, one devoid of virtue. "One whose virtue has lapsed" (*sīlavipanno*) means one whose virtue has perished, one whose restraint is broken.

"On account of negligence" (*pamādādhikaraṇaṃ*) means by reason of negligence. And this sutta is presented from the perspective of householders, yet it certainly applies to those who have gone forth as well.
For a householder, by whatever craft or occupation he maintains his livelihood— whether it be agriculture or trade— if he is heedless through such acts as the taking of life,
he will be unable to carry out those tasks at their proper time, and thus his capital will perish. Furthermore, even during the festival season,
if he commits the taking of life, theft, and so forth, he will face great [consequences] by way of punishment.

He incurs ruin regarding enjoyments. A monk who has gone forth but is immoral, due to negligence, incurs ruin regarding virtue, the word of the Buddha, meditative absorption, and the seven treasures of the noble ones.
Regarding a householder, [people say] in the midst of the four assemblies: "Such-and-such a person, born in such-and-such a family, is immoral and of evil character;
having abandoned both this world and the next, he does not give even so much as a ticket for a meal."
An evil reputation spreads abroad. For one who has gone forth, it spreads thus: "So-and-so was unable to guard his virtue or master the Buddha’s word;
he lives by means of medical practice and the like, and is possessed of the six kinds of disrespect. As for the lack of confidence:
first, a householder thinks, "Surely in this assembly of many people, someone will find out about my work..."
Then, thinking, "They will reprimand me, or they will hand me over to the royal family," he approaches with fear.
He sits down dejected, with shoulders drooping and face cast downward, scratching the ground with his toe;
being lacking in confidence, he is unable to speak. Even though he has gone forth, [he thinks], "Many monks have assembled; surely someone will [expose] my deed..."

"Once they know, they will set aside my Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies, deprive me of my status as a recluse, and cast me out"—thinking thus, he approaches with fear and is unable to speak with confidence.
On the other hand, there is one who, though immoral, behaves as if he were arrogant; yet even he is inwardly humiliated by his own disposition.
“He dies deluded”: for as he lies upon his deathbed, the place where he undertook and practiced unvirtuous deeds comes into his range of vision.
Opening his eyes, he sees this world; closing them, he sees the other world.
The four states of misery appear before him, as if a hundred spears were being struck into his head. He cries out, “Stop! Stop!”
One dies full of fear. Therefore it is said: “He passes away deluded. The fifth phrase is self-evident.
The discourse on the benefits should be understood as the reverse of what has been stated.
4. Commentary on the Bahubhāṇi Sutta.

214. In the fourth [verse], "one who speaks much" refers to one who speaks at length without having delimited [the matter] through wisdom (*paññā*). "One who speaks with deliberation" (*mantabhāṇī*): "deliberation" (*manta*) is said to be wisdom; it refers to one who speaks after having delimited [the matter] by means of that [wisdom].
5. Commentary on the First Discourse on Intolerance (Paṭhama-akkhanti-sutta) 215.

In the fifth [verse], "one full of enmity" (*verabahula*) means one who has much enmity, whether toward other persons or toward unwholesome states (*akusala*). "One full of faults" (*vajjabahula*) means one who is full of hatred (*dosa*).
6. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Forbearance (Dutiyaakkhantisutta) 216.
In the sixth [verse], "cruel" (*luddo*) means harsh and hard-hearted. "Remorseful" (*vippaṭisārī*) means possessed by a sense of shame or embarrassment.
7. Commentary on the First Discourse on What is Unattractive (Paṭhamaapāsādikasutta)

217. Regarding the seventh, "uninspiring" (*apāsādika*): this refers to one who is possessed of uninspiring bodily actions and so forth. "Inspiring" (*pāsādika*) refers to one whose conduct is pure and who inspires confidence. The eighth and ninth [sections] have meanings that are self-evident.
10. Commentary on the *Madhurā-sutta*: 220.
Regarding the tenth, "Monks, there are these five dangers in Madhurā," at one time the Blessed One was surrounded by the community of monks.
While wandering on his journey, having reached the city of Madhurā, he began to enter the city.
Then a certain female spirit (yakkhinī) of wrong views, appearing naked and stretching out her two hands, lolling her tongue, stood before the One of Ten Powers.
Without entering the city, the Teacher departed from that very spot and went to the monastery.
The great multitude, taking with them both hard and soft food as well as honors and respect, went to the monastery and gave alms to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
For the purpose of subduing that city, the Teacher began this discourse.
In that context, "uneven" means not level; "full of dust" refers to the mass of dust raised when the wind blows through the lattices.
It is as if it were completely enveloped. The rest is clear everywhere.
Thus ends the second chapter, the Chapter on Abusers.
(23) 3. The Chapter on Long Journeys.
1. Commentary on the First Discourse on Long Wanderings 221.
Regarding the first [section] of the third [discourse]: "Wandering without a fixed residence" means wandering without a settled place.
"He does not purify what he has heard" means that even though he possesses what he has heard, he is unable to purify it. "He lacks confidence in some of what he has heard" means...
Even when there is some slight learning present, he does not attain joy through that knowledge. "Samavatthacāre" means one whose conduct is well-established.
The second [sutta] has a meaning that is already clear.
3–4. Commentary on the *Atinivāsa-sutta* and others.

223–224. In the third [case], "one with many goods" means one with many requisites (*parikkhāra*). "One with many medicines" means one who has many medicines due to the abundance of ghee, fresh butter, and so forth.
"Distracted" (*byatta*) means attached. "Intimately associated" (*saṃsaṭṭha*) means having become intimately associated through the fivefold intimacy.

"In a manner not conformable" (*ananulomika*) means in a way that is unsuitable for the Dispensation (*sāsana*). In the fourth [case], "one who is stingy regarding praise" (*vaṇṇamaccharī*) means one who is stingy regarding virtues (*guṇa*).
"One who is stingy with the Dhamma" means one who is stingy with the scriptures (*pariyatti*).
5–6. Commentary on the *Kulūpaka-sutta*, etc., 225–226.
Regarding the fifth [offense], "he incurs [the offense] by wandering without having informed": "being invited and having already partaken of a meal, while there is a monk present..."
She incurs the offense stated in the training rule: “Without having asked permission, she should not enter among families before a meal or after a meal.
The phrases such as “sitting in private” are also to be understood according to their respective training rules.
In the sixth [offense], “at an improper time” means a time that has exceeded the proper measure. The seventh is self-evident.
8. Commentary on the Ussūrabhatta Sutta (228).
Regarding the eighth [verse], *ussūrabhatte* means when the meal is cooked too late in the day.

*Na kālena paṭipūjentī* means not preparing the rice-gruel at the time for rice-gruel, the snacks at the time for snacks, or the main food at the time for the main food; that is, they fail to attend to the appropriate and proper times.
Because they have been delayed, they do not offer worship at the proper time; they merely give with their own minds.
Consequently, when those [offerings] also arrive at their own homes, they act in the same way.

Even the deities who receive offerings by family tradition, receiving their gains only at the appropriate time, protect and guard them without causing any affliction. However, when they receive them at an improper time, [they think]: "These..."
“Because they show us no respect,” people do not provide protection.
Ascetics and brahmins also do not perform rites that ought to be performed during auspicious or inauspicious occasions, thinking, “In their house there is no food at the time of the meal;
they give it only when midday has passed. Thus, they turn away from work, thinking, “We receive nothing in the morning.”
"Oppressed by hunger, we are unable to work," they say, and having abandoned their work, they sit down.

"It lacks nutritive essence (*ojā*)" means that what is eaten at an improper time is unable to carry nutritive essence. The bright side (*sukkapakkha*) is to be understood by reversing what has been stated [in the dark side].
9. Commentary on the First Black Snake Sutta (*Paṭhamakaṇhasappasuttavaṇṇanā*)
229. In the ninth [verse], "one who is timid" means one who sleeps with a heavy sleep. "One who is fearful" means that fear arises depending upon him;
therefore, he is fearful. "One who betrays friends" means he harms or injures even a friend who provides him with food and drink.
The same principle applies to women as well.
10. Commentary on the Second Black Snake Sutta (Sutta 230).

"Possessing terrible venom" (*ghoravisa*) means having harsh venom. "Having split tongues" (*dujjivha*) means having tongues that are split in two. "By reason of terrible venom" (*ghoravisatāya*); the same method applies to the other two cases as well.
The third section, the Chapter on Long Journeys (*Dīghacārikavagga*), is concluded.
(24) 4. The Chapter on Residents (Āvāsikavagga). 1. Commentary on the Sutta of the Residents (Āvāsikasuttavaṇṇanā).

231. Regarding the first [offense] of the fourth [chapter]: "Not endowed with proper deportment" means not being endowed with the deportment of a recluse. "Is not one who should be cultivated" means he is not one who should be increased [in virtue]. The second [offense] is self-evident.
3. Commentary on the Sobhana Sutta (233).
In the third [sutta], "capable" means capable because of being endowed with both physical strength and the power of knowledge.
4. Commentary on the Bahūpakāra Sutta.

234. In the fourth [verse], "cracks and fissures" (*khaṇḍaphulla*) refers to places that have fallen apart and places that have broken. "He repairs" (*paṭisaṅkharoti*) means he restores them to their original condition. "He informs" (*āroceti*) is said with reference to families that have already invited him for a meal.
5. Commentary on the *Anukampa-sutta* (Discourse on Compassion) 235.

In the fifth [verse], "in higher virtues" (*adhisīlesu*) means in the five precepts. "He establishes in the vision of the Dhamma" (*dhammadassane niveseti*) means in the vision of the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths.
He establishes [the mind]. "Gone to the state of the Arahants" means that the Triple Gem alone has gone to that which is worthy of all honors;
the meaning is: "Establish reverence toward the Three Objects. The sixth [sutta] is self-evident. 7.
Commentary on the Second Sutta on Those Worthy of Censure.

237. Regarding the seventh [precept]: "One who is greedy for a dwelling" (*āvāsapaligedhī*) refers to one who stands as if having swallowed the dwelling through the power of intense greed. All the rest is self-evident.
The fourth chapter, the Chapter on Dwelling (*Āvāsikavagga*), is concluded.
(25) 5. The Chapter on Bad Conduct (*Duccaritavagga*).
1. Commentary on the First Discourse on Bad Conduct (Paṭhamaduccaritasuttavaṇṇanā) 241.
Regarding the first [verse] of the fifth [discourse]: "In bad conduct and good conduct"—this is stated without distinction.

"In bodily misconduct," and so forth, is stated by way of the distinction of the doors, such as the door of the body. "True Dhamma" means from the standpoint of the ten courses of wholesome kamma. "Not-true Dhamma" means...
In the unwholesome states (assaddhamma) comprised of the courses of unwholesome action (akusalakammapatha).
9. Commentary on the Sivathika Sutta: 249.

Regarding the ninth [verse], "at the cemetery" (sivathikāya) means at the charnel ground (susāna). "Weeping place" (ārodanā) means a place of lamentation. "By the impure" (asucinā) means by that which is loathsome.
10. Commentary on the Discourse on Confidence in Persons (Puggalappasādasutta) 250.

Regarding "confidence in persons" (*puggalappasāda*) in the tenth [discourse]: it refers to the confidence that has arisen toward a single person. "He seats him at the end" means he seats him at the edge of the seating area for the monks. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, the Chapter on Misconduct (*Duccaritavagga*).
The Fifth Fifty is finished. (26) 6.
The Chapter on Ordination (Upasampadāvagga). 1–3.
Commentary on the Suttas concerning those to be ordained, etc.
251–253. Regarding the first [case] of the sixth [sutta]: "one should be ordained"—meaning one should be ordained while acting as a preceptor (upajjhāya). Regarding the second:
"the dependence (nissaya) should be given"—meaning the dependence should be given while acting as a teacher (ācariya). Regarding the third:

"the novice (sāmaṇera) should be attended to"—meaning the novice should be accepted while acting as a preceptor. Thus, these three suttas also pertain to those whose taints were exhausted during the First Enlightenment.

[The preceding sections] have been explained. The fourth and subsequent [sections] are self-evident from the word-by-word commentary (*anupada-vaṇṇanā*). 1. Commentary on the Abbreviated Formulae (*peyyāla*) concerning Conventional Designations, etc. 272.
The detailed exposition regarding the designators of meals (*bhattuddesaka*) and so forth is according to the method set forth in the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
“Should be known. “One who has been appointed should not be sent” means that one who is normally appointed [to a task] should not be sent with the instruction, “Go and assign the meals.

273–285. “Receiver of the rains-bathing cloth” means the one who causes the *vassikasāṭikā* (the rainy-season bathing cloth) to be received. “Receiver of the bowl” refers to the receiver of the bowl mentioned in the passage: “And whichever bowl is the last among that assembly of monks, it should be given to that monk.
293–302. “Ājīvaka” means a naked wanderer. “Nigaṇṭha” means one whose front part [of the body] is covered. “Muṇḍa-sāvaka” means...
A *nigaṇṭha-sāvaka* is a disciple of the Jains. A *jaṭila* is an ascetic with matted hair. A *paribbājaka* is a wandering mendicant who conceals his status.

The followers of Māgandiya and others are likewise merely sectarian outsiders (*titthiya*). However, because they lack the practice of fulfilling the precepts, they are not included in the "bright side" (*sukkapaṅkha*).
The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the Pañcaka-nipāta of the Manorathapūraṇī,
the commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya, is completed.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Chapter of Sixes in the Aṅguttara Nikāya: 1.
The First Fifty Discourses (Paṭhamapaṇṇāsaka)
1. The Chapter on Those Worthy of Offerings (Āhuneyyavagga) 1. Commentary on the First Discourse on Those Worthy of Offerings (Paṭhama-āhuneyyasutta-vaṇṇanā) 1.
Regarding the phrase "In this case, monks, there are bhikkhus" at the beginning of the first discourse in the Section of Sixes (Chakkanipāta): "In this" means in this teaching, O monks.

The monk: "He is neither elated nor dejected" means that he is not elated by joy accompanied by lust toward a desirable object, nor is he dejected by grief accompanied by aversion toward an undesirable object.

"He dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending" means that he maintains a state of equanimity through the absence of non-equanimity—that is, through equanimity as ignorance—regarding a neutral object.

Without falling into [either extreme], being mindful and clearly comprehending, he dwells with equanimity toward the object. In this sutta, the constant dwelling of one whose taints are destroyed is explained.
2. Commentary on the Second Āhuneyya Sutta.
2–4. "The various kinds of supernormal power" and so forth are explained exactly as they are stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.
"Taintless through the destruction of the taints" means being taintless by means of the destruction of the taints, not through their non-existence in the manner of eye-consciousness and the rest.
In this sutta, the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) of one whose taints are destroyed are taught in succession; in the third and fourth [suttas], one whose taints are destroyed is described.
5–7. Commentary on the Triad of *Ājānīya* Suttas 5–7.

In the fifth [sutta], "by means of five factors" (*aṅgaihīti*) refers to the factors of virtue (*guṇa-aṅga*). "Patient" (*khamo*) means one who endures. "Of forms" (*rūpānaṃ*) means of objects consisting of visible forms.

"Endowed with beauty" (*vaṇṇasampanno*) means endowed with the beauty of the body. In the sixth, "endowed with strength" (*balasampanno*) means endowed with physical strength. In the seventh, "endowed with speed" (*javasampanno*) means...
Endowed with speed of foot.
8–9. Commentary on the *Anuttariya-sutta* and others. 8–9.

Regarding the eighth [sutta], "the unsurpassed" (*anuttariyāni*) means those things that are without a superior, being devoid of anything else more excellent. "The unsurpassedness of vision" (*dassanānuttariyaṃ*)...
It is the unsurpassed among the sights of forms. This same method applies to all the following terms. For the sight of the elephant-treasure and so forth is not the unsurpassed sight;

rather, for one whose faith is established, the sight of the One Possessing the Ten Powers (the Buddha), or the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus, or of any one of the kasiṇa-motifs, the foulness-motifs, and so forth, by virtue of established affection, is called the unsurpassed sight. Hearing talk of the virtues of Kṣatriyas and others is not...

The unsurpassed hearing is the hearing of the qualities of the Three Jewels or the hearing of the Buddha’s word contained in the Tipiṭaka by one who is established in faith through established affection.
The acquisition of gems, jewels, and so forth, is not the unsurpassed acquisition;
rather, the acquisition of the sevenfold noble wealth is called the unsurpassed acquisition. Training in elephant-lore and other such skills is not the unsurpassed training.
The fulfillment of the three trainings, however, is called the unsurpassed training. Service rendered to kshatriyas and others is not the unsurpassed service;
rather, service rendered to the Three Jewels is called the unsurpassed service.
Recollection of the virtues of kshatriyas and others is not the unsurpassed recollection; rather, recollection of the virtues of the Three Jewels is called the unsurpassed recollection.

Thus, these six unsurpassables (anuttariya), both mundane and supramundane, have been explained. In the ninth [section], "recollection of the Buddha" (buddhānussati) refers to mindfulness having the qualities of the Buddha as its object.
The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.
10. Commentary on the Mahānāma Sutta.
10. Mahānāma: This refers to a certain Śākya king, the son of the Blessed One’s junior father.

“He approached the Blessed One” means that, having finished his morning meal and being surrounded by his servants and retinue, he took perfumes, garlands, and other offerings and went to where the Teacher was.
“One who has attained the fruit” (*āgataphala*) means that the fruit of the Noble Ones has come to him; it means that the teaching of the three trainings has been understood by him.
"Viññātasāsano" (one who has understood the teaching). Thus, this king, asking "I ask about the dwelling-place of support for one who has entered the stream," spoke as follows.
"Nevassa rāgapariyuṭṭhitaṃ" means it was not seized by lust arising and rising up.
"Ujugataṃ" means it has gone straightly into the meditation subject of the recollection of the Buddha. "Tathāgataṃ ārabbha" means with reference to the qualities of the Tathāgata.
*Atthaveda* means the joy and gladness that arise based on the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). *Dhammaveda* means the joy and gladness that arise based on the canonical text (*pāḷi*).
*Dhammūpasañhita* means that which arises based on both the canonical text and the commentary.
*Pamuditassa* means for one who is gladdened by the two kinds of gladness. *Pīti jāyati* means that the fivefold joy is produced.
"The body becomes tranquil" means that both the mental body (*nāmakāya*) and the physical body born of karma (*karajakāya*) become tranquil through the subsiding of distress.
"Happiness" refers to bodily and mental happiness. "Becomes concentrated" means it is properly established upon the object.

"For beings who have gone astray" refers to sentient beings who have fallen into the unevenness of passion, hatred, and delusion. "Attained to evenness" means having attained equanimity and tranquility.
"With ill will" means with suffering. "Has entered the stream of the Dhamma" means he has entered the stream of the Dhamma known as insight (vipassanā).
"He develops the recollection of the Buddha" means he cultivates and increases the meditation subject of the recollection of the Buddha.
The meaning is to be understood in this manner throughout. Thus, Mahānāma asked about the dwelling-place of one who is a stream-enterer.
The Teacher spoke to him about that very same thing. Thus, in this sutta, it is the stream-enterer alone who is mentioned.
The first chapter, the Chapter on Those Worthy of Offerings, is concluded. 2. The Chapter on Kindness.
1. Commentary on the First Sāraṇīya Sutta 11.

Regarding the first [of the two], "sāraṇīya" means worthy of being remembered. "Loving bodily action" (mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ) refers to bodily action that should be performed with a mind of loving-kindness.
The same method applies to verbal and mental actions as well. And these, moreover, are for the monks...

These [actions] have come down by way of [the tradition], and they are found even among householders. For monks, the fulfillment of the duties of proper conduct (*ābhisamācārika-dhamma*) with a mind of loving-kindness is called "loving-kindness bodily action" (*metta-kāyakamma*). Among householders, it includes going for the purpose of worshipping a shrine (*cetiyavandana*), worshipping the Bodhi tree (*bodhivandana*), or inviting the Saṅgha;
and upon seeing monks who have entered a village for alms, going out to meet them, receiving their bowls, and preparing seats.
"Following after," and so forth, is called loving bodily action (*metta-kāyakamma*).

Teaching the monks the rules of conduct (*ācāra-pannatti*) with a mind of loving-kindness, speaking of meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*), teaching the Dhamma, and even the entire word of the Buddha consisting of the Three Piṭakas, is called loving verbal action (*metta-vacīkamma*). [Teaching] householders, "Let us go to pay homage at the cetiya..."
"Let us go to pay homage at the Bodhi tree; let us listen to the Dhamma; let us perform an offering of flower garlands and lamps;
let us undertake and practice the three types of good conduct; let us give tickets for meals and other offerings; let us provide the rains-retreat gifts;
today we shall provide the four requisites for the Saṅgha; having invited the Saṅgha, prepare hard foods and other provisions."
When one says such words as, “Prepare the seats, set out drinking water, go out to meet the Saṅgha and lead them here, and having seated them on the prepared seats,
perform service with a spirit of enthusiasm,” this is called verbal action of loving-kindness (*mettā-vacīkamma*).

Furthermore, when one rises early in the morning for the bhikkhus, attends to their physical needs, performs duties such as the rites at the shrine courtyard (*cetiyāṅgaṇa*), and [leads them] to a secluded seat—
Sitting down and thinking, "May the bhikkhus in this monastery be happy, free from enmity, and free from ill will," is called loving-kindness as mental action (*mettā-manokamma*).
Thinking, "May the laypeople be happy, free from enmity, and free from ill will," is called loving-kindness as mental action.
"Both openly and in private" means both in their presence and in their absence. In that regard, acting as a companion to novices in tasks such as making robes is [loving-kindness].

"Face-to-face loving bodily action" refers to such acts as washing the feet of the elders; indeed, all forms of respectful service (*sāmīcikamma*) toward them are called face-to-face loving bodily action.

"Behind one's back loving bodily action" refers to the act of putting away wooden vessels and other items that have been poorly placed by both oneself and others, doing so without showing contempt for them, as if they were one's own belongings that had been poorly placed.
Addressing them by name, saying, "The Elder Deva, the Elder Tissa," in this way, speaking words of loving-kindness in their presence is called verbal action of loving-kindness (*mettā vacīkamma*).
However, when they are not present in the monastery, asking about them and saying, "Where is our Elder Deva?
Where is our Elder Tissa? When will he return?"—such speech of endearment is loving-kindness in verbal action in their absence (*parammukhā mettā vacīkamma*).

As for the name: opening eyes that are moistened with the affection of loving-kindness (*mettā*) and looking with a serene face is called loving-kindness as mental action (*manokamma*) in the presence of another.
The mental attention, "May the Elder Deva, may the Elder Tissa, be healthy and free from illness," is called loving-kindness as mental action in the absence of another.

"Gains" refers to requisites such as robes that have been obtained. "Righteous" means those acquired through the practice of alms-gathering in accordance with the Dhamma and justice, having avoided wrong livelihoods such as hypocrisy and the like.
"At least as much as what has fallen into the bowl" means, at the very minimum, even the amount contained within the bowl, consisting of two or three spoonfuls of alms-food.

Regarding the phrase "one who shares his enjoyments without making distinctions": here, there are two kinds of distinctions—distinction regarding material things (*āmisapaṭivibhatta*) and distinction regarding individuals (*puggalapaṭivibhatta*).
Among these, "distinction regarding material things" refers to a mental differentiation such as, "I will give this much, I will not give that much.
"Distinction regarding individuals," however, refers to a mental differentiation such as, "I will give to such-and-such a person, I will not give to such-and-such a person."
[This is] the name. He who, without doing either of those two, eats what has not been apportioned is called one who eats what is unapportioned.
Regarding the phrase "one who shares enjoyments with virtuous fellow-celibates," this is the characteristic of one who shares enjoyments:
whatever excellent thing he receives, he does not seek to exchange that gain for a non-gain by means of householders.

He gives it, but does not consume it himself; and when receiving it, he takes it with the thought, "May it be common property for the Saṅgha," and having struck the gong, he consumes it while regarding it as belonging to the Saṅgha.
Now, who fulfills this duty of courtesy (*sāraṇīya-dhamma*), and who does not fulfill it? First of all, one who is immoral does not fulfill it; for indeed—
The virtuous take what belongs to him. However, one who is pure in virtue fulfills the duties without breaking them.
Herein, this is the duty: for he who gives to his mother, father, teacher, preceptor, or others after making it a specific designation, he is giving what ought to be given;
yet for him, there is no "quality of endearment" (*sāraṇīya-dhamma*), but rather it is called "tending to an impediment. This is the quality of endearment.

For one whose impediments have been removed, it is permissible. However, when distributing specifically designated portions, they should be given to the sick, those attending the sick, newcomers, those departing, and to one who has newly gone forth, provided they do not know how to take up their outer robe and bowl.
Having given these, the remainder should be distributed starting from the seat of the senior elder; rather than giving small amounts to everyone, each person should be given as much as they can take.
When nothing remains, one should go out again for alms and, starting from the seat of the senior monks, give whatever is choice to each person and eat what is left over.
Because of the words "by those who are virtuous," it is even permissible not to give to one who is immoral.
However, this *sāraṇīya-dhamma* (courteous duty) is fulfilled by a well-trained assembly; indeed, it is by a well-trained assembly that it is fulfilled.
One who receives from another does not take it; even if one does not receive from another, one takes only what is measured, not more than that.
Furthermore, this *sāraṇīya-dhamma* is fulfilled after twelve years of giving whatever is obtained by wandering for alms again and again, and not before that.
For if, in the twelfth year, the fulfiller of the *sāraṇīya-dhamma*—
Having placed his alms-bowl full of food in the sitting hall, he went to bathe. The senior monk of the Saṅgha asked, "Whose bowl is this?
When it was said, "It belongs to the one who fulfills the qualities of courtesy," the senior monk said, "Bring it here!
He then ate, having first distributed all the alms-food, and set down the empty bowl. Then that monk, seeing the empty bowl...
If he gives rise to dejection, thinking, “They consumed [the food] without leaving anything for me,” the *sāraṇīya-dhamma* is broken;
it must be fulfilled again for twelve years. For this is similar to the probation (*parivāsa*) for those of other sects (*titthiya*): once a breach has occurred, it must indeed be fulfilled anew.
However, one who thinks, “It is a gain for me, it is a great blessing for me, that what was placed in my bowl... [is not so affected].
When he generates joy thinking, “My fellow celibates are enjoying [the requisites] even without asking for permission,” that is called *puṇṇa*.
For one who has thus fulfilled the quality of being endearing, there is neither envy nor stinginess;
he is dear to human beings, dear to non-human beings, and his requisites are easily obtained. Even when what is given from his bowl is consumed, it is never exhausted.
In place of an ordinary vessel, one obtains a superior vessel; or when danger or famine arises, the deities exert themselves [to provide for one].
Here are some examples: it is said that the Elder Tissa, a resident of Senagiri, lived near Mahāgirigāma.
Fifty great elders, while traveling to Nāgadīpa to pay homage to the cetiya, went for alms in Girigāma and—
Having received nothing at all, they departed. As the Elder was entering, he saw them and asked, "Venerable sirs, did you receive anything?
"We wandered about, friend," they replied. Knowing that they had received nothing, he said, "Venerable sirs, please remain right here until I return.
"Friend, we are fifty men and have not obtained even enough to moisten our bowls. "Venerable sirs... [he continued].
"Residents" means those who are capable; even if they do not receive [alms], they know the path common to the route for alms-gathering.
The elders waited. The elder entered the village. At the very house where he was staying, a great female lay devotee had prepared milk-rice and stood watching for the elder.
As soon as the elder reached her door, she filled his bowl and gave it to him. He took it and—
Having gone into the presence of the elders, he said to the senior of the Saṅgha, "Take it, venerable sir.
The elder thought, "We so many have received nothing, yet this man has come back having already taken it; what could be the reason? He looked toward the faces of the others.
By the very manner of their looking, the elder understood and said, "Venerable sirs, it was obtained righteously and fairly; take it without any scruple."
From the very beginning, he gave as much as they required to everyone, and he himself ate as much as he required.
Then, at the conclusion of his meal, the elders asked him: "Friend, when did you penetrate the supramundane Dhamma?
"Venerable sirs, I have no supramundane Dhamma. "Friend, have you attained the jhānas? "Venerable sirs, I do not have that either."
"But, friend, is this not a marvel? "Venerable sir, I have fulfilled the duty of recollection;
from the time I fulfilled it, even if there were a hundred thousand bhikkhus, what was in my bowl would not be exhausted. "Excellent, excellent, good man! This is worthy of you.
This, first of all, is the basis for the statement: "What was in the bowl did not become exhausted."

Then this elder, having gone to the place of almsgiving for the Great Giribhaṇḍa-pūjā on Cetiyapabbata, asked, "What is the most excellent gift in this offering? "Two robes, venerable sir. "Will these reach me?
When the minister heard this, he informed the king: "A young man speaks thus. [The king said: "Such is the mind of a youth."
"But for the great elders (*mahātherā*), fine garments are permitted," he said, and thinking, "I shall give them to the great elders," he set them aside.
As he was giving them to the community of monks standing in order, although those garments were placed upon the heads of the elders, they would not come into their hands;
instead, other [garments] came into their hands. But at the time of giving to the junior monk, they came into his hand. He [placed them] in that junior monk's hand.
Setting aside the minister’s face and having the youth seated, he gave a gift, dismissed the Saṅgha, and sat down beside the youth, asking:

"Venerable sir, when did you penetrate this Dhamma? Without speaking even indirectly of what was non-existent, he replied: "Great King, I possess no supramundane Dhamma. [The king thought: "Is it not..."
“Venerable sir, you have indeed said so before. “Yes, great king, I am one who fulfills the qualities that create concord;
from the time I began fulfilling those qualities, the finest goods have come to me in the place where distributable goods are kept.
“Excellent, excellent, venerable sir! This is truly worthy of you,” he said, and then departed. This is the finest of the goods in the place where distributable goods are kept.
"Reaches [the destination]"—this is the subject matter here.
However, during the time of the danger from Brāhmaṇatissa, the inhabitants of Bhātaragāma fled without having informed the Elder Nun Anāthapiṇḍika.
At dawn, the Elder Nun said to the junior nuns, "The village is exceedingly quiet; let us investigate it first."
Having gone and learned that they had all departed, they returned and informed the elder nun.
Upon hearing this, she said, "Do not worry about their departure; apply yourselves solely to your own study, inquiry, and systematic reflection.
Then, at the time for the alms-round, she dressed herself and stood at the village gate at the foot of a banyan tree, accompanied by twelve other nuns.
The deity dwelling in the tree gave alms-food to all twelve bhikkhunīs and said, "Noble ladies, do not go elsewhere;
you should always come here. Now, the Elder had a younger brother named Nāgatthera, who thought, "There is great danger;
it is impossible to survive here. I shall go to the other shore," and set out with twelve companions.
Having departed from his own dwelling place, he came to his brother’s village thinking, “I shall go after seeing the Elder Nun.
Hearing that the Elders had arrived, the Elder Nun went into their presence and asked, “What is it, Noble Ones?
He related the circumstances to her. She said, “Stay for one day today in the monastery and depart tomorrow. The Elders went to the monastery.
On the following day, the Elder Nun, having walked for alms at the foot of a tree, approached the Elder and said, "Please partake of this alms-food.
The Elder replied, "It will suffice, Elder Nun," and remained silent. "Dhamma-faring is this alms-food, dear one;
partake of it without anxiety. "It will suffice, Elder Nun? She took the bowl.
He threw it into the air, and the bowl remained suspended in the sky.
The Elder said, "Even though it is situated at the height of seventy palm trees, this is still the meal for the bhikkhunīs, sister. Then he thought, "Fear does not exist at all times;
when fear has subsided, while I am speaking of the Noble Lineage, may I not be reproached in my mind by [the thought], 'O alms-collector, you spent your time eating the bhikkhunīs' meal!'"
“I shall not be able to steady myself; be heedful, O elder nuns,” he said, and set out on his way.
A tree deity, standing there thinking, “If the Elder eats the almsfood from the hand of the elder nun, I will not turn him back;
if he does not eat it, I will turn him back,” saw the Elder’s departure.

Having descended from the tree and said, "Venerable sir, give me your bowl," she took the bowl, led the Elder back to the foot of the tree, prepared a seat, gave him almsfood, and after he had finished his meal, obtained his promise [to stay].
For seven years, she attended upon twelve bhikkhunīs and twelve bhikkhus. This is what is meant by "the deity exerted herself."
This is the basis for the story. For in that case, the Elder Nun was one who fulfilled the qualities conducive to harmony (*sāraṇīyadhamma*).

Regarding the terms "unbroken" (*akhaṇḍa*) and so forth: if, among the seven classes of offenses, a training rule (*sikkhāpada*) has been broken at either the beginning or the end of a particular [set], one's virtue (*sīla*) is called "broken" (*khaṇḍa*), like a garment torn at its edge. However, if it has been broken in the middle, [it is called "rent," *chidda*].

For that [body], there is what is called "perforated," like a garment with holes. For one whose [bones] are broken two or three in succession, there is what is called "spotted," like a cow of a color such as black or red arising on the back or belly due to a discordant color.
For one whose [bones] are broken at intervals, there is what is called "speckled," variegated with discordant spots here and there.

It is called "stained" (*kammāsa*) like a cow that has been soiled. However, for one whose [precepts] are entirely unbroken in every respect, those virtues are called "unbroken, flawless, unblemished, and unstained.

Furthermore, because they liberate one from slavery to craving and establish one in freedom, they are "free" (*bhujissa*); and because they are praised by the wise, such as the Buddha and others, they are "praised by the wise" (*viññuppasattha*).
They are called "unadhered-to" (*aparāmaṭṭha*) because they are not adhered to by craving or views, and because it is impossible for anyone to claim, "You have previously fallen into this.
They are called "conducive to concentration" (*samādhisaṃvattanika*) because they lead to access concentration (*upacārasamādhi*) or absorption concentration (*appanāsamādhi*).
"He dwells having attained the commonality of virtue" means that his virtue has reached a state of equality with those monks dwelling in various regions.

He dwells. For the virtue of those who have entered the stream (sotāpanna) and so forth remains exactly the same as the virtue of other stream-enterers and so forth, even when they dwell in the midst of the ocean or in the world of the devas;
there is no difference in the virtue of the Path (maggasīla). It is with reference to this that it was said:
"This view" refers to right view associated with the Path. "Noble" means faultless. "Leads out" means it is conducive to deliverance (niyyānika).
"Of one who acts thus" means of one who acts accordingly. "For the destruction of suffering" means for the purpose of the destruction of all suffering.
"Having attained the commonality of view" means having entered into a state of shared view, he dwells [therein].
2. Commentary on the Second Sāraṇīya Sutta.

12. In the second [verse], those qualities which one fulfills cause one to be dear to one’s fellow practitioners; thus they are called "endearing" (*piyakaraṇā*). They cause one to be respected; thus they are called "respect-inspiring" (*garukaraṇā*).
"For the sake of gathering" (*saṅgahāya*) means for the purpose of bringing together. "For the sake of non-dispute" (*avivādāya*) means for the purpose of avoiding contention.

"For the sake of concord" (*sāmaggiyā*) means for the purpose of being in harmony. "For the sake of unity" (*ekībhāvāya*) means for the purpose of oneness, for the purpose of making no distinction. "They conduce to" (*saṃvattanti*) means...
They proceed; they continue. 3.
Commentary on the Discourse on Emancipation (Nissāraṇīyasutta). 13.
In the third [discourse], "the elements of emancipation" refers precisely to the elements of escape. For my liberation of mind is loving-kindness (mettā).
Here, loving-kindness consisting of the threefold and fourfold jhānas is called "liberation of mind through loving-kindness" because it is liberated from opposing states.
"Developed" means increased. "Cultivated" means done repeatedly. "Made a vehicle" means made like a well-yoked carriage.
"Made a foundation" means established as a base. "Steadfast" means resolved upon. "Fully consolidated" means gathered and heaped up on all sides.
“Accumulated”: well undertaken through the performance of excellent qualities. “It remains having exhausted [them]”: it remains having consumed and grasped them.
“He should be told: ‘Do not speak thus’”: because he explains what has not occurred as an explanation, therefore he should be told, “Do not speak in this way.
“That is to say, the liberation of mind through loving-kindness”: that which is this liberation of mind through loving-kindness.

This is the escape from ill will; the meaning is that it is escaped from ill will. However, for one who has emerged from the third or fourth jhāna of loving-kindness, comprehended formations, attained the third path, and sees Nibbāna through the third fruit, thinking "ill will exists no more," his mind is the absolute escape from ill will.
By this same method, the meaning should be understood in all cases.

"Signless liberation of mind" (*animittā-cetovimutti*) refers to powerful insight (*balava-vipassanā*). However, the Dīgha reciters say it is the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship (*arahatta-phala-samāpatti*);
for that is called "signless" because of the absence of the signs of lust and so forth, as well as the signs of form and so forth, and the signs of permanence and so forth.
"One who follows the sign" (*nimittānusārī*) means one whose nature is to follow the various types of signs already mentioned.
"I am" is the conceit "I am. "This I am" means: among the five aggregates, "this one named 'I' am.
To this extent, the state of an Arhat is declared. "The dart of doubt and perplexity" means the dart of doubt and perplexity that has become doubt itself.
"He should be told: 'Do not speak thus'" means: if doubt to be abandoned by the first path arises in you, [then] the declaration of Arhatship—
It is false; therefore, one should be restrained by saying, "Do not grasp what is unreal. "The uprooting of the conceit 'I am'" refers to the path of arahantship.
For when Nibbāna is seen through the fruit of the path of arahantship, the conceit "I am" no longer exists;
thus, the path of arahantship is called "the uprooting of the conceit 'I am'. Thus, in this sutta, that which is called "false declaration" is explained.
4. Commentary on the Bhaddakasutta 14.
In the fourth [verse], "not auspicious" (*na bhaddaka*) means not favorable.
In that regard, for one who dies in a state of extreme terror, death is not auspicious; for one who takes rebirth in the woeful states (*apāya*), the passing away is not auspicious.
It exists. Regarding the terms *kammārāma* and so forth: *āramaṇaṃ* means *ārāmo*; the meaning is "delight.
One who has a *ārāma*—that is, a work-project—such as the construction of a monastery, is a *kammārāma*. One who delights (*rato*) in that very work is a *kammarata*.

One who is devotedly engaged (*anuyutto*) in that same state of delighting in work (*kammārāmata*) again and again is one who is "devoted. This method applies everywhere. And here, *bhassa* refers to conversation and discussion; *niddā* refers to sleep.
“Congregation” (*saṅgaṇikā*) means the congregation of a group. It should be understood in such a manner as: “one has a second, two have a third,” and so forth.
“Association” (*saṃsagga*) is the state of being closely associated that occurs by way of seeing, hearing, conversation, sharing enjoyments, and physical contact.
“Proliferation” (*papañca*) is the proliferation of defilements established in the form of intoxication, occurring by way of craving, views, and conceit.

"Sakkāya" refers to the cycle of existence within the three realms. "For the sake of making a complete end to suffering" means for the purpose of establishing the boundary and limit of the entire suffering of the cycle through the method of its cause.
"The path" (magga) is like a path. "In the state free from proliferation" (nippapañca-pada) means in the state of Nibbāna.
"He accomplished" (ārādhayi) means he fulfilled it; he brought it to completion.
5. Commentary on the *Anutappiya Sutta* (Sutta 15):

"To be regretted" (*anutappiya*) means that which should be mourned over, causing remorse. In both of these suttas and their verses, the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*) are explained.
6. Commentary on the *Nakulapitu Sutta* (Sutta 16)

16. In the sixth [case], "severely ill" means extremely ill. "She said this": being unable to cure the illness after preparing medicine for her husband, she now sat down nearby, uttered a "lion's roar," and performed an act of truth (*saccakiriya*) to cure the illness, saying these words beginning with, "May you not...
"Full of longing" means possessed of craving. "Not Nakulamātā" [is the name].
Here, the word *na* (not) cannot [be applied directly]; thus it must be construed with the following word.

"To spread" (*santharituṃ*) means to make without holes; the meaning is "to arrange. "To comb out the braid" (*veṇiṃ olikhituṃ*) means, having clipped the sheep's wool and disentangled it, to form a braid.
"She will go to another house" (*aññaṃ gharaṃ gamissati*) means she will take another husband. "The household celibacy for sixteen years" (*gahaṭṭhakaṃ brahmacariyaṃ*).
"Samāciṇṇaṃ" means that for sixteen years from this point, his residence in the household life while practicing the holy life (brahmacariya) was customary.

"Dassanakāmatarā" means those who more intensely desire to see him. Having let out a lion's roar with these three factors, he performed an act of truth (saccakiriya), saying: "By this truth, may the illness in your body be relieved."

Now, having made the Blessed One his witness, he spoke the words beginning with "It may be that for you... in order to perform an act of truth (*saccakiriya*) by means of his own qualities such as virtue (*sīla*).

In this context, "one who fulfills" (*paripūrakārinī*) means one who practices completely. "Of mental tranquility" (*cetosamathassa*) refers to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) of concentration (*samādhi*).

"One who has reached a foothold" (*ogādhappattā*) means one who has attained entry into a foothold (*ogādha*). "One who has reached a firm standing" (*patigādhappattā*) means one who has attained a firm footing (*patiṭṭha*).
"Attained. "Attained to consolation" means attained to reassurance (*assāsa*), that is, to a place of refuge. "Attained to fearlessness" means attained to the knowledge of joy (*somanassa-ñāṇa*).
"Not dependent on others": "dependence on others" refers to faith in another or reliance on another; the meaning is that she was devoid of such [dependence].
With these three factors, she performed an act of truth (*saccakiriya*) concerning her own virtues. "Recovered from illness."
Having been ill, he has recovered. "As many as" means however many there are. "One among them" means one from within that group.

"Compassionate" means compassionate toward their welfare. "Exhorter" means one who gives exhortation. "Instructor" means one who gives instruction. 7. Commentary on the *Soppasutta* (The Discourse on Sleeping).

17. "In the seventh [case], 'emerged from seclusion' means emerged from the state of reflecting on the Dhamma for the sake of solitude, and from the dwelling in the attainment of the fruit (*phalasamāpatti*).
'To their respective dwellings' means to the dwelling where each of them lived. 'Nine' refers to those who were new to the going-forth; they numbered five hundred.
