'Chattering like crows' means making the sound of crows while gnashing their teeth. 'The Elders'..."
They have attained stability. "Tena nu" means "by that indeed. *Seyyasukha* and so forth have their meanings already explained in the preceding section.
A *raṭṭhika* is one who enjoys a kingdom. A *pettaṇika* is one who enjoys what was enjoyed and used by his father.
A *senāpati* is the leader of an army. A *gāmagāmaṇika* is the ruler of a village. A *pūgagāmaṇika* is the leader of a group. One who lacks insight (*avipassaka*).
"Of wholesome states" means being one who does not seek after or search for wholesome states.
"Of the states conducive to enlightenment" means of the thirty-seven states conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*).
8. Commentary on the Fisherman’s Sutta (*Macchabandhasutta-vannanā*)
18. In the eighth [verse], *macchika* means a fish-killer. *Hatthiyāyī* means one who travels by elephant;
the same applies to the following terms as well. *Vajjhe* means those to be killed. *Vadhāyūpanīte* means brought forward for execution. *Pāpakena manasā* means with a base, murderous mind.
In the canonical text (*pāḷi*), however, it is written as *vadhāyupanīte*. *Māgaviko* means a deer-killer. Who?
As for the phrase "let alone one who has become human": if even one who has become human and harbors an evil mind toward another fails to attain prosperity, what need is there to speak of others?
This was said to demonstrate that such an evil deed results in an undesirable fruit.
However, as for those who, despite performing such a deed, still obtain fame, that [fame] is due to [other factors] supported by that unwholesome action.
It should be understood that the wholesome ripens; however, because it has been impaired by that unwholesome kamma, its fruition does not endure for long.
In this sutta, only the side of the unwholesome is discussed.
9. Commentary on the First Discourse on Mindfulness of Death.
19. In the village named Nādikā; in the Giñjakāvasatha, that is, in the brick hall.
*Amatogadhā* means plunged into the Deathless (*nibbāna*), having Nibbāna as their foundation—this is the meaning. *Bhāvetha no* means "should you cultivate?
*Maraṇassati* is the meditation subject of mindfulness of death. *Aho vata* is a particle used in the sense of aspiration. "Ah, may much indeed have been accomplished by me!"
Much would have been accomplished by me in your teaching. "In that interval" means that interval, moment, or opportunity.
Regarding the phrase "having inhaled, I shall exhale": here, inhalation (*assāsa*) refers to the air entering within, while exhalation (*passāsa*) refers to the air exiting outward.
Thus, this bhikkhu [observes] from the time the air that has entered within exits outward, until the air that has exited outward enters within.
As he was entering, wishing for life, he spoke thus. "Slowly" means sluggishly, heavily, not proceeding quickly.
"For the destruction of the taints" means for the sake of the fruit of arahantship. In this sutta, mindfulness of death is explained as having been brought to the attainment of arahantship.
10. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Mindfulness of Death (*Dutiyamaraṇassatisutta-vaṇṇanā*)
20. "In the tenth [chapter], 'having entered upon' means having practiced. 'Thus he reflects' means he reviews it in this way.

'It would be an obstacle for me'—here, the obstacle is threefold: an obstacle to life, an obstacle to the ascetic’s duty (samaṇadhamma), and for one who dies as an ordinary person (puthujjana), an obstacle to heaven and an obstacle to the Path. He said this with reference to all of these. 'It might cause affliction'..."
It might fail due to indigestion and so forth. "Excessive" (*adhimatta*) means powerful. "Zeal" (*chanda*) is the desire to act.
"Effort" (*vāyāma*) is the energy of application. "Exertion" (*ussāha*) is the energy of uplifting. "Striving" (*ussoḷhi*) is the energy of accomplishment.
"Unyielding" (*appaṭivāni*) means lack of weariness and lack of turning back. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
The Second Chapter: On Recollections.
3. The Chapter on the Unsurpassed. 1–2.
Commentary on the Sāmaṅka Sutta and others.
21–22. In the first [case], "in the village of Sāmagāma" means in the village so named because of the abundance of *sāmaka* grass.

"In the lotus pond" means in the monastery named after the lotus pond (*pokkharaṇī*). "When the night had advanced" means when the first watch of the night had passed and the middle watch had arrived.
"Of surpassing beauty" means of exceedingly lovely and pleasing appearance. "The whole extent" means...
"For an entire eon. "Having illuminated the lotus pond" means having pervaded the great monastery named Pokkharani with one's own radiance.

"In agreement" means having a similar inclination and a similar mind. "Difficult speech" (dovacassatā) is the state of being hard to speak to. "Bad friendship" (pāpamittatā) is the state of having inferior friends.
In this sutta, only the factors of decline are mentioned; in the second [sutta], the factors of non-decline are [mentioned].
These are explained as being mixed with the supramundane.
3. Commentary on the Bhaya Sutta. 23.
In the third [verse], *kāmarāgarattāyaṃ* means "this one is stained by sensual lust. *Chandarāgavinibaddho* means "bound by desire and lust."
"Bound. "Fear" refers to the fear of mental terror. "Mire" refers to the mire of the defilements (*kleśa*).
"Both attachment and mire"—both this attachment and this mire are what is meant by "both. These are called "sensual pleasures" (*kāma*), wherein the ordinary person (*puthujjana*) is stuck;
that is, in which attachment and mire the ordinary person is stuck, clung to, and obstructed. "Grasping" refers to the fourfold [grasping].
Regarding "clinging": "in the arising of birth and death" means in the presence of birth and death as conditions for their occurrence.
"Being liberated through non-clinging" means being liberated without clinging. "In the destruction of birth and death" means in Nibbāna, which is designated as the destruction of birth and death;
the meaning is that they are liberated by means of liberation having Nibbāna as its object. At this point, having turned away [from the round of existence]...
This bhikkhu has indeed attained arahantship. Now, in order to praise him as one whose taints are destroyed, the Blessed One spoke the verse beginning with "They have attained security.
In that context, "they have attained security" means they have reached a state of safety. "Happy" means they are made happy by supramundane happiness.
"Extinguished in this very life" means they are extinguished right here and now due to the absence of defilements within. Having explained only the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) in this sutta...
In the verses, the closing and opening [of the cycle] are explained.
4. Commentary on the Himavanta Sutta: 24.
In the fourth [verse], "he would split" means he would break. "Chavāya" means by one who is wretched. One who is skilled in the attainment of concentration...
"He becomes skilled" means that, having discerned suitable food and a suitable climate, he is dexterous, capable, competent, and able to enter into concentration (*samādhi*).
"Skilled in the maintenance of concentration" means skilled in the stability of concentration;
the meaning is that he is able to sustain concentration. "Skilled in emerging from concentration" means skilled in the emergence from concentration.
The meaning is that one is able to emerge according to the specific determination [of the object].
"Skilled in making concentration pliant" means skilled in the pliancy of concentration; the meaning is that one is able to make the mind of concentration fit and capable.
"Skilled in the range of concentration" means having avoided those states that are unsuitable and unhelpful for concentration, [one is skilled] in those that are suitable and helpful...
Even while practicing, one who knows, "This has the sign of concentration as its object;

this has the characteristic as its object," is called skilled in the range of concentration. One who is skilled in the directing of concentration is called skilled in the directing of concentration because he is able to direct the concentration of the first jhāna and so forth for the purpose of attaining higher and higher attainments.
Thus, having emerged from the first jhāna, he enters the second; from the second jhāna... [and so on] ...having emerged from the third jhāna, he enters the fourth.
5. Commentary on the Discourse on the Bases of Mindfulness (Anussatiṭṭhānasutta)

25. “The five subjects of recollection” (*pañca anussatiṭṭhānāni*) means the bases for recollection. “‘Such indeed is the Blessed One’ and so forth” have already been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.
“Having made this, monks, a supporting object” means having made this meditation subject of recollecting the Buddha (*buddhānussati-kammaṭṭhāna*) a supporting object.
“They are purified” means they reach supreme purification, which is Nibbāna. The rest is the same everywhere.
The meaning is exactly as stated above. However, it should be understood that in this sutta, the six bases for recollection (*anussati-ṭṭhāna*) are taught in a combined manner.
6. Commentary on the Mahākaccāna Sutta 26.

In the sixth [verse], "in confinement" (*sambādhe*) means in the confinement of the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*). Regarding "attainment of space" (*okāsādhigama*): here, "spaces" (*okāsa*) are so called...
The six bases of recollection; their attainment. For the sake of purification means for the purpose of becoming purified.
For the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation means for the purpose of transcending both sorrow and lamentation. For the subsiding [of suffering] means for the purpose of its passing away.
For the attainment of the method means for the purpose of attaining the path together with insight.
"For the realization of Nibbāna" means for the purpose of directly experiencing the unconditioned final Nibbāna (*apaccaya-parinibbāna*).
"In every way" means in all its modes. "Equal to space" means similar to space in the sense of being unattached and in the sense of being unobstructed.
"Vast" means not limited. "Exalted" means having attained greatness, or [shared] by great noble disciples (*ariyasāvaka*).
"By one who has gone, by one who has practiced"—this is the meaning. "Immeasurable" means immeasurable by way of its pervasiveness.

"Harmless" means free from unwholesome enmity and from persons who are enemies. "Free from ill will" means devoid of anger and suffering. All of this is stated with reference specifically to the mind of recollection of the Buddha.
The same method applies further on as well. "Phenomena of purification" means those whose intrinsic nature is to be purified. In this [context] too...
In the Sutta, the six subjects of recollection are taught as being mixed together.
7. Commentary on the First Samaya Sutta:

Regarding the seventh [sutta], "of one who is mind-developing" (*manobhāvanīya*): here, one who develops (*bhāveti*) or increases the mind (*mana*) is called "mind-developing. "For the sake of seeing" (*dassanāya*).

"For the purpose of seeing" means for the sake of vision. "Escape" means departure and pacification. "He teaches the Dhamma" means he explains the meditation subject of foulness (*asubha-kammaṭṭhāna*) for the purpose of abandoning sensual lust.

In the second section and those following, [he teaches] the meditation subject of loving-kindness (*mettā-kammaṭṭhāna*) for the abandonment of ill-will; the meditation subject for dispelling sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha-vinodana-kammaṭṭhāna*) for the abandonment of sloth and torpor;
or else the perception of light (*ālokasaññā*), or one of the bases for arousing energy (*vīriyārambhavatthu*), and so forth.

It should be understood that he teaches the Dhamma while speaking on the theme of the qualities of the Three Jewels for the abandoning of restlessness and remorse, and for the abandoning of doubt. "Having approached" (āgamma) means having taken as a basis.

"Attends to" (manasikaroto) means for one who applies it to the mind by way of an object. "Immediately thereafter there is the destruction of the taints" (anantarā āsavānaṃ khayo hoti) means that the destruction of the taints occurs without interval.
8. Commentary on the Second Samaya Sutta 28.
In the eighth [sutta], "in the maṇḍalamāḷa" means in the dining hall. "Fatigue from wandering" refers to the fatigue arising from going for alms.
"Fatigue from food" refers to the distress caused by eating. "In the shade of the monastery" means in the shade at the edge of the monastery. Whatever of his...

"The sign of concentration has been attended to during the day" means that very same sign of serenity (*samatha-nimitta*) which was previously made the object of his mind during the earlier part of the day.
"That alone manifests for him at that time" means that at that moment, while he is sitting during his midday rest, that very same sign moves within his mind-door (*manodvāra*).
"Abiding in nutritive essence" (*ojaṭṭhāyī*) means established and firmly grounded in nutritive essence (*ojā*). Of one who is at ease...
"It becomes comfortable" means it becomes pleasant for him. "In his presence" means in the place where he is speaking.
"Hearing" means heard by the ear. "Accepted" means accepted by the mind.
9. Udāyīsutta Commentary.
29. Regarding the ninth [discourse], concerning the Elder Lāḷudāyin: "I hear, friend," he said; "Friend, I am not deaf;
I hear the Blessed One’s words, but I am examining the question. "The higher mind" refers to the mind of concentration (*samādhi*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
"This, venerable sir, is a basis for recollection" means this cause for recollection, which consists of the three meditative absorptions (*jhāna*). For dwelling in happiness in this very life...
"It conduces" means it proceeds for the sake of dwelling in happiness within this very selfhood (*attabhāva*).
"Perception of light" is the perception arisen regarding the sign of light. "He resolves on the perception of day" means he establishes the perception of "day.
"As by day, so by night": just as the perception of light was attended to by him during the day, he attends to it in the same way at night; and as by night...
"Likewise by day" means that just as the perception of light was attended to by him during the night, he attends to it in the same way during the day.
"Open" means manifest. "Unshrouded" means unenveloped by the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
"He develops a luminous mind" means that for the sake of the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*), he cultivates and increases a mind accompanied by light. That which...
However, when it is said, "he attends to the perception of light," that should be understood as referring to the perception of light for the purpose of dispelling sloth and torpor,
not to the light of the knowledge of the divine eye. "For the attainment of knowledge and vision" means for the attainment of the knowledge and vision known as the divine eye.

Whatever needs to be said regarding the passage beginning with "this very body," all of that has been stated in full detail in the *Visuddhimagga* within the section on the meditation subject of mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*).
"For the abandoning of lust for sensual pleasures" means for the purpose of abandoning the lust associated with the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).
"As if he were to see" means as though he were seeing. "A corpse" means a dead body. "Cast away in a charnel ground" means...
Cast away in a charnel ground. That which has been dead for one day is "one-day-dead" (*ekāhamata*). That which has been dead for two days is "two-day-dead" (*dvīhamata*).

That which has been dead for three days is "three-day-dead" (*tīhamata*). Like a bellows filled with air, because it has become bloated by the gradual emergence of putrefaction following the exhaustion of life, it is "bloated" (*uddhumāta*);
being bloated, it is "the bloated" (*uddhumātaka*). Because of its repulsiveness...
Or, it is called *uddhumātaka* because it is loathsome and bloated. *Vinīla* refers to that which has changed color; *vinīlaka* is simply *vinīla*.
Or, it is called *vinīlaka* because it is loathsome due to its repulsiveness and its bluish-black color. In the places where the flesh has protruded, there is a red color;
in the places where pus has accumulated, there is a white color; and for the most part, there is a blue-black color—like one draped in a blue garment over the blue parts.
This is a designation for the physical body. Pus that is oozing from nine places of decomposition or from the openings of wounds is "putrid";
it is "putrefied" (vipubbaka) because it has become putrid. Alternatively, it is "putrid" (vipubbaka) because it is loathsome and foul-smelling.
That which has become putrid, having reached such a state, is "become putrid" (vipubbakajāta).
"Thus, with regard to this very body": that bhikkhu brings this body of his into comparison and aligns it with that [other] body by means of knowledge.
How? "This body, too, is of such a nature, of such a character, and not exempt from such a fate. This is what is meant:
through the presence of these three factors—vitality, heat, and consciousness—this body is capable of standing, walking, and so forth.
"But with the disappearance of these [factors], this too is of such a nature, of such a putrid essence.

"It will become thus" means it will become exactly so, characterized by the various stages such as bloating (*uddhumātaka*). "Not having passed beyond this state" means not having transcended the state of bloating and so forth.
"Being devoured" means sitting upon the belly and other parts, repeatedly tearing away the flesh of the belly, the flesh of the lips, the flesh of the eyes, and so on.
“Being eaten”: “with flesh and blood remaining” means it is still joined with some residual flesh and blood. “Smeared with blood though devoid of flesh”:
even when the flesh has been consumed, the blood does not dry up; it is with reference to this that it is said, “smeared with blood though devoid of flesh.
“By another”: by another direction or part. “A hand-bone”: the sixty-four types of bones in the hand are each counted individually.
Scattered individually. The same method applies to foot-bones and so forth. "More than a year old" means having passed a full year.
"Putrid" means that those kept in the open air become putrid after just more than a year due to contact with wind, heat, and rain;
however, those buried underground remain for a longer time. "Reduced to powder" means having become crumbled and scattered into dust.
In all instances, the application should be made according to the method stated as "he [perceives] this very [body] being devoured," and so forth.
"For the uprooting of the conceit 'I am'" means for the purpose of uprooting the ninefold conceit that occurs as "I am.

"For the penetration of the various elements" means for the purpose of penetrating the various elements. "Mindful he advances" means that while walking, he is indeed endowed with mindfulness and wisdom.
"He goes. "Mindful he returns" means that even when turning back, he returns endowed with mindfulness and wisdom (*sati-paññā*).

The same principle applies to the remaining phrases as well. "For the sake of mindfulness and clear comprehension" (*satisampajaññāya*) means for the purpose of both mindfulness and knowledge (*ñāṇa*).
Thus, in this sutta, mindfulness and knowledge are taught in combination.
10. Commentary on the *Anuttariya Sutta* (30).
In the tenth [sutta], "high and low" (*uccāvacam*) means whatever is great or small, or high and low. "Inferior" (*hīnam*) means base.
"Vulgar" (*gāmam*) means the view of village-dwellers. "Of the common folk" (*pothujjanikam*) means belonging to ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*). "Unnoble" (*anariyam*)...
It is not noble, not supreme, and not utterly pure. "Not connected with the goal" means it is not dependent upon the goal.

"Not for disenchantment" means not for the purpose of becoming disenchanted with the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*). "Not for dispassion" means not for the purpose of the fading away of lust and the other defilements.

"Not for cessation" means not for the cessation that is the non-arising of lust and the other defilements. "Not for peace" means not for the purpose of the subsiding of lust and the other defilements. Not...

"Abhiññāya" means not for the sake of higher knowledge (*abhijānanatthāya*). "Na sambodhāya" means not for the sake of penetrating the knowledge of the four paths, which is designated as "awakening" (*sambodhi*).
"Na nibbānāya" means not for the realization of *nibbāna*.
"Niviṭṭhasaddho" means one whose faith is established. "Niviṭṭhapemo" means one whose affection is established. "Ekantagato" means having gone to the absolute end.
"Gone" means having attained immovability (*acala*). "Deeply confident" means exceedingly serene.
"This is unsurpassed" means this is the supreme. "He trains in elephant-riding" means he trains in the art of elephants, that which is to be trained in for the sake of the elephant-sign.
The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. "High and low" means he trains in crafts both great and small.
"Attentive to service" means established in service. "They develop mindfulness" means they develop supreme mindfulness.
"Connected with seclusion" means having made it dependent on Nibbāna. "Secure" means free from danger.
"Leading to the Deathless" means leading to Nibbāna; the meaning is that they develop the Noble Path. "Rejoicing in heedfulness."
They are delighted and rejoiced in heedfulness, which is defined as non-separation from mindfulness. "Vigilant" means endowed with circumspection (*nepakka*).
"Restrained by virtue" means restrained and shielded by virtue. "They indeed understand at the proper time" means they know when the time has come for application.
"Where suffering ceases" means in that place where the entire suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*) comes to an end.
Those bhikkhus know that deathless, great Nibbāna. In this sutta, the six kinds of unsurpassed excellence (*anuttariya*) are taught in combination.
This concludes the third chapter, the Chapter on the Unsurpassed Excellence.
4. The Chapter on Devas.
1. Commentary on the Sekha Sutta (31).

Regarding the first [sutta], "of one in training" (*sekhassa*) refers to the sevenfold person in training (*sekha*). As for the worldling (*puthujjana*), there is simply nothing to be said. "For the sake of decline" (*parihānāya*) means for the sake of declining from higher and higher qualities.
2–3. Commentary on the Two Suttas on Non-decline.

32–33. Regarding "veneration for the Teacher" (*satthugāravatā*): it is the state of regarding the Teacher with reverence. Regarding "veneration for the Dhamma" (*dhammagāravatā*): it is the state of regarding the ninefold supramundane Dhamma (*lokuttaradhamma*) with reverence.

Regarding "veneration for the Saṅgha" (*saṅghagāravatā*): it is the state of regarding the Saṅgha with reverence. Regarding "veneration for the training" (*sikkhāgāravatā*): it is the state of regarding the three trainings (*tisso sikkhā*) with reverence.

Regarding "veneration for heedfulness" (*appamādagāravatā*): it is the state of regarding heedfulness (*appamāda*) with reverence. Regarding "veneration for hospitality" (*paṭisanthāragāravatā*): [it is the state of regarding] the two kinds [of hospitality], namely, that consisting of the Dhamma and that consisting of material goods (*āmisa*).

"Veneration in hospitality" means having a sense of reverence toward hospitality. "One who venerates the Teacher" means one for whom the Teacher is revered. "One who venerates the Dhamma" means one for whom the Dhamma is revered. "One of intense veneration" means one whose veneration is profound.

"One who has veneration for hospitality" means one who possesses veneration toward hospitality. In the third [verse], "one who is deferential" means one who is respectful and reverent toward those who are senior.
However, in this context, shame (*hiri*) and fear of wrongdoing (*ottappa*) are spoken of as combined.
4. Commentary on the Mahāmoggallāna Sutta 34.
In the fourth [sutta], "The monk named Tissa" refers to the Elder’s own pupil (saddhivihārika).

"Possessed of great psychic power and great majesty": he is called *mahiddhika* because he possesses great psychic power (*iddhi*) in the sense of success (*ijjhana*). He is called *mahānubhāva* because he possesses great majesty (*ānubhāva*) in the sense of radiating influence (*anupharaṇa*).
"Of great power. "It has been a long time, dear Moggallāna, since you made use of such an occasion"—this is a form of naturally affectionate address used in the world.
For when worldly people see someone of a pleasing kind who has arrived after a long absence, even if they have never met before, they say:
"Whence have you come? It has been a long time since you came; how was your journey here?"
“[He is] well-known; why are you lost as to the path? and so forth—others say this.
But he spoke thus because he had previously come here. For the Elder indeed goes to the Brahma-world from time to time. “He made an occasion there” means he made his turn.
“Namely, for the sake of coming here” means that he made long awaited the turn for coming here. “This seat... [is provided].
"Having prepared" means having prepared a very costly Brahmā-couch; he spoke thus. "With verified confidence" means with the unshakable confidence in the Path that has been attained.
In this sutta, the knowledge of the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga-ñāṇa*) is explained.
5. Commentary on the *Vijjābhāgiya-sutta*.

35. "Conducive to true knowledge" (*vijjābhāgiya*) means belonging to the category of true knowledge. "Perception of impermanence" (*aniccasaññā*) is the perception arisen in the knowledge of the contemplation of impermanence.

"Perception of suffering in the impermanent" (*anicce dukkhasaññā*) is the perception arisen in the knowledge of the contemplation of suffering. "Perception of non-self in what is suffering" (*dukkhe anattasaññā*) is the perception arisen in the knowledge of the contemplation of non-self.

"Perception of abandoning" (*pahānasaññā*) is the perception arisen in the knowledge of the contemplation of abandoning. "Perception of dispassion" (*virāgasaññā*) is [the perception arisen] in the knowledge of the contemplation of dispassion.
"Perception arisen. "Perception of cessation" refers to the perception arisen in the knowledge of the contemplation of cessation.
6. Commentary on the *Vivādamūla Sutta* (Discourse on the Roots of Dispute).
36. In the sixth [sutta], "roots of dispute" means the roots of dispute. "One who is angry" refers to one characterized by anger, which has the characteristic of being prone to wrath.
"Endowed with. "Malicious" means endowed with malice (*upanāha*), which is characterized by the failure to relinquish enmity.
Regarding the phrase "for the harm and suffering of gods and humans": how does a dispute between two monks lead to the harm and suffering of gods and humans?
As in the *Kosambaka-kkhandhaka*, when two monks have fallen into a dispute, in that situation—
In the monastery, their resident pupils quarrel; receiving their instruction, the community of nuns quarrels.
Consequently, their lay supporters quarrel, and then the protective deities of the people split into two factions.

Likewise, the protective deities of those who speak according to the Dhamma become speakers of the Dhamma, while those of those who speak contrary to the Dhamma become speakers contrary to the Dhamma.
Then the earth-deities, who were friends of the protective deities, break away.
In this manner, by successive stages up to the Brahma-world, all gods and humans—excluding the noble disciples (ariyasāvaka)—fall into two factions.

However, those who speak according to the Dhamma are fewer, while those who speak contrary to the Dhamma are more numerous. Consequently, they go over to whichever side is taken by the majority. Having abandoned the Dhamma, they indeed become the majority.
They grasp at what is non-Dhamma. Dwelling with non-Dhamma as their priority, they are reborn in the states of deprivation.
Thus, the dispute between two monks leads to the harm and suffering of both gods and humans. "Internally" means within your own assembly;
"externally" means in the assembly of others.

*Makkhī* means one possessed of *makkha*, which has the characteristic of smearing over the virtues of others. *Paḷāsī* means one possessed of *paḷāsa*, which has the characteristic of grasping with both hands [at what belongs to oneself].
*Issukī* means one possessed of *issā*, which has the characteristic of envying the honor and so forth of others.

*Maccharī* means one possessed of the five kinds of stinginess, such as the stinginess regarding dwelling places (*āvāsamacchariya*). *Saṭho* means a deceiver (*kerāṭiko*). *Māyāvī* means one who conceals what has been done.

"One of evil desires" (*pāpiccha*) means one who is immoral and seeks honor for what he does not possess. "One of wrong view" (*micchādiṭṭhi*) refers to a nihilist, a proponent of causelessness, or a proponent of non-action.
"One who clings to his own views" (*sandiṭṭhiparāmāsī*) means one who clings only to what he himself has seen. "One who holds firmly" (*ādhānaggāhī*) means one who grasps tenaciously.
"One who is difficult to release" (*duppaṭinissaggī*) means it is impossible to make him relinquish what he has grasped. In this sutta, only the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is discussed.
7. Commentary on the Dānasutta 37.
Regarding the seventh [verse]: "Veḷukaṇḍakī" means a resident of the city of Veḷukaṇḍaka. "Endowed with six factors" means endowed with six qualities as constituent parts.
"He establishes a sacrificial gift" means he gives a gift. "Before giving, he is glad" means [he thinks], "I shall give a gift."
From the half-month or month [prior to the giving], he becomes filled with joy.

For in this context, "prior volition" (pubba-cetanā) is obtained for one who thinks, starting from the moment the thought arises, "I will give," and beginning with the selection of the field [of merit], thinking, "I will give a gift from what has been produced here.
However, the "volition of relinquishment" (muñca-cetanā), described as "while giving, he gladdens the mind," is obtained only at the very time of giving. Having given...
"He is gladdened" refers to a subsequent volition that arises in one who recollects [the qualities] again and again.

"Those free from lust" means those whose lust has departed, the ones whose taints are destroyed. Or, "those practicing for the removal of lust" means those practicing the path leading to the removal of lust.
This is a teaching given in its highest sense; however, it applies not only to those whose taints are destroyed, but also to non-returners, once-returners, and stream-enterers.
Even a gift given to a novice monk who has merely taken charge of the requisites on the day he went forth possesses all six factors.
For he too has gone forth for the very purpose of attaining the path of stream-entry.
"The perfection of the sacrifice" means the completeness of the giving. "Self-restrained" means restrained by the restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃyama*). "Having rinsed one's own mouth" means...
Having washed his own hands and feet and rinsed his mouth; "with his own hands" means with his own hands (the reading *sayehi* is also found).
"Faithful" means one who has faith in the qualities of the Triple Gem. "With a mind liberated" means with a mind freed from avarice regarding gain and other such defilements.
"The blissful world free from affliction" refers to the celestial realm (*devaloka*), which is devoid of suffering and abounds in sublime happiness and joy.
8. Commentary on the Attakārīsutta 38.
Regarding the eighth [case]: "I saw" or "I heard"—do not say, "I did not see," having opened my eyes;
do not say, "I did not hear that he dwells in such-and-such a place"; or do not say, "I did not hear the words of one who was speaking. "How indeed could this be? means by what [reason]?
It is by way of its name as a cause. The "element of initiative" (*ārambha-dhātu*) is energy that functions by way of undertaking.

The "element of exertion" (*nikkama-dhātu*) is energy whose intrinsic nature is the departure from indolence. The "element of striving" (*parakkama-dhātu*) is the state of striving. The "element of firmness" (*thāma-dhātu*) is the state of firmness.
The "element of stability" (*ṭhiti-dhātu*) is the state of stability. The "element of application" (*upakkama-dhātu*) is the state of application. And all this [is so] in its respective manner.
This is simply a name for energy that has already arisen.
9–10. Commentary on the *Nidāna-sutta* and others, 39–40.
In the ninth [sutta], "of kamma" means of kamma leading to the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*). "For the sake of origination" means for the purpose of forming a mass. "Source" (*nidāna*)...

*Paccayo*: "Born of greed" means born from greed. "Are not discerned" means they are not seen [to have been] produced by such-and-such karma. In the bright side (*sukkapakkha*), "of karmas" refers to karmas leading to the turning away from the cycle of existence (*vivaṭṭagāmika-kamma*).
Thus, in this sutta, the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and the turning away from it (*vivaṭṭa*) are explained.
In the tenth [section], "in the Nicula grove" means in the Mahāmucalinda grove. "True Dhamma" (*saddhamma*) means the true Dhamma of the Dispensation (*sāsana*).
11. Commentary on the Dārukkhandha Sutta 41.
In the eleventh [sutta], "one who has attained mastery over the mind" means one who has attained mastery over the consciousness.
"One should resolve upon it as earth alone" means one should discern the stiffened aspect as the earth element. "Depending upon that" means depending upon that existing stiffened aspect.
Relying on the earth element, one should resolve upon this log of wood as "earth" itself, thinking, "The earth element exists here.
By this method, the remaining terms should also be understood.

For just as there is the earth element in the form of hardness in that [log], so too there is the water element in the form of moisture, the fire element in the form of heat, the air element in the form of distension, and in the case of a red color...
In its core, it has the beautiful color of a lotus flower; but when it has become rotten, its powder, sapwood, and bark have an unattractive color—the aspect of foulness (*asubhadhātu*).
Relying on that, one should resolve upon and observe that log of wood as nothing but foulness.
In this sutta, what is called "mixed abiding" (*missakavihāra*) is taught.
12. Commentary on the Nāgita Sutta 42.

In the twelfth [sutta], "dwelling in a village" (*gāmantavihārin*) means one who dwells in a lodging within a village. "Seated in concentration" (*samāhitaṃ nisinnam*) means seated after having entered into meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in that village lodging.
"Now" (*idāni*) means at this time. "He will cause him to fall from concentration" (*samādhimhā cāvessati*) means he will cause him to be displaced from that state of meditative absorption.
"He will arouse himself from concentration. "I am not pleased" means I am not satisfied. "Drooping" means being drowsy. "Oneness" means a single nature;
the meaning is that he will bring the perception of the forest alone to mind, which has become one-pointed. "He will guard it" means he will favor it.
Or, "he will liberate the unliberated mind" means a mind that was unliberated at another time.
Now he will liberate [beings] by means of the five kinds of liberation. "He abandons" means he discards or relinquishes. "Having turned away" means having pushed aside or cast off.
"For the purpose of the work of voiding excrement and urine" means for the sake of performing the acts of defecation and urination.
By this much, the Teacher has described the praise of forest lodgings. However, in the first section of the sutta, that which...
It should be stated that this has already been explained above.
The fourth chapter, the Chapter on Deities, is concluded.
5. The Chapter on the Righteous (Dhammika-vagga).
1. Nāgasuttavaṇṇanā 43.
Regarding the first [sutta] of the fifth [chapter], the phrase "together with the Venerable Ānanda" is stated because [the Buddha] went there after addressing the Elder thus: "Come, Ānanda.
However, the Teacher went there surrounded by no fewer than five hundred bhikkhus.
It is to be understood thus. "He approached him" means he approached surrounded by those same five hundred bhikkhus.

"Having bathed" is a figurative expression; the meaning is "having washed. "Arranging his upper robe" means having put on the inner robe (*rattadupaṭṭa*) and holding the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga-cīvara*) with both hands, placing the western world-system behind his back and facing toward the eastern world-system.
The meaning is that he stood making his limbs appear like raw flesh due to the state of being waterless.
The community of monks also, having descended to various spots, bathed, and ascended back out, stood surrounding the Teacher alone.
Thus, at that moment, the sun—like a red-gold earring falling from the sky—was entering the western world-system.
He set out; like the moon with its perfectly pure silver disc rising from the eastern world-system,
the Perfectly Enlightened One, surrounded by a retinue of five hundred bhikkhus, stood upon the bank of the Pubbakoṭṭhaka River, adorning the world as he emitted the six-colored rays of a Buddha.
Now at that time... [as before] ...there was an elephant named Seto, so called because of his white color; he was a great elephant.
"With the sounding of great musical instruments" means with a great performance of musical instruments, cymbals, and instrumental music.
In this context, the first striking is called *tāḷita*, and what follows is called *vādita*. "The people" refers to the great multitude gathered for the purpose of seeing the elephant.
"Having seen him, he spoke thus": having rubbed the limbs and members [of the elephant], bathed him, brought him out, and set him on the bank;
then, having dried his limbs with water and seeing that great elephant adorned with hand-ornaments, he uttered this word of praise: "Oh, how handsome he is!
"Endowed with a body" means endowed with the excellence of a physical form, possessing complete limbs and members.
The meaning [of the passage] is as follows: "The Venerable Udāyī" refers to the Elder Kāḷudāyī, who had attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).

"He said this" means that, seeing the great multitude praising the beauty of the elephant, he thought: "These people are praising the beauty of an elephant born with a non-causal rebirth-linking (*ahetuka-paṭisandhi*);
they do not praise the Buddha-elephant. Now, by using this noble elephant as a simile, I shall [praise] the Buddha-elephant."
Thinking, "I shall speak in praise [of him]," he uttered these words beginning with, "Venerable sir, is it indeed an elephant?
In this context, "great" means endowed with height; "lofty" means endowed with girth. "Thus he spoke" means he says this.
Now, as for this word "nāga," it refers not only to an elephant, but also to a horse, an ox, a serpent, a tree, and a human being.
Because it occurs [in this way], he said, "Even a hand... and so forth.
"Āgu" refers to evil, wretched, unwholesome states (*akusaladhamma*).
"That I call a non-naga" means that because I do not perform the ten courses of unwholesome action (*akusalakammapatha*) or the twelve unwholesome thoughts through these three doors, I am a non-naga.
I say this: for he is a *nāga* in the sense that he does not perform evil deeds.
"With these verses I express my appreciation" means that with these sixty-four words in sixteen verses, I express my appreciation and rejoice.
"Become human" means having become a human being specifically, without having entered the state of a deity or other such beings. "Self-tamed" means by oneself alone...

Tamed, not brought to taming by others. For the Blessed One is tamed, peaceful, extinguished, and completely extinguished in these six places—tamed even by the eye, by the ear, by the nose, by the tongue, by the body, and by the mind—by means of the very taming of the path he himself has produced.
Therefore he said: "Self-tamed. "Concentrated" refers to both kinds [of concentration].

"Concentrated by means of concentration" means composed through *samādhi*. "While acting" means while dwelling [in the practice]. "On the Brahma-path" means on the supreme path, the deathless path, the path to *nibbāna*.

"Delighting in the tranquility of the mind" means having stilled the five hindrances by means of the first *jhāna*, thought and examination by means of the second *jhāna*, rapture by means of the third *jhāna*, and pleasure and pain by means of the fourth *jhāna*.
Having stilled [the mind], they revere and delight in that tranquility of the mind.
"They revere" means they revere with the body, revere with speech, revere with the mind, and revere through practice in accordance with the Dhamma;
they honor and hold them in high esteem. "One who has gone beyond all phenomena" means one who has transcended all aggregates, bases, elements, and phenomena.

He has reached the further shore through the sixfold reaching of the further shore: he is one who has gone to the further shore of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), of full understanding (*pariññā*), of abandoning (*pahāna*), of development (*bhāvanā*), of realization (*sacchikiriyā*), and of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
He has reached the further shore, attained the beyond, and reached the summit. "Even the gods pay homage to him":
this refers to all those dwelling in the ten-thousandfold world-system, both those who have fallen into suffering, such as the divine son Subrahma and others, and those who have attained happiness.

"Even the gods pay homage to you. By saying "Thus have I heard from the Arahant," he indicates that he has heard this very teaching in the presence of you who have received the designation "Arahant" for four reasons.
"One who has transcended all fetters" means one who has passed beyond all ten kinds of fetters. "One who has come from the forest to the forestless state" means...
Nirvana has come—that is, it has been attained—from the forest of defilements, being itself devoid of the forest of defilements. "Delighting in renunciation from sensual pleasures":

because it has emerged from the two kinds of sensual pleasures, the going-forth (pabbajjā), the eight meditative attainments (samāpatti), and the four noble paths (ariyamagga) are called "renunciation from sensual pleasures";
one delights in and takes pleasure therein. "Like gold freed from ore": like gold that has been released from its mineral matrix, it is similar to pure gold.
*Sabbe accaruci* means having a preference that extends beyond all beings.

For one who has a preference extending beyond the eighth-person (the worldling on the path) is called *accaruci*, namely the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*). One who has a preference extending beyond the stream-enterer is the once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*)...
[and so on] ...one who has a preference extending beyond the one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) is the paccekasambuddha; and one who has a preference extending beyond the paccekasambuddha—

The Perfectly Enlightened One is named Accaruci. "As Himavā, the other mountain peaks" means that just as Himavā, the king of mountains, outshines all other mountains, so too does he outshine them; this is the meaning. "Truly named" means his name is real, his name is true;
because he does not commit any evil, he is "Nāga"—thus his name is not false.

*Soraccaṃ* means pure virtue (*suci-sīla*). *Avihiṃsā* refers to compassion (*karuṇā*) and the preliminary stage of compassion. "Those two forefeet of the Nāga" refers to the two front feet of the Buddha-Nāga.
*Tapo* is the undertaking of the ascetic practices (*dhuta*). *Brahmacariya* is the virtue of the Noble Path (*ariya-magga-sīla*).
"Those other two feet of the Nāga" refers to the other two rear feet of the Buddha-Nāga. *Saddhā-hattha* means endowed with the trunk made of faith (*saddhā-mayā soṇḍā*).
“Whose tusks are white with equanimity” means he is endowed with the white tusks consisting of the sixfold equanimity (*upekkhā*).

“Mindfulness is the neck”: just as the neck is the support for the network of veins among the limbs and members of an elephant, so too is mindfulness the support for the qualities such as gentleness (*soracca*) in the Elephant-Buddha.
Therefore it is said: “Mindfulness is the neck. “Wisdom is the head”: just as [in the case of] a noble elephant...
The head is the supreme limb; likewise, the omniscient knowledge of the Buddha-elephant is the head. For it is by means of that [knowledge] that he knows all phenomena.

Therefore it is said: "Wisdom is the head. "Investigation is the thinking of the Dhamma" means that just as the elephant’s trunk is called "investigation," for by means of it he investigates what is hard and soft, and what is fit to be eaten and unfit to be eaten. Then...

Just as one abandons what is to be abandoned and takes up what is to be taken up, even so is the reflection on the Dhamma—termed the knowledge that discerns the divisions of the Dhamma—of the Buddha-elephant.
By means of that knowledge, he knows who is capable and who is incapable. Therefore it is said: “Investigation is reflection on the Dhamma.
Regarding the phrase “the sunshade of the Dhamma-womb”: here, “Dhamma” refers to the concentration of the fourth jhāna; the womb itself...

*Samātapo* means the heat of the belly (*kucchisamātapo*). *Samātapo* refers to a place of heating. That which has the phenomena (*dhamma*) as its internal heat is called "having the phenomena as its internal heat" (*dhammakucchisamātapo*).
For those various phenomena, such as the supernormal powers (*iddhividha*), succeed for one established in the concentration of the fourth jhāna;
therefore, that [concentration] is called the internal heat. "Seclusion" (*viveka*) refers to seclusion of body, mind, and requisites (*upadhi*). Just as...
Just as flies ward off the tail of a nāga, so does the seclusion of the Tathāgata ward off householders and those who have gone forth.
Therefore, it is called "the tail.

"A meditator" means one who meditates by means of the two kinds of jhāna. "From the stream of breath" means that, just as there are inhalations and exhalations for a nāga, so too for the Buddha-nāga...
The attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*); the meaning is that one delights therein and cannot exist without it, just as one cannot exist without inhalation and exhalation.
"Restrained in all respects" means restrained at all the sense-doors. "Blameless" refers to food obtained by right livelihood.
"Blameworthy" refers to food obtained by way of the fivefold wrong livelihood.
"Minute and gross" means both small and large. "Having cut all bonds" means having severed all ten kinds of fetters (*saṃyojana*).
"Is not smeared by the world" means he is not defiled by the world through the stains of craving, conceit, and views. "A great fire" means a great conflagration.
"Taught by the wise" refers here specifically to the Venerable Kāḷudāyin, who had attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).

"By one wise and learned"—this is the meaning of "taught by him. "The great Nāgas will understand"—the other Nāgas who have destroyed the taints (*khīṇāsava*) will recognize the Buddha-Nāga as taught by the Nāga Udāyī Thera.
"The Nāga, casting off his body, will attain final Nibbāna"—he who was already extinguished through the extinction of defilements (*kilesaparinibbāna*) at the seat of enlightenment (*bodhipallaṅka*).
He will attain final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue within the Yamaka Sāla grove.
Thus, having attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), the Elder Udāyī concluded his teaching by praising the One of Ten Powers with sixteen verses and sixty-four lines.
The Blessed One expressed his approval. At the conclusion of the teaching, eighty-four thousand living beings drank the drink of the Deathless (amatapāna).
2. Commentary on the Migasālā Sutta 44.
In the second [verse], "In what way, in what way indeed" (*kathaṃ kathaṃ nāma*) means by what various reasons.

"One who should be known" (*aññeyyo*) means one who is to be understood. "In that very thing" (*yatra hi nāma*) refers to in which state or phenomenon. "Equal in their destination" (*samasamagatikā*) means they have an identical destination by virtue of being equal. "They will be" (*bhavissanti*).

"Born. "One who has attained the fruit of a once-returner (sakadāgāmipatta) has been reborn in the Tusita realm"—meaning that having become a person who is a once-returner, he was reborn specifically in the Tusita abode.
"How, how indeed?"—by what various reasons? Having known what, was it taught, or rather, without knowing?
Not knowing the reason, the Elder said: "It was indeed thus declared by the Blessed One, sister."

"A foolish woman, with the wisdom of a foolish woman" means that, being a woman, she was possessed only of the perception of a woman. And what is the "knowledge of the higher and lower faculties of persons"?
Here, "knowledge of the higher and lower faculties of persons" refers to the knowledge of the higher and lower faculties of persons by way of their being sharp or dull.
Therefore, who is the foolish Migasālā, and who are those whose range regarding the knowledge of the higher and lower faculties of persons is unimpeded?
"Both these are far apart, very far apart"—this is the summary here.
Now, showing his own distance from Migasālā, he said: "These six, Ānanda," and so forth.
"He is gentle" (*sorato*) means he is well-restrained and abstains from evil. *Surato* is also a reading. "His fellow-celibates rejoice because of his dwelling in unity."
Together with him, his fellow practitioners of the holy life (sabrahmacārī) rejoice and are satisfied. There is also a reading "ekantavāsena," which means "by constant dwelling.
"Even by hearing it has not been accomplished" means that what is worthy of being heard has not been heard.
"Even by great learning (bāhusacca) it has not been accomplished": here, "great learning" refers to energy (vīriya); thus, what is worthy of being done through energy has not been done.
The meaning is "it occurs. "It is not penetrated even by view" means that what ought to be penetrated by view is not penetrated.
"He does not obtain even temporary liberation" means that he does not obtain rapture and gladness based on hearing the Dhamma from time to time.
"He goes only toward decline" means that he undergoes only deterioration.

"Pamāṇikā" means those who take the measure of individuals. "Paminanti" means they begin to measure or weigh [them]. "One is inferior" means one is deficient in virtues; "one is superior" means one is excellent in virtues. "That" refers to that act of measuring.

"More excellent" means more beautiful; "more refined" means more supreme. "The stream of Dhamma carries him away" means that the knowledge of insight (vipassanā-ñāṇa) which has arisen as something courageous carries him away, leading him to the plane of the Noble Ones (ariya-bhūmi). "Who could know what happens immediately after that?"
The meaning is: "Who other than the Tathāgata could know that interval and that cause?
"Anger and conceit" means anger and conceit. "States of greed" means greed itself. "Verbal formations" means words themselves by way of conversation and discourse.
"Or whoever else might be like me" means whoever else, even another, might be like me—the Perfectly Enlightened One himself.
"Of him," the meaning is: "he would take a measure among persons. "Is wounded" means he reaches the wounding of his virtues. "These, Ānanda, are the six persons":
two who are gentle, two who have attained the states of anger, conceit, and greed, and two who have attained the mental formations of anger and conceit—these are the six persons.
"Destination" means the destination of knowledge. "Deficient by one factor" means deficient by each respective factor of virtue. [As for] Pūraṇa, by virtue...
Pūraṇa excelled in virtue, while Isidatta excelled in wisdom. Pūraṇa’s virtue stood in the place of Isidatta’s wisdom, and Isidatta’s wisdom stood in the place of Pūraṇa’s virtue.
3. Commentary on the Debt Sutta (Iṇasutta)
45. In the third [verse], *dāliddiyaṃ* means the state of being poor (*daliddabhāvo*). *Kāmabhogino* refers to a being who enjoys sensual pleasures.
*Assako* means one who is devoid of what belongs to oneself. *Anāḷhiko* means not wealthy. *Iṇaṃ ādiyati* means that, being unable to maintain a livelihood, one incurs debt.
*Vaḍḍhiṃ paṭissuṇāti* means that, being unable to repay, one promises, "I will give interest. *Anucarantipi*...
They follow closely behind, causing harm by casting dust, throwing dirt, and so forth, in the midst of assemblies or crowds.
"There is no faith" means there is not even the slightest degree of conviction-based faith (*okappanaka-saddhā*).
"There is no shame" means there is not even the slightest form of a sense of shame (*hirīyanākāra*). "There is no dread" means there is not even the slightest form of fear (*bhāyanākāra*).

There is none. "There is no energy" means there is not even the slightest physical energy. "There is no wisdom" means there is not even the slightest wisdom regarding one's own actions as one's own property (*kammassakatapaññā*).
"I speak of taking on debt" means I speak of the act of borrowing money. "May they not know me" means may they not recognize me.
"Poverty is suffering" means the state of being destitute of wealth is suffering. "Longing for the acquisition of sensual pleasures" means [longing for] the attainment of sensual pleasures.
"Of those making aspirations. "The unraveling of evil karma" means that which increases evil karma.
"Crawls about" means it writhes. "Knowing" means one who knows. "Born of remorse for whom" means those things born from his remorse.
"One or another womb" means a certain animal womb. "Giving, they gladden the mind" means one who gives while gladdening the mind.
"Kaṭaggāho" means the seizing of victory; it is the seizing of non-offense. "Gharamesino" refers to one who is seeking a household life or one who is living in such a state.
"Cāgo puññaṃ pavaḍḍhati" means that merit, which has come to be designated as "cāga," increases.
Alternatively, the reading is "cāgā puññaṃ. "Paṭiṭṭhitā" means established faith, which is the faith of a stream-enterer. "Hirimano" means...
"With a mind endowed with moral shame" (*hirisampayuttacitto*). "Spiritual happiness" (*nirāmisaṃ sukhaṃ*) is the happiness arising in dependence upon the three *jhānas*.
"Equanimity" (*upekkhā*) is the equanimity of the fourth *jhāna*. "One who has aroused energy" (*āraddhavīriyo*) is one whose energy is fully exerted.

"Having attained the *jhānas*" (*jhānāni upasampajja*) means having reached the four *jhānas*. "Unified, prudent, and mindful" (*ekodi nipako sato*) means possessing a one-pointed mind as well as the mindfulness of the knowledge that one's actions are one's own property (*kammassakatañāṇa*).
"Having known thus as it really is": having understood this much of the cause according to its true nature.
"In the destruction of all fetters" means in Nibbāna. "In every way" (*sabbaso*) means in all aspects. "Without clinging" (*anupādāya*) means without grasping. "The mind is rightly liberated":
this is what is meant—by means of the correct cause, having not clung in any way whatsoever to that which is called Nibbāna, the destruction of all fetters.
“By means of this method, the path-consciousness is liberated. Furthermore, it is written in the Pāḷi: “Having known this as it really is, [there is] the destruction of all fetters”;
the meaning of this is: “having known this Nibbāna, which is designated as the destruction of all fetters, as it really is.
However, this does not cohere with what precedes and follows.
"Of him who is rightly liberated": of that one who is rightly liberated, whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*). "Knowledge arises": reviewing-knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*) arises.

"Such a one" (*tādino*): of one established in that state. "Unshakable" (*akuppā*): it is unshakable because its object is unshakable and because of the absence of the defilements (*kilesa*), which are the causes of shaking.

"Liberation" (*vimutti*): both path-liberation (*maggavimutti*) and fruition-liberation (*phalavimutti*). "In the destruction of the fetters of existence" (*bhavasaṃyojanakkhaye*): [in the destruction of the fetters of existence].
It has arisen in Nibbāna, which is defined as the destruction of the fetters of existence, and at the very moment of that destruction of the fetters of existence.
"This indeed is the supreme knowledge" means that this knowledge of the path and its fruit is called supreme knowledge (*paramañāṇa*).

"Bliss unsurpassed" means that this very bliss of the path and its fruit is called unsurpassed bliss. "The debtlessness supreme" refers to one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), who is among all those free from debt.
"Supreme freedom from debt": therefore, by means of the fruit of arahantship, he took up the climax of the teaching that "freedom from debt is supreme.
And in this sutta, having spoken only of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) [in the prose], the verses speak of both the round and its reversal (*vaṭṭavivaṭṭa*).
4. Commentary on the Mahācunda Sutta.
46. *Catutthe cetīsūti*: in the Cetiraṭṭha country. *Sayaṃjātiyan*ti: in the town named after itself. *Mahācundo*: the younger brother of the Dhammasenāpati (Sāriputta). *Dhammayogā*:
those for whom there is application (*yoga*) or devoted practice (*anuyoga*) toward the Dhamma; this is a name for preachers of the Dhamma. *Jhāyantīti jhāyī*:
they meditate, thus they are "meditators" (*jhāyī*). *Apasādentīti*: they disturb or harm. *Jhāyantīti*: they reflect. *Pajjhāyantīti* and so forth...
[The words] are augmented by means of prefixes. "What are these meditating? (kiṃ ime jhāyanti) means: what indeed are these meditating? "Why are these meditating? (kinti ime jhāyanti) means:
for what purpose are these meditating? "How are these meditating? (kathaṃ ime jhāyanti) means: by what cause are these meditating?
"Dwelling having touched with the body the deathless element" (amataṃ dhātuṃ kāyena phusitvā viharanti) refers to the meditation subject (kammatthāna) directed toward the deathless Nibbāna-element.
Having grasped it, as they dwell [in meditation], they gradually come to dwell having touched that with the mental body (*nāmakāya*).

"A profound word of meaning" refers to the hidden and concealed meaning of the aggregates (*khandha*), elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), and so forth. "They see by piercing through with wisdom" means they see after having penetrated [the truth] with the path-wisdom (*maggapaññā*) accompanied by insight (*vipassanā*).
In this context, however, both the wisdom of comprehension (*sammasanapaññā*) and the wisdom of inquiry (*paripucchāpaññā*) are also applicable.
5–6. Commentary on the Two Suttas on the Evident (Sandiṭṭhika-sutta-dvaya-vaṇṇanā) 47–48.
In the fifth [sutta], “whatever exists internally” (*santaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ*) refers to that which is present within one’s own internal domain.

By the terms “greed” (*lobha*) and so forth, the three unwholesome roots are shown. By the terms “states of greed” (*lobhadhamma*) and so forth, the phenomena associated with them are indicated. In the sixth [sutta], “corruption of body” (*kāyasaṃdosa*)...
The aspect of corrupting the door of the body. The same method applies to the other two as well. In these two suttas, only reflective contemplation (*paccavekkhaṇā*) is explained.
7. Commentary on the *Khemasutta* (Sutta 49).

"One who has lived" (*vusitavā*) means one who has completed the dwelling in the holy life (*brahmacariya*). "One who has done what was to be done" (*katakaraṇīyo*) refers to that which is to be accomplished by means of the four paths.

Having done so, he stands. "One who has laid down the burden" means one who stands having set down the burden of the aggregates (*khandha*), the burden of the defilements (*kilesa*), and the burden of volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*).
"One who has attained his own goal": the "own goal" is called *arahatta*; the meaning is that he has reached it. "One whose fetters of existence are completely destroyed":
one whose bonds to existence are exhausted. "Liberated through perfect knowledge": liberated by knowing correctly through the cause and reason. Of him—

By the phrases "It does not occur to him: 'I am superior,' etc.," the three types of conceit—namely, the conceits "I am superior," "I am equal," and "I am inferior" regarding one who is superior—are rejected.
For one whose taints are destroyed, there is no conceit such as "There is someone superior to me," "There is someone equal to me," or "There is someone inferior to me.
By the phrases "It does not occur to him: 'I am not superior,' etc.," those very same [conceits] are rejected. For one whose taints are destroyed, [there is no conceit] such as "I alone..."
The conceit (*māna*) arises thus: "I am better," "I am equal," "I am inferior," or "there are none others who are better and so forth.
"Not long after they had departed" means that they had departed shortly after having declared their attainment of *arahantship*.
"They declare another" means they speak of [another] attainment of *arahantship*. "As if laughing while declaring another" means they speak as if they were laughing. "Affliction" (*vighāta*).
"They fall into" means they fall into suffering.

"Neither among the superior, nor among the inferior, nor among equals do they lead themselves [by pride]"—here, "superior" (ussā) refers to those persons who are elevated; "inferior" (omā) refers to those who are low;

"equal" (samatto) refers to those who are similar. Thus, among these three—superior, inferior, and equal—the ones whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) do not lead themselves by way of conceit (māna).
"They do not bring [them], they do not approach"—this is the meaning. "Birth is exhausted" means their birth is exhausted.
"The holy life has been lived" means the holy life of the Path has been lived. "They wander, freed from fetters" means they wander having become liberated from all fetters.
In both the sutta and the verse, the one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*) is described.
8. Commentary on the *Indriyasaṃvara-sutta* 50.

In the eighth [verse], "has its proximate cause destroyed" (*hatūpanisaṃ*) means it has its supporting condition (*upanissaya*) destroyed. "Of one deficient in virtue" (*sīlavipannassa*) means of one whose virtue is ruined.

"Knowledge and vision according to reality" (*yathābhūtañāṇadassanaṃ*) refers to the knowledge of nascent insight (*taruṇavipassanāñāṇa*). "Disenchantment and dispassion" (*nibbidāvirāga*): here, "disenchantment" (*nibbidā*) is powerful insight.
Dispassion is the Noble Path. Regarding "knowledge and vision of liberation": here, "liberation" refers to the fruit of Arhatship, and "knowledge and vision" refers to the knowledge of review.
"It becomes endowed with decisive support" means it possesses a fulfilled decisive support.
In this discourse, the guarding of virtue and the restraint of the sense faculties are explained.
9. Commentary on the Ānanda Sutta 51.
Regarding the ninth [question], "To what extent" (*kittāvatā*) means by how much. "Never heard before" (*assutañceva*) means not previously heard at another time.
"Do not go to forgetfulness" (*na sammosaṃ gacchantī*) means they do not go to destruction. "Formerly touched by the mind" (*cetaso samphuṭṭhapubbā*) means formerly contacted by consciousness.
“They practice” means they operate at the mind-door (*manodvāra*). “And he cognizes what has not been cognized” means he knows a cause that was not previously cognized at another time.

“Masters” means they handle or recite [the texts]. “Teach” means they explain. “He causes another to recite” means he causes another to learn. “Those for whom the tradition has come down” (*āgatāgama*):

among the *Dīgha* and other [Nikāyas], whatever tradition (*āgama*) has come down—that belongs to them; thus, they are “those for whom the tradition has come down. “Bearers of the Dhamma” means bearers of the Sutta Piṭaka.
"Vinayadharas" means those who uphold the Vinaya Piṭaka. "Mātikādharas" means those who uphold the two Pātimokkhas.
"Paripucchati" means he asks about the sequence of the connections, both preceding and following. "Paripañhati" means he deliberates and discriminates, thinking, "I shall ask this and that.
[He asks: "Venerable sir, how is this? [meaning] "Venerable sir, how does this sequence of connections, both preceding and following, come to be?"
He asks: "What is the meaning of this? means he asks, "What is the meaning of this statement? "Unopened" means not yet revealed.
"They reveal" means they make it manifest. "In matters that are grounds for doubt" means in those things that serve as causes for doubt.
In this context, it should be understood that whatever phenomenon gives rise to doubt is itself called a "ground for doubt."
10. Commentary on the *Khattiya-sutta* 52.
In the tenth [verse], "with the aim of wealth" means having an intention established for the purpose of amassing wealth; it refers to an inclination that has arisen.
"Investigations for the sake of wisdom" means investigations that have arisen for the purpose of wisdom, thinking, "May we be possessed of wisdom. This very...
Their investigation ranges over the mind. "Based on power" means based on a body of power; for having obtained a body of power, they are said to have gained a firm footing.
"Intentions directed toward earth" means intentions formed in the mind for the sake of earth, thinking, "We shall become lords of the earth.
"Ending in sovereignty" means ending in the consecration of kingship; for the consecration—
Having reached [the end], they are said to have attained the conclusion. In this manner, the meaning is to be understood in all instances.
Regarding the remaining terms here, this is the intended sense: first, the brahmins, having received the mantras, are said to have gained their footing;
the householders, whatever craft [they may have]; women, a son who is the heir and master of the family estate; and thieves, whatever [they may have].
The weapon of the ascetics is the sword of virtue; they are said to have "gained a firm footing. Therefore, the phrases beginning with "founded on mantras" and so forth were spoken.
As for the brahmins, their minds become fixed on the thought, "We shall perform a sacrifice," and when they reach the Brahma-world, they are said to have "reached the ultimate goal.
Therefore, it was said that their "adherence to sacrifice has the Brahma-world as its ultimate goal. For the purpose of performing work...

"Attachment to work" (*kammantābhinivesā*) means that the mind adheres to these [tasks]. "The completion of finished work" (*niṭṭhitakammantapariyosānā*) means that when the work is finished, they have reached their conclusion.

"Having men as their aim" (*purisādhippāyā*) means having an inclination directed toward men. "That in which the mind ranges for the sake of adornment" (*alaṅkāratthāya mano upavicarati etissā*) refers to this [woman].

"Adorned with ornaments and reflecting on their beauty": "Asapattībhini-vesā" (non-rival fixation) means that her mind becomes fixed on the thought, "Having become rival-less, may we two live alone in the house.
"Issariyapariyosānā" (culmination of sovereignty) means that when they have attained mastery over household life, they are said to have reached the culmination.
"Ādānādhippāyā" (intent on seizing) means that their intention is the taking away of another's goods. "Gahane nilīyanatthāne etesaṃ" (in hiding places for these to lie concealed).
They are "investigations of grasping" because the mind investigates by way of grasping. They are "adherence to darkness" because their minds are intent upon the state of darkness.
They are "ending in non-seeing" because they reach a conclusion that results in not seeing [the truth].
They are "intent on forbearance and gentleness" because their underlying purpose lies in patient endurance and a pure moral character.
Their minds are intent upon the state of nothingness and the state of non-grasping; thus, they are "intent upon nothingness" (*ākiñcaññābhinivesā*).
They have reached Nibbāna, they have reached the ultimate goal; thus, they are "having Nibbāna as their consummation" (*nibbānapariyosānā*).
11. Commentary on the *Appamāda-sutta*.
53. *Samadhiggayha* means having grasped well. *Jaṅgalānaṃ pāṇānaṃ* refers to creatures that move upon the surface of the earth, namely those animals possessing feet.
*Padajātāni* means footprints. *Samodhānaṃ gacchantī* means they go toward a convergence, that is, toward being placed together.
*Aggamakkhāyati* means it is declared to be the best, the most excellent. *Pabbajalāyaka* means one who cuts the *pabbaja* grass.
“Shakes off” means he shakes [the fruit] from below. “Shakes all around” means he shakes it from both sides.
“Conceals” means he strikes it with his arm or strikes it against a tree. “By a cluster of mangoes” means by a cluster of mango fruits.
“Attached to the stalks” means bound to the stalks or fixed upon the stalks. “They follow after that” means they conform to the stalks.
"They become," means they become followers of the "mother-gatherer" (ambapiṇḍidaṇḍaka). "Minor kings" (*khuddarājāno*) means small kings, or perhaps natural kings.
12. Commentary on the *Dhammikasutta* 54.
"In all" (*sabbaso*) means in all [of them]. "In the seven monasteries" (*vihāresu*) means in the seven cells (*pariveṇa*). "He reviles" (*paribhāsati*)...
He treats with contempt; he displays fear. "He harms" means he torments. "He pierces" means he stabs.
"He offends with speech" means he provokes with words. "They depart" means they go away in various directions.
"They do not stay" means they do not remain. "They abandon" means they cast off or relinquish. "We should expel them" means we should drive them out. "Handa" is used in the sense of an exhortation.
"nipāto. "Alaṃ" is appropriate; the meaning is "let him go forth. "Kiṃ te iminā" means "what use have you for this dwelling in your native land?
"Tīradassiṃ sakuṇaṃ" refers to a directional crow. "Muñcanti" means they release it for the purpose of seeing the directions. "Sāmantā" means nearby.
There is also the reading "samantā," which has the same meaning as "sāmantā. "Abhiniveso" means...
The "nesting" refers to the settling of branches that have spread out. "The nesting of the roots and the creepers" refers to the settling of the roots.
"A pot for a measure of rice" is a vessel for cooking a meal consisting of one *āḷhaka* of rice. "Honey from bees" is honey produced by small flies (*khuddamakkhikā*) on stalks.
"Unadulterated" means free from defects. And they do not harm each other's fruits.
The fruits do not harm one another’s portions. There is no one who cuts the root, the bark, or the leaf from their own portion;
they enjoy only those fruits that have fallen beneath their respective branches.
Even when a fruit has moved from one person’s portion to another’s, [the owner thinks], "This fruit is not from my branch."
"Knowing this, they do not eat. "Having eaten as much as desired" means having eaten until their throats were full.

"Breaking off a branch" means cutting it to the size of a parasol and providing shade before departing. "For indeed" (*yatra hi nāma*) means "for whoever indeed. "He will depart" means he has already departed.
"He did not take" means that by the power of the deity, he took nothing but the fruit; for she had made such a resolution.
"He approached him" means that when the inhabitants of the countryside had gone and said, "Great King, the tree did not bear fruit;
is it perhaps our fault or yours?", he replied, "There is no fault on my part, nor on the part of the country-folk.
In my kingdom, what is called 'unrighteousness' does not prevail. For what reason has the tree not borne fruit? Let us approach Sakka."
Thinking, “I shall ask him,” he approached Sakka, the lord of the devas. *Pavattesi* means he turned it over. *Ummūlamakāsi* means he uprooted it.
*Api nu tvam* means “Indeed, for you? *Aṭṭhitāyeva* means “precisely because it was not firmly established.
*Sacchavīni* means having the same color, remaining in their natural state. *Na paccakkosati* means “he does not protest.”
"Quarreling" means striking one another. "Brawling" means hitting one another.

"Sunetta" (Fair-eyed): "netta" refers to the eyes; he is "fair-eyed" because of the beauty of those eyes. "A founder of a sect" (*titthakara*) means a maker of a ford for entering upon a happy destination.
"Free from lust" (*vītarāga*) means one whose lust has been removed by way of suppression. "He produces" means he obtains. "Endowed with right view" (*diṭṭhisampanna*).
"One endowed with vision" means one who has attained the stage of stream-entry (*sotāpanna*). "Patience" (*khanti*) refers to the enduring of the disparagement of one's own virtues.

"As this [is] toward fellow practitioners of the holy life" (*yathāmaṃ sabrahmacārīsu*): the meaning is that I do not speak of any other such patience regarding virtues as this reviling and abuse directed toward fellow practitioners of the holy life. Regarding the phrase "not equal among our fellow practitioners of the holy life" (*na no samasabrahmacārīsu*):
here, "equal persons" (*samajano*) refers to one's own kin (*sakajano*). Therefore, it is not...
The meaning here is that their minds will not become corrupted toward their fellow practitioners of the holy life (*samānabrahmacārī*).
As for Jotipāla and Govinda: by name he was Jotipāla, but by position he was Mahāgovinda.

"Seven household priests" (*sattapurohita*) means he was the household priest to the seven kings beginning with Reṇu. "Non-violent ones of the past" (*ahiṃsakā atītaṃse*) means these six teachers were non-violent in the past.
They were. "Free from the stench of raw flesh" (*nirāmagandhā*): free from the stench of the "raw flesh" of anger. "Delivered through compassion" (*karuṇā-vimuttā*):

intent upon the jhāna of compassion, and established in both compassion and its preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*). "Yet" (*yetā*): these [beings]; or rather, *ayam eva* is the reading. "One should not approach one who is of good character" (*na sādhurūpaṃ āsīde*):
one should not strike at one whose nature is virtuous. "One who has abandoned the sixty-two views" (*diṭṭhiṭṭhānappahāyinaṃ*): one who has abandoned the sixty-two types of speculative views.
"Seventh" means the seventh starting from arahantship. "Not free from lust" means not devoid of lust;
by this, he rejects the state of a non-returner (*anāgāmin*). "The five faculties are dull" means the five insight-faculties are dull;

for him, these are indeed called dull compared to those of a once-returner (*sakadāgāmin*). "Insight" is the knowledge of discerning formations (*saṅkhāra-pariggaha-ñāṇa*). "He is already afflicted beforehand" means...
It is harmed even earlier. "Unharmed" means being unharmed and uninjured by the destruction of one's virtues (*guṇa*).
The rest is clear everywhere.
The fifth chapter, the *Dhammika-vagga*.
The First Fifty [Discourses] is concluded.
2. The Second Fifty [Discourses], Chapter Six:
The Great Chapter (Mahāvagga).
1. Commentary on the Soṇa Sutta 55.
Regarding the first [verse] of the sixth [chapter]: "Soṇa" refers to the Elder Soṇa Sukhumāla. "In Sītavana" means in the charnel ground of that name.
It is said that five hundred successive leaf-huts for walking meditation (*caṅkama*) were constructed there; in those, the Elder [dwelt]. His own...
Taking up a suitable walking meditation, he practiced the duty of a recluse.
As he walked with such exerted energy, his soles were worn through; as he walked on his knees, his kneecaps and palms were also worn through and became perforated.
Even while dwelling thus with such exerted energy, he was unable to manifest even a mere sign of light. To him—
To show the thought that arose in him as he sat upon a stone slab at the edge of the forest, his body exhausted by exertion, the passage beginning with "Then, venerable sir...
was spoken. Therein, "one who has aroused energy" means one whose energy is fully exerted.

"The mind is not liberated from the taints through non-clinging" [is said because] if I were one who understands through a condensed teaching (*ugghaṭitaññū*) or one who understands through an elaborated teaching (*vipañcitaññū*), [then it would have been liberated].

"Whether I am one who is to be led or not, surely my mind would be liberated. But certainly I am merely one for whom words are the limit, because of which my mind is not liberated"—having made this determination, he reflected on the passage beginning with "But there do exist," and so forth.
In that context, the word *bhogā* (possessions) is used in the nominative case (*paccatta*) in the sense of the accusative (*upayoga*).

"Pāturahosi" (He appeared): Having known the Elder’s state of mind, [the Buddha thought], "This Soṇa is sitting today on the meditation ground in the Sītavana forest and is reflecting upon this thought;
having gone there, I shall grasp his thought at its very source and teach him the meditation subject of the lute simile.
Thus he became manifest before him. Regarding the phrase "on the prepared seat": the bhikkhus who were practitioners of meditation [were staying] in their own respective dwellings.
Having prepared a seat as was available for the Blessed Buddha who had come to give exhortation, they applied themselves to striving;
and failing to find anything else, they even spread out old leaves and placed their upper robes (saṅghāṭi) upon them.
The Elder also prepared a seat and applied himself to striving. It is with reference to this that it is said: "on the seat prepared."
"What do you think?"—the Teacher said this, beginning with "What do you think," in order to tell the parable of the lute, thinking: "This bhikkhu has no need for other meditation subjects;
he is skilled and experienced in the art of music (gandhabba-sippa), and when something is spoken within his own domain, he will quickly comprehend it.
Skill in the strings and tones of the lute is indeed [skill] in the lute.
He was skilled in playing musical instruments, and he was proficient therein. For his parents thought, "If our son learns another craft, he will weary his body;
however, this can be mastered even while sitting on a couch," and so they had him learn the craft of music alone. As for him—
“Seven notes, three scales, twenty-one finger-measures for tuning, and forty-nine positions—such are these circles of notes.
Thus, he became proficient in the entire craft of music. *Accāyatā* means excessively long; *kharamucchanā* refers to a harsh tuning.
“Saravatī” means endowed with sap. “Kammaññā” means fit for work, suitable for work. “Atisithilā” means loosely plucked.
“Same guṇe patiṭṭhitā” means having been placed on a middle pitch, they are plucked.
