“Accāraddhaṃ” means too tight. “Uddhaccāya saṃvattatī” means it leads to agitation. “Atilīnaṃ” means...
"Too lax. "For the sake of laziness" means for the purpose of a state of indolence.
"He resolves upon energy and calm" means he resolves upon calm associated with energy; the meaning is: "Join energy with calm. And "he penetrates the evenness of the faculties" means:
resolve upon the evenness, the state of balance, of the faculties beginning with faith. In that regard, [balance] faith with wisdom, and wisdom with...
By one who joins faith with energy, and energy with concentration, and concentration with faith, the evenness of the faculties is said to be established.
Mindfulness, however, is all-beneficial; it must always be strong.
Furthermore, that method of joining them has already been explained in the *Visuddhimagga*. And therein, regarding the instruction "take up the sign," in that...
"When there is equanimity, take up and produce that sign by which the sign should arise— just as the reflection of a face appears in a mirror— whether it be the sign of serenity,
the sign of insight, the sign of the path, or the sign of the fruit. Having thus directed him toward Arahantship,
the Teacher explained the meditation subject.
And there he grasped the sign (*nimitta*); that is, he grasped both the sign of serenity (*samatha-nimitta*) and the sign of insight (*vipassanā-nimitta*).
"Six bases" (*cha ṭhānāni*) means six causes. "He is intent upon" (*adhimutto hoti*) means he stands having penetrated and made [the truth] directly manifest (*paccakkhaṃ*).
"Intent upon renunciation" (*nekkhammādhimutto*) and so forth—all this is stated specifically with reference to Arahantship. For Arahantship is [freed] from all defilements (*kilesa*).

It is called renunciation (*nekkhamma*) because of its departure [from the world]; it is called seclusion (*paviveka*) because of its being secluded from those very things; it is called non-affliction (*abyāpajjha*) because of the absence of malice;

it is called the destruction of craving (*taṇhākkhaya*) because it arises at the end of the destruction of craving; it is called the destruction of clinging (*upādānakkhaya*) because it arises at the end of the destruction of clinging;
and it is called non-delusion (*asammoha*) because of the absence of delusion.
"Merely faith alone" means merely faith devoid of penetration, unmixed with the wisdom of penetration.

"Accumulating" means increasing through repeated performance. "Because of being free from lust" means that precisely because lust has departed through the penetration of the Path, he stands having penetrated and realized the state of Arahantship known as renunciation, by means of the dwelling in the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
"He dwells" means that his mind is inclined toward that very thing. The same method applies to the remaining phrases as well.
"Gain, honor, and renown" refers to the acquisition of the four requisites, the fact that those very things are well-prepared, and the speaking of praise about them.
"Desiring" means wishing for or longing for. "Devoted to seclusion" means intent upon seclusion; [the Blessed One] is an Arahant.
The meaning is that he thus declares [his attainment of] Arahatship.

"Adherence to rules and observances" (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*) refers merely to the grasping undertaken after having misapprehended both moral conduct (*sīla*) and vows (*vata*). "Returning to it as the essence" (*sārato paccāgacchanto*) means knowing it as being the essential core.
"Devoted to non-affliction" (*abyāpajjhādhimutto*) means he declares Arahatship, which is free from affliction. By this very [statement],...
The meaning should be understood in all instances according to this method. Furthermore, some say:
"In this very [verse], 'resolute upon renunciation' refers to Arahantship, while in the remaining five, it refers to Nibbāna. Others say:
"In this very [verse], 'resolute upon non-delusion' refers to Nibbāna, while in the remaining ones, it refers to Arahantship. However, the essential point here is this: in all [cases]...
Among those, both arahantship and Nibbāna have indeed been explained.
"Powerful" means strong, resembling divine forms. "They do not overwhelm his mind" means they are unable to seize and remain within the mind of this one whose taints are destroyed;
for it is when defilements arise that they are said to "seize" the mind. "Unmixed" means...
For the defilements mix the mind together with their object; because they are absent, it is "unmixed. "Steady" means firmly established.
"Attained to imperturbability" means attained to immovability. "And he contemplates its passing away" means that he sees both the arising and the passing away of that mind.
"A violent wind and rain" means a powerful mass of wind. "It would not even shake" means...
"One would not be able to move it by even a single part. "One would not cause it to tremble" means one would not be able to make it shake from all sides, like a pillar.
"One would not cause it to quake" means one would not be able to make it shake violently or cause it to fall.
"For one intent on renunciation" refers to an Arahant who has realized the state of destruction of the taints (*khīṇāsava*) and stands firm. The same applies to the remaining phrases.
Only arahantship has been described. In the phrase "of the destruction of clinging" (*upādānakkhayassa*), the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative.

"And non-delusion of the mind" (*asammohaṃ ca cetaso*) means for one who is intent upon the non-delusion of the consciousness. "Having seen the arising of the sense-bases" (*disvā āyatanuppādaṃ*) means having seen both the arising and the passing away of the sense-bases.
"The mind is rightly liberated" (*sammā cittaṃ vimuccati*) means by way of the correct cause and method, through this practice of insight.
By means of the attainment of fruition, the mind is liberated; it resolves upon Nibbāna as its object.

Alternatively, this describes the path of one whose taints are destroyed. For, having seen the arising of the sense-bases, his mind is rightly liberated from all defilements through the power of the Noble Path attained by means of this insight. Thus, for him who is rightly liberated... [and so forth].
It is not found. In that context, "one whose mind is peaceful" means one whose mind is extinguished (*nibbuta*). The rest here is of obvious meaning.
2. Commentary on the Phaggunasutta 56.
In the second [verse], "he has fallen away" (*samadhosi*) indicates the manner of his falling. "They retreat" means they decline; "they do not advance" means...
They do not increase. "One should wrap the head" means that one should wrap the head and bind it with a cord so that it is turned all around.

"The faculties became serene" means that at the time of death, the six faculties were clear and tranquil. "In the investigation of the meaning" means in the examination of what is beneficial and what is not, and what is the cause and what is not the cause.
"In the unsurpassed destruction of acquisitions" means in Nibbāna. "Not liberated" [refers to those who have not attained final release].
"It becomes" means it is inclined toward the fruit of arahantship.
3. Commentary on the *Chaḷabhijātisutta* 57.
In the third [sutta], "six classes of birth" (*chaḷabhijāti*) means six types of births. "In this regard" (*tatridaṃ*) means "in this case. "Cruel" (*luddā*) means harsh. "Bhikkhus..."
"Those who live by thorns" means these ascetics. "Wearing a single cloth" means those who cover themselves in front with only a single piece of rag.
"They would hang [me] on a spit against my will" means that when the army was marching and an ox had died, they were dividing and eating it for the sake of obtaining the price of the beef;
then, making a portion of the beef for one who did not even desire it, they said, "And this must be eaten by you."
"And the root must be given"—this means they would hang that [root], which is reckoned as a section, upon the hole, or they would force it into the hand.
"By one who does not know the field" means by one who does not know the field according to the classification of noble birth (*abhijāti*).
"Listen to that" means listen to this my classification. "One of dark birth" means one of black birth; one who is born into dark states, thus having a dark nature.

"Having sacrificed, one is born; one is reborn, or one is born into a dark lineage (*kaṇhābhijāti*). One 'is born into nibbāna' means one attains nibbāna, or one is born into the lineage of nibbāna, which is designated as the plane of the Noble Ones (*ariyabhūmi*).
4. Commentary on the Discourse on the Taints (*Āsavasutta-vannaṇā*)
58. "In the fourth [case], they are to be abandoned by restraint (*saṃvara*)," meaning they are to be abandoned through restraint.

The same method applies to the remaining cases as well. "Here" (*idha*) means in this teaching (*sāsana*). "Having reflected" (*paṭisaṅkhā*) means having discerned; the sense is "having reviewed. "By way" (*yoniso*) means by means of a method or path.
And here, it should be understood that "reflection on the danger in non-restraint" (*asaṃvare ādīnavapaṭisaṅkhā*) is what is meant by "wise reflection" (*yoniso paṭisaṅkhā*). And this—

“Monks, it is better for the eye-faculty to be thoroughly rubbed by a red-hot iron rod—blazing, flaming, and glowing—than to grasp at the signs and secondary characteristics in forms cognizable by the eye,” and so forth; thus it should be understood through the discourse on burning.
Regarding the phrase “he dwells restrained with the restraint of the eye-faculty”: here, it is the eye itself...
The faculty is the eye-faculty. "Restraint" (*saṃvara*) means from the sense of restraining;
it is said to mean covering or closing. This is a designation for mindfulness. Restraint of the eye-faculty is "eye-faculty-restraint.
Even though this arises in the impulsion (*javana*), it is called "eye-faculty-restraint" because it prevents the arising of defilements at that door. One who is restrained...
He is endowed with that restraint. For it is said in the analysis (*vibhaṅga*) of the phrase "restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha":
"By means of this restraint of the Pātimokkha, he is endowed... [etc. ...he is possessed of it. Alternatively, *saṃvuto* means "one who restrains" (*saṃvarī*);
it means he has closed or shut [the senses]. "Restrained by the restraint of the eye-faculty" means [restrained] by that which is designated as the restraint of the eye-faculty.
He "secured" (saṃvari) the door of the eye with mindfulness, just as one secures a house door with a bolt; "he closed it" is what is meant.

This very meaning is the most excellent here, for this same meaning is seen in these passages: "for one who dwells with the faculty of the eye unrestrained," and "for one who dwells with it restrained."
In the passage beginning with “yaṃ hissa,” the meaning is: for that bhikkhu who dwells without having restrained—that is, without having closed and secured—the eye-faculty (*cakkhundriya*).
Alternatively, this is a substitution of *ya* for the vowel *i*; thus, the meaning is “ye assa” (for whom there are).

“Taints, vexations, and fevers” refers to the four taints (*āsava*) and other afflictive defilements (*kilesa-pariḷāha*) or resultants of suffering (*vipāka-pariḷāha*). For, in the case of the eye-door...
The taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) arises for one who delights in and rejoices over a desirable object that has come into range by way of the gratification of sensual pleasure;
the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*) arises for one who delights in the aspiration for existence, thinking, "I shall obtain such [a state] in another fortunate rebirth";
and the taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*) arises for one who grasps at a "being" or "belonging to a being. All [these taints] arise simultaneously with [the object].

Ignorance is the "taint of ignorance"; thus the four taints arise. Other defilements associated with these, as well as their afflictions and fevers, or their future results, are said to arise for one who dwells without restraint from them.
"In this way they would be for him" means that by this method they do not exist, and not otherwise. [This is] through wise reflection.
The same method applies to such passages as "restrained by the restraint of the ear-faculty" and so forth. These are called "the taints to be abandoned by restraint.
Having taken four [taints] for each of these six doors, it is said that twenty-four taints are to be abandoned by restraint.
Regarding what is to be said concerning such passages as "reflecting wisely on the robe," all of that is found in the *Visuddhimagga* in the discourse on virtue (*sīla*).
This has already been stated. "Whatever" means whatever robe, or one among alms-food and so forth, he may have.
"Not using it wisely" refers to one who does not use it with such wise reflection (*yoniso*).

In this context, the arising of the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) should be understood as occurring for one who longs for robes and so on not yet obtained, or who relishes what has been obtained; thinking, "I shall obtain such things in another fortunate existence."

The taint of existence (*bhavāsava*) arises for one who relishes the aspiration for existence; the taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*) arises for one who establishes the notion of self, thinking "I gain" or "I do not gain," or "this is mine";
and the taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*) arises as co-nascent with all of them.
Thus, the arising of these four taints should be understood both as affliction and fever, and also from the production of the nine kinds of feeling. These...
"Bhikkhus, it is said that 'the taints are to be abandoned by using. Having taken four taints for each of these conditions,
these sixteen taints are said to be abandonable by this reviewing and using, which is called restraint through knowledge."
"Reflecting wisely, he is patient with cold": having reflected by means of the appropriate method and way, he becomes one who endures cold;
he tolerates and withstands cold. He does not, like a man lacking in heroism, waver or tremble at even a slight cold, nor does he abandon his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
The same method applies to heat and the other [sensations]. And here, "the path of speech" (*vacanapatha*) refers simply to the words themselves.

It should be understood [in this way]. Regarding the phrases "painful" (*dukkhā*) and so forth: they are "painful" in the sense of being painful; "sharp" (*tibbā*) in the sense of being intense; "rough" (*kharā*) in the sense of being harsh;
"bitter" (*kaṭukā*) in the sense of being pungent; "disagreeable" (*asātā*) because they are devoid of gratification; "unpleasant" (*amanāpā*) because they do not increase the mind's delight;

and "life-taking" (*pāṇaharā*) because they are capable of taking life. "Whatever among these" means that even if there were only a single factor among the cold and so forth. "Because it cannot be endured" means:
This refers to one who does not endure or tolerate [the sensations]. The arising of the taints (*āsava*) here should be understood as follows:

when one touched by cold longs for heat, the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) arises; so it is in all cases. When one longs for existence, thinking, "In the state of a happy destination there is neither cold nor heat," the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*) arises.
The grasping that "this is cold for me" or "this is hot for me" is the taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*).
"The taint of ignorance is associated with all [of these]. Regarding the phrase "these are called":

the meaning is that these numerous taints—four being grouped for each of the cold and so forth—are said to be abandonable by means of this endurance known as restraint through patience (*khanti-saṃvara*).
"By reflecting wisely, he avoids a fierce elephant" means: "I am an ascetic," and thus he does not [approach] the fierce elephant.
One should stand at a distance. For on that account there might arise even death or suffering amounting to death;
thus, having reflected by way of this means and method, one avoids and retreats from a fierce elephant. This same method applies everywhere. "Fierce" (*caṇḍa*) means wicked or savage.
"Stump" (*khāṇu*) refers to a khadira stump or the like. "Thorny place" (*kaṇṭakaṭṭhāna*) is where thorns are found.
They disappear into that space. A *sobbha* is a pit whose banks are cut away on all sides. A *papāta* is one whose banks are cut away on only one side.
A *candanikā* is a place for discarding used water, womb-impurities, and so forth.
An *oḷigalla* is a place where those very same muds and such flow; it is filled with impurity even to the depth of the knees. Both of these places—
These are places where non-human beings cause disturbances; therefore, they should be avoided. Regarding "anāsane" (unsuitable seats): here, an "unseated" place is an unsuitable seat (*anāsana*);

in terms of its meaning, it should be understood as a secluded and concealed seat whose location is not fixed. Regarding "agocare" (unsuitable resort): here too, an "unresorted-to" place is an unsuitable resort (*agocara*).
It is fivefold, categorized by types such as those frequented by prostitutes and so forth. Regarding "pāpake mitte" (evil friends): this refers to those who are base and immoral.
“Friends who are not friends. “Evil” means base or low. “They would believe” means they would have conviction or resolve, thinking:
“Surely this venerable one has done it, or will do it. “For whatever among these” means whichever one among the elephants and so forth might belong to him.
Furthermore, the arising of the taints (*āsava*) in this context should be understood as follows: for one who is touched by suffering caused by the elephant and so forth...

The taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) arises for one who longs for pleasure; the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*) arises for one longing for existence, thinking, "In the state of a happy destination, there is no such suffering";
the taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*) is the misconception, "An elephant tramples me" or "A horse [tramples] me";
and the taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*) is associated with all of these. These are called "these four each by way of each [instance], such as the elephant," etc.
Having done this, it is said that "many taints (āsava) are to be abandoned by means of this avoidance known as the restraint of virtue.
As for the phrase "he does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire, having reflected wisely," it refers to the method beginning with: "In this way, this thought is unwholesome;
in this way, it is blameworthy; in this way, it has a painful result; and furthermore, it leads to one's own affliction. And so forth.
Having reflected upon the danger in sensual thoughts through systematic attention, one does not tolerate the sensual thought that has arisen with respect to this or that object;
having brought it to mind, one does not dwell with it, nor does one dwell with it within. This is the meaning.
What does one do when not tolerating it? One abandons it. Is it like throwing rubbish into a basket? No; rather, one dispels it.
It strikes, pierces, and extracts. Is it like driving out an ox with a goad? No;
rather, it brings it to an end, it makes it reach its limit, so that not even its interior remains, not even a mere fragment—thus it treats it.
But how does it treat it thus? It causes it to go to non-existence; it causes it to go to non-existence bit by bit.
By means of suppression-abandonment (*vikkhambhanappahāna*), he acts so that [the thought] is well-suppressed.

This same method applies to the other two types of applied thought (*vitakka*) as well. "As each one arises" (*uppannuppanne*) means with each and every arising; it is said to mean "as soon as it has arisen.
Having dispelled it once it has arisen, he does not remain indifferent toward it a second time, even if it arises a hundred times over.
"Only by dispelling": "evil unwholesome states" refers specifically to those thoughts of sensual desire and so forth, or alternatively, to all nine great types of thought.
Among these, three have already been mentioned; the remaining ones are:

"thought of relatives, thought of the country, thought of immortality, thought associated with compassion for others, thought associated with gain, honor, and fame, and thought associated with not being despised."

And these six. Regarding the phrase "whatever among these thoughts": whatever there may be among these thoughts, the thought of sensual desire (*kāmavitakka*) here is simply the taint of sensuality (*kāmāsava*);

the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*) is its specific differentiation; the taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*) is that which is associated with it; and ignorance (*avijjā*) present in all thoughts is the taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*).
Thus should the arising of the taints be understood. "These are called" refers to these taints described according to their modes as thoughts of sensual desire and so forth.
By means of this removal— known as restraint through energy— accompanied by the contemplation of the danger in each respective thought,
they are said to be abandoned.
"He develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor by wisely reflecting" refers to the danger in non-development and the benefit in development.
Having reflected by way of this method, one develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor (*satisambojjhaṅga*). This same method applies everywhere.

The development of the enlightenment factors has already been explained in detail below. Regarding the phrase "whatever among these": it refers to whichever [defilements] might arise from among these enlightenment factors.

However, in this context, regarding the arising of taints (*āsava*), those taints such as the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) which would otherwise arise do not do so because these enlightenment factors associated with the Noble Path have been developed.
This method should be understood thus: "The taints do not exist for one who develops [the path] in this way. Regarding the phrase "these are called":
these taints, such as the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) and so forth, are said to be abandonable by means of this supramundane development of the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*).
Praising the bhikkhu whose taints have been abandoned through these six modes, he said: "When, O bhikkhus... and so forth. Therein, *yato* is used in the genitive case.
The word *to* means "of which," as it were. However, the ancients explain it as "in which time.

Regarding the phrase "those taints that are to be abandoned by restraint have been abandoned": this means that those taints which are to be abandoned by restraint have indeed been abandoned by restraint itself;
one does not merely perceive them as abandoned while they are actually unabandoned.
5. Commentary on the Dārukammika Sutta 59.
In the fifth [sutta], "dārukammiko" refers to a certain lay follower who made his living by trading in wood.
"Kāsikacandanaṃ" means fine sandalwood. "Aṅgena" means by way of its parts; in the bright fortnight, it is by way of its qualities. "Nemantaniko" means one who receives invitations.
The recipient [thought]: "I shall give a gift to the Sangha. He said, "I shall give it to the community of monks," and having spoken thus, he paid homage to the Teacher and departed.
Later on, five hundred monks who were his family-visitors fell away from the religious life and returned to the state of householders.

When it was said to him, "Those family-visiting monks have fallen away," he replied, "What does that matter to me? and did not allow even the slightest difference in the arising of thoughts [to arise].
"He did not do so. It was with reference to this that the Teacher said, "The mind of one giving a gift to the Saṅgha will become serene.
6. Commentary on the Hatthisāriputta Sutta 60.
In the sixth [sutta], "discourse on the Abhidhamma" means a discourse mixed with the Abhidhamma. "How does he instill it? refers to those [listeners].
How does he speak his own discourse after having interrupted [others]? "Of the elder bhikkhus" is a genitive case used in the sense of the instrumental;
the meaning is "together with the elder bhikkhus. The meaning is that he is also able to speak whatever Abhidhamma discourse those elders have.
"Cetopariyāya" means the range of the mind. "Idha" means in this world. "Soratasorato" means...
"Tranquil as it were tranquil" means endowed with serenity; "as it were humble" means humble in conduct.
"Peaceful as it were peaceful" means truly peaceful. "He draws away from the Teacher" means he departs from the presence of the Teacher.
"Of one who is socially intimate" means of one who is intimate through the five kinds of social intimacy.
"Of one who has been released" means of one who has been let go.

"Of one whose faculties are clear" means of one whose senses are unimpaired. "A consumer of grain" means one who eats grain. "Should cause to disappear" means should destroy. "Cows and goats" means both cows and she-goats.
"Shells and snails" means both shells and snails. "Gravel and pebbles" means both gravel and pebbles. "Stale from the previous day" means...
The food of kudrūsaka, whose faults are well known. “It would not please him” means it would not be agreeable to him.
In that context, the accusative case “purisaṃ bhuttāviṃ” (a man who has eaten) should be understood in the sense of the genitive. “Amuṃ hāvuso, purisaṃ” means, “friend, that man.
“Of all signs” means of all signs such as the sign of permanence and so forth. “Signless concentration of mind” means...

Strong insight-concentration (*balava-vipassanā-samādhi*). "The sound of the *cīrika*" means the sound of the *jhallika* (a type of drum). "He will remember renunciation" means he will remember the virtue of going forth (*pabbajjā*).
"There was one among the Arahants" means that among the Blessed One’s disciples who were Arahants, he was one Arahant.
For this elder, having been a householder seven times, went forth seven times. For what reason? During the time of the Sammasambuddha Kassapa.
This was not because he praised the state of a householder to a certain bhikkhu.

Rather, while the necessary conditions for attaining *arahantship* already existed through that very deed, the man wandered seven times between the life of a householder and the life of a renunciant; on his seventh round, having gone forth, he attained *arahantship*. 7.
Commentary on the Middle Sutta (*Majjhesuttavaṇṇanā*).
61. In the seventh [chapter], the *Metteyya-pañha* within the *Pārāyana*, concerning the question of the youth Metteyya at the assembly of the *Pārāyana*:
"Having understood both ends" means having known both ends, that is, both divisions. "The wise one is not stained in the middle": here "wisdom" (*mantā*) refers to discernment (*paññā*).
Having understood both ends by means of that wisdom, one is not stained in the middle; one is not stained in the intermediate state.
"Transcending the seamstress" means having gone beyond craving, which is designated as "sewing. "Contact" refers to this personal existence (attabhāva) because it is produced by way of contact.
"One end" means this one portion. "The origin of contact": that which has contact as its origin is the "origin of contact";
this refers to a future personal existence produced with the contact of kamma performed in this present personal existence as its condition.
"The second end" means the second division. "The cessation of contact" is Nibbāna.
In the sense of having cut the sewing of craving and making [existence] twofold, Nibbāna is called the "middle. For craving sews it;
that is, craving sews and joins together this contact—which is reckoned as the two types of personal existence—and the origin of contact. Why? Because of each respective state of becoming (*bhava*).
Regarding rebirth: for if craving did not sew [them] together, the production of this or that state of existence would not occur.
At this point, they take up the simile of the two arrow-ends. For when two arrows are placed together and sewn together in the middle with a thread, it is called "the middle of the ends.
When the thread is cut, both arrows fall apart in opposite directions. So it is here.
The two ends are like the two pieces of the arrow-shaft described above; craving is like the thread that remains after having been sewn through them.
Just as when the thread is cut, both pieces of the arrow-shaft fall apart, so too when craving has ceased, the two ends necessarily cease.
"By this much" means: by this much, having understood both ends, one should directly know [the middle] by way of being unstained by craving.

He is said to directly know the Dhamma of the Four Truths; and by means of the full understanding through scrutiny and the full understanding through abandoning, he is said to fully understand the two mundane truths that are to be fully understood.
"In this very life" (*diṭṭheva dhamme*) means in this very personal existence. "He makes an end of suffering" means he makes an end of the suffering of the round of rebirths;
he is one who effects its limit and its complete enclosure.

In the second instance, the simile should be understood by way of three arrows. For when three arrows are bound together with a string and the string is cut, the three arrows fall in three separate places;

even so, here the aggregates of the past, future, and present are like the triad of arrows, while craving is like the string. For that [craving] connects the past with the present, and the present with the future.

It is woven together with craving. Just as when the thread is cut, the triple-strand rope falls apart at its three points, so too, when craving has ceased, the aggregates (khandhas) of the past, future, and present have ceased.
In the third instance, "the neither-painful-nor-pleasant is in the middle" means it is in the middle by way of being between the two types of feeling.
For there is no interval between pleasure and pain, or between pain and pleasure.
"Craving is the seamstress" means that delight and lust for feelings prevent the cutting off of those feelings; thus it is said to "sew.

In the fourth section, "consciousness is the middle": both the rebirth-linking consciousness and the remaining consciousnesses are called the "middle" of name-and-form because they have arisen with name-and-form as their condition.

On the fifth occasion, "consciousness is in the middle" means that kamma-consciousness is in the middle; or, because the door of the mind (manāyatana) among the internal bases has grasped the kamma, any consciousness whatsoever here is said to be "in the middle"; or, because the adverting [consciousness] at the mind-door is dependent on an internal base, the impulsion-consciousness (javana-viññāṇa) is said to be "in the middle."
On the sixth occasion, "personality" (*sakkāya*) refers to the round of existence in the three realms. "The origin of personality" (*sakkāyasamudaya*) is the truth of the origin.

"The cessation of personality" (*sakkāyanirodha*) is the truth of cessation. "By way of method" (*pariyāyena*) means by that very same reason [in each case]. The rest is to be understood everywhere according to the method already stated. 8.
Commentary on the Discourse on Knowledge of the Male Faculty (*Purisindriyañāṇasutta-vaṇṇanā*)
62. In the eighth [case], "a certain one" refers to a single individual belonging to Devadatta’s faction.

"Having reflected" means having directed his attention. He asks with the underlying intention: "Was this spoken by the Blessed One after he had understood, or without understanding? Was it spoken categorically, or was it spoken analytically?
"One bound for the states of deprivation" (āpāyika) means one who is to be reborn in the woeful states. "One bound for hell" (nerayika) means...
One who goes to hell. "A kalpa-dweller" means that because of having performed an action that results in dwelling for a kalpa, he will remain for a kalpa.

"Incurable" means it is not possible to treat. "Dvedhā" means a state of being twofold. "The measure of a hair-tip's protrusion" means just enough to be shown by the tip of a hair, or just the falling of the tip of a hair. "Knowledge of the male faculty."
The meaning is: the knowledges of the degree of the faculties of individual persons; that is, the knowledges that discern whether the faculties are sharp or dull.
"Wholesome states and unwholesome states that exist" means: "I know that there are this many wholesome states existing, and this many unwholesome states existing.
"Disappeared" means they have gone out of sight. "Manifested" means by way of their active occurrence (*samudācāra*).

They became manifest. "Root of the wholesome" (*kusalamūla*) means an inclination toward the wholesome. "Wholesome, wholesome" means that from that inclination toward the wholesome, further wholesomeness will also be produced.
"Having taken the essence" (*sāradāni*) means having grasped the essence, or produced in the month of Sarada (autumn).
"Well-stored" (*sukhasayitāni*) means well-accumulated. "In a good field" (*sukhette*) means in a fertile field. "Planted" (*nikkhittāni*) means sown.
“With counterparts” means similar. “At midnight” means at the time of midnight; “when midnight has arrived.
“At the time of the meal” means at the time designated as the mealtime for royal families.
“Subject to decline”—who was known by the Blessed One to be so? King Ajātasattu. For he, relying on evil friends, had fallen away from the paths and fruits.
Furthermore, Suppabuddha, Sunakkhatta, and others were known by the Blessed One. Who was known by the Blessed One as one whose nature is not subject to decline?
The wanderer Susīma and others of that sort. Who was known by the Blessed One as one who would attain final Nibbāna?
The minister Santati and others of that sort.
9. Commentary on the Nibbedhika Sutta 63.
Regarding the ninth [sutta]: "Nibbedhika-pariyāya" means that which pierces and shatters the mass of greed (*lobha-kkhandha*) and so forth, which have not been pierced before nor shattered before;
the meaning is "the cause for piercing. "Nidāna-sambhava" refers to that which lies down in or produces sensual pleasures (*kāma*), owing to its capacity for their arising.
“Niyyādeti” means the source (nidāna). “Sambhavati tato” means it arises from that; thus, the source itself is the origin, hence “nidānasambhavo.
“Vemattatā” means differentiation.

“Kāmaguṇā” means objects of desire in the sense of being desirable (kāmayitabba), and “guṇā” in the sense of fetters (bandhana), as in the expression “antaguṇa” and so forth. “Cakkhuviññeyyā” means cognizable by the eye.
They are to be seen by eye-consciousness. "Desirable" means they are either sought after or not;
the meaning is that they have become desirable objects. "Pleasant" means lovely. "Agreeable" means increasing the mind's satisfaction. "Of a dear nature" means born of what is dear.
"Connected with sensual desire" means connected with the sensual desire that arises taking them as its object. "Lust-inducing" means being the cause for the arising of lust.

"These are not sensual pleasures" means that these do not become what are called "sensual pleasures" (kāma) in the sense of being desirable (kamana). "Lust of intention" (saṅkapparāga) is lust arisen by way of intention (saṅkappa).
"Sensual pleasure" (kāma)—this is what must be abandoned by those practicing for the abandonment of sensual pleasure; it is called "sensual pleasure" in the sense of being desirable.
"Variegated" (citra) means having variegated and diverse objects (ārammaṇa).
"Contact" means co-nascent contact. "Desiring" means desiring sensual pleasure. "Corresponding, corresponding" means of a similar nature, of a similar nature.

"Partaking of merit" means that for one who, having aspired to celestial sensual pleasures, is reborn in the world of the devas through the fulfillment of good conduct, that individual existence is called "partaking of merit";
whereas for one who is reborn in the states of deprivation through the fulfillment of misconduct, that individual existence is "partaking of demerit."
"Name. This, monks, is called "the result of sensual pleasures. Both of these types, because they arise dependent upon the pursuit of sensual pleasures, are called "the result of sensual pleasures.

"He understands this penetrative [practice]" means that the monk understands this supreme conduct which brings about penetration regarding the thirty-six bases. "The cessation of sensual pleasures" refers to that which has received its name from the very cessation of sensual pleasures.
For in this context, it is the path—designated as the holy life (*brahmacariya*)—that is called the cessation of sensual desire.
"Material" (*sāmisā*) means associated with the material of the defilements (*kilesāmisasampayuttā*). In this manner, the meaning is to be understood in all instances.

Furthermore, here "resulting in conventional expression" (*vohāravepakkā*) means having conventional expression as its result (*vohāravipāka*). For conventional expression, which consists of discourse, is indeed called the result of perception (*saññā*). Just as...

The phrase "yathā nanti ettha naṃ" is merely a particle (*nipātamatta*). Thus, because it is said that "in whatever way one perceives, in exactly that way one becomes one who possesses such a perception," the meaning is that [perception] ripens as conventional expression (*vohāravepakkā*).
"Ignorance" (*avijjā*) refers to the dense ignorance consisting of non-knowing regarding the eight points. "Leading to hell" (*nirayagamaniyā*) means those things which cause one to go to hell.
The meaning is: "the condition for rebirth in hell. The same method applies to the remaining cases as well. "I say 'volition'" (*cetanāhaṃ*) means "I [say] volition" (*cetanaṃ*).

Here, the volition that encompasses all [factors] (*sabbasaṅgāhikā saṃvidahanacetanā*) is taken. "Having willed" (*cetayitvā*) refers to the volition proceeding through the sense doors. "By the mind" (*manasā*) means by the consciousness associated with volition.
"To be experienced in hell" (*nirayavedanīyaṃ*) means that which yields its result in hell. The same method applies to the remaining cases as well.
*Adhimattaṃ* means intense suffering. *Dandhavirāgī* means suffering that fades away slowly rather than quickly, being heavy and gradual.
*Urattāḷiṃ kandati* means he weeps while beating his breast. *Pariyeṭṭhiṃ* means searching.
*Ekapadaṃ dvipadaṃ* means either a one-word verse or a two-word verse; the meaning is, "Who knows this verse? *Sammohavepakkam* means having delusion as its result.
For delusion regarding suffering is indeed called its "outflow-result" (*nissanda-vipāka*). The same principle applies to the second term as well;
for seeking (*pariyesanā*) is also its outflow-result. In this sutta, the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*) are explained.
10. Commentary on the Sīhanāda Sutta.
64. "The tenth: the place of the bull (āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ)" means the supreme, immovable position. "The lion’s roar" means the roar of fearlessness, the preeminent roar.

"The Brahma-wheel" means the supreme wheel of knowledge, namely both the knowledge of penetration and the knowledge of teaching. "From the standpoint of the possible and the impossible" means from the standpoint of cause and non-cause.
"By which [knowledge]" refers to that specific knowledge. "This too belongs to the Tathāgata" refers to this very knowledge of the possible and the impossible.
The Tathāgata possesses what is called the power of a Tathāgata. In this way, the meaning should be understood for all the terms. Regarding "of the undertaking of kamma" (*kamma-samādānānaṃ*):
it refers to wholesome and unwholesome kamma performed after having undertaken it; or, "undertaking of kamma" (*kamma-samādāna*) is simply the kamma itself.

"According to the situation and the cause" (*ṭhānaso hetuso*) means according to both the condition (*paccaya*) and the cause (*hetu*). In that context, the destination, the basis, the time, and the application are the "situation" (*ṭhāna*) for the result, while the kamma is the "cause" (*hetu*).
“Of the jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments” means: of the four jhānas, the eight liberations, the three concentrations, and the nine successive attainments.
“Corruption” refers to states conducive to decline. “Purification” refers to states conducive to distinction.
“Emergence” means that purification itself is emergence; it is the emerging from each respective concentration.
"Emergence is also emergence"—thus it is said that both the familiar jhāna and the fruition-attainments (phalasamāpatti) are included.
For each successive lower familiar jhāna serves as the proximate cause (padatthāna) for each successive higher one;
therefore, "purification is also emergence" is stated. However, emergence from all jhānas occurs by means of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and [emergence] from the fruition-attainment...
Emergence occurs from the attainment of cessation. With reference to this, it is said: "Emergence from each respective concentration is also emergence.
The terms "in various ways" and so forth have been explained in the *Visuddhimagga*. The knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya-ñāṇa*) has already had its meaning explained above.
For one who desires a detailed exposition of the preceding three knowledges as well, [one should consult] the *Majjhima-aṭṭhakathā*.
The commentary on the "Great Lion’s Roar" (*Mahāsīhanāda*) should be consulted. "Of one who is concentrated" (*samāhitassa*) means of one whose mind is one-pointed.

"Concentration is the path" (*samādhi maggo*) means that concentration is the means for the attainment of these knowledges. "Lack of concentration" (*asamādhi*) means a state of non-one-pointedness. "A wrong path" (*kummaggo*) means a false path.
In this sutta, the power of knowledge (*ñāṇabala*) of the Tathāgata is explained.

Fifty-Section 1. The Chapter on Wealth (Dhanavagga) 1–5. Commentary on the First Discourse on the Dear One and Others The term *paṇṇāsaka* refers to a collection of fifty discourses. This section comprises five discourses beginning with the "First Discourse on the Dear One" (*Paṭhamapiyasutta*). The commentary (*vaṇṇanā*) upon these follows. **Commentary on the First Discourse on the Dear One:** In this discourse, the Blessed One teaches that there are four things that are dear, beloved, and pleasing to oneself, yet which one must eventually relinquish. These are: wealth, relatives, health, and life itself. The Blessed One further explains that while these things are cherished by worldly beings, they are impermanent, subject to change, and inevitably lead to suffering. He contrasts this with the practice of the Noble One, who, through wisdom and renunciation, does not cling to such worldly attachments, thereby attaining liberation from suffering. **Commentary on the Second Discourse on the Dear One:** This discourse elaborates on the same theme, emphasizing that although these four things—wealth, relatives, health, and life—are naturally dear to all living beings, they are nonetheless transitory. The wise person understands their nature and does not become overwhelmed by grief when they pass away, whereas the foolish person, failing to see their impermanence, suffers greatly at their loss. **Commentary on the Third Discourse on the Dear One:** In this teaching, the Blessed One addresses the inevitability of separation from what is dear. He illustrates this through various examples, showing how even the most cherished possessions, kin, and physical well-being must eventually be left behind. He urges his disciples to cultivate detachment and to take refuge in the Dhamma, which is the only true and lasting source of security. **Commentary on the Fourth Discourse on the Dear One:** This discourse focuses on the distinction between the "dear" (*piya*) and the "pleasing" (*manāpa*). The Blessed One explains that while these qualities are universally desired, they do not bring ultimate happiness. True happiness arises from the cessation of craving for these things. By understanding the nature of desire and its consequences, one can transcend attachment and attain peace of mind. **Commentary on the Fifth Discourse on the Dear One:** The final discourse in this series provides a practical guide for those who wish to live in accordance with the Dhamma despite the presence of worldly attachments. The Blessed One advises his followers to maintain mindfulness and clear comprehension regarding their possessions, family, health, and life. By doing so, they can remain undisturbed by the vicissitudes of existence and progress toward the goal of Nibbāna. Thus concludes the commentary on the first five discourses of the Chapter on Wealth. These teachings collectively serve as a profound reflection on the nature of human attachment and the path to liberation from it.

In the fourth [sutta], "one liberated in both ways" means one who is liberated by two parts: from the material body by means of the formless attainments.

He is liberated from the mental body by means of the path. He is fivefold: by way of those who have attained Arahantship after emerging from each of the four formless attainments and comprehending formations;
and by way of the Non-returners who have attained Arahantship after emerging from cessation.
Regarding this, the text says: "And what kind of person is one liberated in both ways? Herein, a certain person..."
“A person dwells having touched the eight liberations with the body; and having seen with wisdom, his taints are completely destroyed.
Thus it is said with reference to one who has attained the eight liberations.
“Liberated by wisdom” means one liberated through wisdom (*paññāvimutta*). He is a dry-insight practitioner (*sukkha-vipassaka*) who, having emerged from the four jhānas, attains Arahantship.

It is fivefold by way of these four [types of individuals] and the one who has attained [the fruit]. However, the canonical text here is presented specifically by way of the negation of the eight liberations.
As it is said: "He does not dwell having touched the eight liberations with the body;
yet, having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed. This person is called one liberated by wisdom."
One who has realized that which is touched is a body-witness (*kāyasakkhī*). He first touches the contact of jhāna and subsequently realizes cessation, Nibbāna.
He is of six kinds, beginning from the stage of the fruit of stream-entry up to the stage of the path of arahantship.
Therefore it was said: "In this case, a certain person dwells having touched the eight liberations with the body, and [having attained] through wisdom..."
Upon seeing this, some of his taints (āsava) are completely exhausted. This person is called a "body-witness" (kāyasakkhī).
One who has reached the view is a "view-attainer" (diṭṭhippatto). Herein is the brief definition:
when it is known, seen, understood, realized, and touched by wisdom that "formations are suffering and cessation is bliss," one is a view-attainer.
In detail, however, this person also is of six kinds, just like the body-witness (kāyasakkhī). Therefore it was said: "Here, a certain person understands as it really is:
'This is suffering'... [and so on] ...he understands as it really is: 'This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
And the teachings proclaimed by the Tathāgata have been clearly seen and scrutinized by his wisdom... [and so on]."
“This person is called one who has attained through vision.
One who is liberated by faith is a faith-liberated one (*saddhāvimutta*). He too is sixfold according to the method already stated. Therefore it was said:
“Here, a certain person understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’ … [and so on] … ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.’”
He understands things as they truly are, and the teachings proclaimed by the Tathāgata have been clearly seen and thoroughly mastered by his wisdom...
[as before] ...but not yet attained through the realization of right view. This person is called one liberated by faith (*saddhāvimutta*).
For at the moment of the preliminary path, this one liberated by faith is as if believing and as if resolving with confidence.

For one who is resolving [on this], there is the destruction of the defilements; for one who has attained vision, at the moment of the preliminary path, the knowledge that severs the defilements proceeds unhindered, sharp, and courageous.
Therefore, just as when cutting a plantain tree with a sword that is not too sharp, the cut surface is not smooth, the sword does not proceed swiftly, and there is a sound...
A sound is heard, a more powerful effort must be exerted; such is the development of the preliminary path for one liberated through faith (*saddhāvimutta*).

However, just as when a very sharp sword cuts a plantain tree, the cut surface is smooth, the sword glides swiftly, no sound is heard, and no great effort is required—such is the case for one liberated through wisdom (*paññāvimutta*).
The development of the path in its prior stage should be understood.
One who recollects the Dhamma is a "Dhamma-follower" (dhammānusārī). "Dhamma" here means wisdom; the meaning is that he develops the path preceded by wisdom.
The same method applies to the "faith-follower" (saddhānusārī) as well. Both of these are still at the stage of the stream-entry path (sotāpatti-magga). And this has also been said:

“For that person who has entered upon the practice for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, if the faculty of wisdom is predominant, they develop the Noble Path, which is carried by wisdom and preceded by wisdom. This person is called a ‘follower of the Dhamma.
For that person who has entered upon the practice for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, if the faculty of faith is predominant...”
“He possesses faith and develops the Noble Path with faith as its vehicle and faith as its precursor. This person is called a ‘follower by faith.

This is the summary here; however, this detailed discussion on those liberated in both ways and so forth is set forth in the *Visuddhimagga* in the section on the development of wisdom (*paññābhāvanā*).
Therefore, it should be understood according to the method explained therein.

It rises up. "Sādhu" means beautiful, auspicious, and excellent. "It only declines" means it diminishes, just like water poured onto a slope.
"Having emerged, he sees clearly and looks around" means that having risen up, he sees clearly and looks around in the direction he must go.
"He crosses over" means he is said to cross over facing the direction he must travel. "He has reached a firm footing" means having risen, looked around, and crossed over.
"He has reached a firm footing in one place" means he stands there and does not return.

"He has crossed over, gone to the further shore, and stands on dry land" means that having crossed the flood of all defilements and gone to the further shore, he is established in the ground of Nibbāna.
