6. Commentary on the Discourse on Contemplating Impermanence (Aniccānupassīsutta) 16.
In the sixth [verse], one who contemplates by striking with wisdom thus, "Impermanent," is "one who contemplates impermanence" (*aniccānupassī*).

One who has such a perception as "impermanent" is "one who perceives impermanence" (*aniccasaññī*). One who has experienced this through knowledge thus, "Impermanent," is "one who experiences impermanence" (*aniccapaṭisaṃvedī*).
“Constantly” means at all times. “Continuously” means in such a way that the subsequent consciousness is joined to, approached by, and touched by the preceding consciousness.
“Uninterrupted” means without interval, unmixed with any other state of mind. “Resolving with the mind” means determining with the mind.
“Plunging with wisdom” means penetrating with the knowledge of insight (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*).
"Neither before nor after" means neither earlier nor later, but at one and the same moment. Here, the "one who attains final nibbāna with the head even" (samasīsī) is described. He is fourfold:
one who attains it with the head even through disease, one through feeling, one through posture, and one through life.
Among these, for one who is afflicted by some kind of disease, the subsiding of that disease and the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya) occur simultaneously.

This is called "the simultaneous summit of illness. However, for one who experiences a certain feeling and for whom the subsiding of that feeling and the destruction of the taints occur simultaneously, this is called "the simultaneous summit of feeling.

Furthermore, for one who possesses a certain posture among the postures such as standing and so forth, and who is practicing insight, the conclusion of that posture and the destruction of the taints occur simultaneously.

This is called "the simultaneous termination of the postures. However, when for someone the exhaustion of the life-faculty and the destruction of the taints occur simultaneously—either through deliberate effort or by the force of nature—this is called "the simultaneous termination of the life-faculty. This is what is intended here.
In this regard, although the exhaustion of the taints occurs with the path-consciousness, the exhaustion of the life-faculty occurs with the death-consciousness.

There is no such thing as the simultaneous occurrence of both. However, because his life comes to an end immediately after the moment of reviewing the destruction of the taints (*āsava*), with no interval being discerned, it is stated thus.
An "antarā-parinibbāyin" is one who, having been born in any of the five Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsa*), attains final Nibbāna at the very moment of rebirth.
Or, having passed slightly beyond [the middle], or standing in the middle, one attains *arahantship*; this is its name.
One who attains *parinibbāna* upon reaching (*upahacca*) is one who attains *arahantship* right there after passing the middle of the lifespan.

One who attains *parinibbāna* without exertion (*asaṅkhāra*) is one who exhausts the defilements by means of non-exertion, that is, without application. One who attains *parinibbāna* with exertion (*sasaṅkhāra*) is...

"One who exhausts the defilements with effort and exertion. "One who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm" refers to one who, having been reborn in any of the four lower Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa), passes away from there and, arising successively through the higher realms, attains Arahantship in Akaniṭṭha.
7–9. Commentary on the Discourses on the Contemplation of Suffering, etc.
17–19. In the seventh [application of mindfulness], "contemplating suffering" means contemplating the mode of oppression as suffering.

In the eighth, "contemplating non-self" means contemplating the mode of lack of mastery as non-self. In the ninth, "contemplating pleasure" means contemplating it as pleasure by means of such knowledge.
10. Commentary on the *Niddasavatthusutta* (The Discourse on the Grounds for Praise).

20. *Dasama-niddasa-vatthūni*: the grounds for the term "niddasa" and so forth; that is, the reasons for speaking thus: "The bhikkhu is *niddasa* (without ten), *nibbīsa*, *nittimso*, *niccattālīso*, *nippaññāso*.
It is said that this question arose during the period of the non-Buddhist sects (*titthiya-samaya*).
For the non-Buddhists say that a Nigaṇṭha who has died at the age of ten is "niddasa. It is further said that he [the Nigaṇṭha] becomes ten years old again.
It does not exist. And it is not only one of ten years; even one of nine years or one year does not exist.
In this same manner, when they have reached twenty years and so forth, they say of a dead Nigaṇṭha: "He is without ten, without thirty, without forty, without fifty.
The Venerable Ānanda, while wandering through the village, heard that talk; having gone to the monastery, he reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said: "No..."
“Ānanda, this is a designation for the followers of other sects; in my teaching, it is a designation for one whose taints are exhausted.

For one whose taints are exhausted, having attained final nibbāna at ten years [of age], does not become ten years old again. Nor only at ten years, but even at nine years... [and so on] ...even at one year.
Nor only at one year, but even at eleven months... [and so on] ...even at one month, or even for a single moment.”
"It simply does not exist. Why? Because there is no further rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). This same principle applies to the terms "free from hunger" (*nibbisā*) and so forth.

Thus, having stated, "In my teaching, this is a designation for one whose taints are exhausted," the Blessed One began this teaching in order to demonstrate the reasons by which one becomes free from craving (*niddaso*).
In this context, "here" means in this teaching (*sāsana*). "He has a keen desire for undertaking the training" means he has a powerful desire for fulfilling the threefold training (*sikkhāttaya*).

"And he possesses undiminished affection for undertaking the training in the future" means that even on future days and so forth, he remains endowed with undiminished affection for fulfilling the training.
"For the sake of settling in the Dhamma" means for the purpose of investigating the Dhamma.
This is a designation for insight (vipassanā). "Discipline of desire" means the discipline of craving (taṇhā). "Seclusion" means solitude.
"Exertion of energy" means the fulfillment of physical and mental energy. "Mindfulness and circumspection" means both mindfulness and the state of being prudent.
"Penetration by view" means the seeing of the Path. The rest is clear in every respect.
The Second Chapter on Latent Tendencies (Anusaya-vagga).
3. The Third Chapter on the Seven [Points] of the Vajjīs (Vajji-sattaka-vagga). 1. Commentary on the Sāraṇada Sutta.
21. "In the first [monastery] at Sārandada Cetiya" refers to the monastery bearing that name.

It is said that before the Tathāgata had appeared, there was a shrine (*cetiya*) there which was the dwelling place of the *yakkha* Sārandada; subsequently, they had a monastery built for the Blessed One there.
Thus, it became known as Sārandada Cetiya. "For as long as" (*yāvakīvañca*) means for whatever length of time. "Frequently" (*abhiṇhaṃ*).
“Frequent assemblies” means that they assemble three times a day, or even at intervals throughout the day; thus, they are indeed frequent assemblies.
“Habitual assembly” means that they do not fall into complacency by thinking, “We have assembled yesterday and the day before;
why should we assemble again today?”—thus they are habitual in their assembly. Licchavis, there is only growth for the Vajjis.
"It is to be expected that there will be decline" means that by not assembling frequently, they do not hear the news arriving from various directions;
consequently, they do not know that "the boundary of such-and-such a village or market town is in turmoil, or that robbers have overrun such-and-such a place.
Then the robbers, perceiving that "the kings are negligent," strike at the villages, market towns, and so forth, and destroy the countryside. Thus...
There is decline for kings. However, when they assemble frequently, they hear of that situation; then, by dispatching an army, they crush their enemies.
Even the thieves, thinking, "The kings are vigilant; it is not possible for us to roam about in organized bands," break up and flee.
In this way, there is growth for kings. Therefore it was said: "Only growth..."
“O Licchavis, this is to be expected for the Vajjis; there will be no decline.

Regarding the passage beginning with “united,” when the drum for assembly has been sounded, those who cause a distraction by saying, “I have business today,” or “I have an auspicious ceremony,” are said not to assemble unitedly.
However, upon merely hearing the sound of the drum, even those who are eating [assemble].
Even while adorning themselves and putting on their robes—half-eaten and half-adorned—they are said to have assembled in harmony as they gather together.

But once assembled, having deliberated and consulted, and having performed what was to be done, if they do not withdraw together, they are not said to withdraw in harmony. For among those who have thus withdrawn, those who [depart] first...
As they go, it occurs to them: "We have heard only external talk; now there will be a discussion on legal matters.

When they emerge from their retreat together, they are said to emerge in concord. Furthermore, having heard that "in such-and-such a place the village boundary or town boundary is disturbed, or it is overrun by thieves," and when it is asked, "Who will go and act as the crusher of enemies? [they respond accordingly].
Even when walking while saying, "I first! I first!", they are said to be rising in harmony.
However, when one person’s work is failing, even if the others send their sons and brothers to support that person’s labor, they do not say to the visiting king, "Let him go to so-and-so’s house;
let him go to so-and-so’s house," but rather [they all go together].

Even when supporting one another, or when a festival, an illness, or some other such pleasure or pain arises for one person, all of them go there as companions and perform what ought to be done together in harmony. Regarding the phrases "unpromulgated" and so forth:
they are called "unpromulgated" when they cause others to bring taxes, tributes, or fines that were not previously established.
They are said to "lay down" [rules]. However, those who do not uphold what has come down through the ancient tradition are said to "abolish" what has been laid down.
When a thief is caught and presented, those who, without investigating, order his mutilation or execution are said to "fail to act in accordance with the ancient Vajjian custom.
For those who lay down what was not previously laid down, people will be oppressed by new taxes and the like.
“‘We are greatly oppressed; who will dwell in their kingdom?’—thinking thus, they enter the borderlands and, becoming thieves or accomplices of thieves, they slaughter the countryside.
By abolishing what has been established and by failing to collect the traditional taxes and duties, the treasury declines.
Consequently, the elephants, cavalry, infantry, women of the harem, and so forth, being unable to receive their regular allowances as assigned, [fall into ruin].”
They decline in strength and power. They become neither capable of fighting nor capable of service.
Because they do not adhere to the ancient Vajjian tradition, the people in the conquered territories, becoming angry, think:
"They have treated our sons, fathers, and brothers as if they were thieves, though they were not thieves," and having cut them down and broken them, they enter the borderlands and become bandits.
Or, having become accomplices with thieves, they plunder the countryside. In this way, there is a decline for kings.

However, when they do not establish what has not been established, people—thinking, "The kings are merely following the traditional lineage"—become joyful and content, and they carry out their occupations such as agriculture and trade.
When they do not abolish what has been established, but continue to collect the traditional taxes and duties, [the kingdom prospers].

The treasury increases; consequently, the elephant corps, cavalry, infantry, and women’s quarters, receiving their respective allowances, become endowed with strength and power, capable both of warfare and of service.

People do not criticize those who conduct themselves by undertaking the ancient Vajjian laws. "The kings act according to the ancient tradition, together with the *aṭṭakula* ministers, generals, and vice-kings..."
“Having surrounded themselves, they in turn surround the ancestral book and, having had it recited, they inflict a fitting punishment;
there is no fault in them, but the fault is ours alone. Thinking thus, they perform their duties with diligence.
In this way, the prosperity of kings comes about.
"Honoring" means that whatever honor they perform for them, they will perform it beautifully. "Revering" means they will perform it by establishing a sense of respect.
"Honoring" means they will hold them dear with affection. "Worshiping" means they will worship them with the offering of requisites.
"Thinking them worthy of being heard" means [going to] attend upon them two or three times a day.
Having gone there, they will think that what those [elders] say should be heard and believed.
In this regard, those who do not perform honors and the like for such great kings, or who do not go to attend upon them for the sake of receiving instruction, become neglected by them;
being without counsel and addicted to play, they fall away from their kingdom. But those who act accordingly—
Those elder kings explain the ancient tradition, saying, "This should be done; this should not be done.
Even when they have entered into battle, they show them the proper method, saying, "One should enter thus; one should withdraw thus.
Being thus advised by them and practicing according to that advice, they are able to maintain the royal lineage. Therefore it was said:
—“Only growth, O Licchavis, is to be expected for the Vajjis. *Kulitthiyo*:
women of good family, i.e., the mistresses of noble households. *Kulakumāriyo*: their daughters who have not yet been married. *Okassa* means either “having pushed aside” or “having forced”;
this is simply a name for the manner of pushing aside. Some also read *okāsā*; in that case, *okassa* means “having cleared away” or “having drawn aside.”
*Pasayha* means having overcome or having overwhelmed; such is the etymological meaning. For those who act in this way, the people within their realm become incensed, thinking:

"They have forcibly seized even our sons and brothers, and even our daughters—who were raised by us after we removed from our mouths their spittle, mucus, and so forth—and are keeping them in their own homes. Thus they enter the borderlands in revolt.

Or, having become thieves or accomplices of thieves, they plunder the countryside. But when they do not act in this way, the people within the realm remain free from anxiety and, performing their own duties, increase the royal treasury. In this manner, the growth and decline [of the kingdom] are to be understood.
As for "the Vajjian shrines of the Vajjis," these are so named because they were objects of veneration (*cetiyata*) by the Vajjian kings in the Vajjian territory.
The abodes of the *yakkhas*. "Internal" means those situated within the city; "external" means those situated outside the city.

"Previously given and previously performed" means both what was given and what was done in the past. "They will not let it fall away" means they will not neglect it, but will carry it out exactly as it has been established.
For when people neglect the lawful tax (*dhammika-bali*), the deities do not provide well-ordered protection.
Even when they are unable to prevent unarisen suffering from arising, they increase coughs, headaches, and other ailments that have already arisen;
when a battle is joined, they do not act as allies. However, for those who do not neglect their protection, they provide well-arranged security;
even when they are unable to produce unarisen happiness, they remove coughs, headaches, and other ailments that have already arisen; at the head of the battle, they are true allies.
"Thus they are. In this way, increase and decrease should be understood here.

Regarding "righteous protection, warding, and guarding": herein, it is "protection" (*rakkhā*) because it wards off (*āvaraṇa*) that which is undesired so that it does not come; it is "warding" (*āvaraṇa*) because of such warding.
It is "guarding" (*gutti*) because of protecting (*gopāyanā*) that which is desired so that it is not lost. Therein, having surrounded [it] with a body of troops...
For those who have gone forth, there is no such thing as "protection" in the sense of lawful guarding, warding, and defense.

However, when they do not cut down trees in the monastery grove, do not let birds build nests, and do not catch fish in the lotus ponds—acting in this manner is what is called lawful guarding, warding, and defense. *Kinti* means: by what cause indeed?
In this regard, those who do not desire the arrival of future Arahants are faithless and lack confidence.
When a renunciant has arrived, they do not go out to meet him; having gone, they do not look upon him;
they do not offer hospitality, they do not ask questions, they do not listen to the Dhamma, they do not give gifts, and they do not hear the expression of thanks.
They do not provide a place for lodging. Then their ill-repute spreads: "Such-and-such a king is faithless and lacks confidence;
when renunciants arrive, he does not go out to meet them... [and so on] ...he does not provide a place for lodging.
Hearing this, even when passing through the city gate, the renunciants do not enter the city. Thus, those who have not yet arrived—

For the Arahants, there is simply no returning. But for those who have already arrived, if there is no comfortable dwelling, even those who came without knowing [the situation] think, "We came thinking we would stay," yet they depart, wondering, "Under this kind of conduct by these kings, who will remain?
Thus, while those who have not come do not come, and those who have come dwell in suffering.
That fault makes it an unfit dwelling for those who have gone forth. Consequently, there is no protection from deities;
when there is no protection from deities, non-human beings find an opportunity. When non-human beings are prevalent, they cause unarisen diseases to arise.

Furthermore, there is no influx of merit based on seeing those possessed of virtue or inquiring after their questions, and so forth. By contrast, this is the opposite of what was stated regarding the dark side.
"The waxing moon increases"—thus should growth and decline be understood here.
2. Commentary on the Vassakāra Sutta. 22.
In the second [sutta], "desiring to attack" means desiring to go for the purpose of overcoming. "The Vajjis" refers to the kings of the Vajjis. "Possessing such great power" means...
"Endowed with such great royal power": by this he expresses their state of being united. "Possessing such great majesty":

by this he expresses their proficiency in the training in elephant-lore and other arts, with reference to which it was said: "Truly well-trained are these Licchavi youths, truly well-trained are these..."

“Licchavi youths, it is truly remarkable that they will cause the arrow to pass through the fine crevice of the palm-leaf with such precision, shot after shot without fail. “I shall cut off” means “I will sever. “I shall destroy” means “I will lead [them] to disappearance.
“Calamity and ruin” means both loss of prosperity and loss of kinsmen. “I shall bring about” means “I will cause [them] to fall into.”
Thus, indeed, while standing or sitting and so forth, he spoke only of this talk of war and commanded his army, saying, "Be ready to march.

Why? It is said that near a certain port town on the Ganges, half a *yojana* was the territory of Ajātasattu and half a *yojana* belonged to the Licchavis. There, from the foot of a mountain, goods of great value—
[The Licchavis] descend. Having heard this, even as Ajātasattu was making arrangements, saying, "I will go today;
I will go tomorrow," the Licchavis arrived earlier in a united and harmonious body and took everything.
Ajātasattu, arriving later, learned of that occurrence and departed in anger. They did exactly the same thing again the following year. Then—
Thus, born of powerful anger, he acted in this way at that time.
Then he thought: "A battle with a multitude is indeed a grave matter; there is no such thing as a single futile blow.
However, one who acts after consulting with a wise man remains free from fault, and a wise man [is like] a Teacher."
“There is no one equal to him, and the Teacher resides not far away in the Dhura Monastery.
Come now, I shall send someone to inquire. If there is some purpose for my going, the Teacher will remain silent;
but if there is no purpose, he will say, ‘What is the King’s business in going there? He then dispatched the brahmin Vassakāra. The brahmin went and...
He reported that matter to the Blessed One. Thus it was said: "Then the king... [omitted] ...I shall cause the Vajjis to be brought under subjection.
While fanning the Blessed One, the Elder stood at the head of his duties and fanned the Blessed One;
yet for the Blessed One there is neither cold nor heat. Having heard the words of the brahmin, the Blessed One did not converse with him.
Desiring to consult with the Elder, he said, "What have you heard, Ānanda? and so forth. That has the same meaning as already stated.
"I have heard this once" was said by the Blessed One in order to demonstrate that this Vajji Sutta had previously been taught to the Vajjīs.
"Not to be done" (*akaraṇīya*) means not to be performed; the sense is "not to be undertaken. *Yadidaṃ* is merely an expletive particle. "Of war" (*yuddhassa*)...

The genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental; the meaning is that he was unable to capture him by means of battle face-to-face. "Except for conciliation" means setting aside conciliation.
Conciliation (*upalāpanā*) is the act of winning over [an enemy] by sending elephants, horses, chariots, silver, gold, and so forth, saying, "Enough with this dispute; let us now be united.
For it is only by making such a conciliation that one is able to capture him through mere trust.
The meaning is: "Except for causing a breach of friendship" means setting aside the breaking of friendships.
By this, he shows: "Even by creating mutual dissension, it is possible to capture them. Having grasped the underlying method (*naya*) in the Blessed One's discourse, the brahmin spoke these words.
But did the Blessed One know that the brahmin had grasped the method through this discourse? Yes, he knew it. Knowing it...
Why did he speak? Out of compassion. For it occurred to him: "Even if I do not tell him, he will go in a few days and seize them all;
but if I do tell him, he will take three years to seize them by creating a schism among those who are united.
Even this much life is better, for while living thus they will perform merit that serves as their own support. Having rejoiced...
"Having rejoiced with his mind. "Having expressed approval" means having expressed approval with his voice, saying, "How well spoken this is by the Blessed Gotama!
"He departed" means he went into the presence of the king. The king, too, having sent him away and having caused them all to be divided, went and brought about their ruin and disaster.
3. Commentary on the First Sutta of the Group of Seven (Paṭhamasattakasuttavaṇṇanā)
23. Regarding the third [point], "frequent assemblies," this is exactly the same as what was stated in the *Vajjiputta Satta*.

Here too, those who do not assemble frequently do not hear the messages arriving from various directions; consequently, they do not learn that "the boundary of such-and-such monastery is in disorder, the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies have been suspended, in such-and-such a place the monks are performing medical treatments, messenger services, and so forth, and they are making many requests for gifts of fruit, flowers, and the like."
They do not know such things as [how] "they make their living.
Even wicked bhikkhus, perceiving that "the Saṅgha is negligent," gather in groups and cause the Dispensation to decline. However, those who assemble frequently hear of that situation;

consequently, they dispatch a community of bhikkhus to straighten out the boundaries (*sīmā*), cause the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies to proceed, and [act] in places where wrong livelihoods are prevalent.
Having dispatched those belonging to the noble lineage, they cause the discourse on the noble lineage to be taught; they cause the holders of the Vinaya to carry out the suppression of evil monks.
Even the evil monks, thinking, "The Saṅgha is vigilant; it is not possible for us to wander about by forming factions," break away and flee.
In this way, the increase and decline therein are to be understood.
Regarding the phrase "united" (*samagga*) and so forth: when the gong or bell is struck merely to call for the Saṅgha to assemble for the purpose of repairing a cetiya,
or for covering the Bodhi-house or the Uposatha-hall, or out of a desire to establish a formal agreement (*katikavatta*), [if one creates] an obstacle by saying,
"I have work on my robes," "my alms-bowl must be baked," or "I have construction work."
When they perform [the formal act] without being in harmony, it is said that they do not meet in harmony.
However, when they set aside all other business and meet simultaneously, each thinking, "I shall be first, I shall be first," it is said that they meet in harmony.
But once they have met, deliberated, consulted, and performed what was to be done, if they do not withdraw together as one, they do not withdraw in harmony.
...so it is called. For when they have risen in this manner, those who go first think: "We have heard only the external talk;
now there will be discussion on the points of legal decision (*vinicchaya*). Those who rise all at once are said to have risen in concord. Furthermore, [they consider]:

"In such-and-such a place the monastery boundary (*vihārasīmā*) is confused, and the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies are suspended; in such-and-such a place there are those performing medical treatments and the like..."
Having heard that "evil bhikkhus have become numerous," when it was asked, "Who will go and subdue them? they each said, "I first! I first!
and even as they were departing, they were called "unitedly setting out.
However, upon seeing a visitor, instead of saying, "Go to this cell; go to that cell; who is this?", [they would not speak thus].
Even though all of them perform their duties— even when seeing worn-out bowls and robes, they seek out bowls and robes for him during his alms-round;
even when seeking medicine for the sick, they do not say to the sick man who is without a protector,
"Go to such-and-such a cell," but rather look after him in their own respective cells— there is still one single knot of a literary work that remains stuck.
Having won over a wise bhikkhu and having had him recite that text, they perform sangha-business in concord; this is what is meant by "performing sangha-business in concord.

Regarding the phrases "not laid down" and so forth: when they adopt a new, unrighteous rule of conduct (*katikavatta*) or a training precept (*sikkhāpada*), they are said to "lay down what has not been laid down," just as the bhikkhus did at Sāvatthī in the case of the old rug. [They act] contrary to the Dhamma and contrary to the Vinaya.

Those who illuminate the Dispensation but abolish what has been prescribed are said to "abolish the established rule," like the Vajjiputtakas of Vesālī when the Blessed One had been parinibbāna for a hundred years.

However, those who intentionally transgress even minor and lesser offenses and do not conduct themselves by undertaking the training rules as they were prescribed are said to "not live according to the training," like Assaji and Punabbasu. But those who do not act in such a way...
They do not prescribe what has not been prescribed, they do not abolish what has been prescribed, and they undertake and practice the training rules exactly as they have been laid down—
just like the Venerable Upasena, the Venerable Yasa Kākaṇḍakaputta, and the Venerable Mahākassapa.
"Only growth" means there is only growth in virtues such as moral discipline, and no decline.

"Elders" (*therā*) means those who have attained stability and are endowed with the qualities that constitute the state of an elder. "Knowing many nights" (*rattaññū*) means they know many nights [of the religious life].

"Long-ordained" (*cirapabbajitā*) means those for whom it has been a long time since their going forth. "Fathers of the Saṅgha" (*saṅghapitaro*) means they stand in the place of fathers to the Saṅgha.
Because they stand in the place of fathers, they hand over the Saṅgha; acting as leaders, [they establish them] in the three trainings.
They are called "leaders of the Saṅgha" because they cause [the Dhamma] to proceed.
Those who do not show them honor and so forth, or who do not attend upon them two or three times for the sake of instruction—
even such people they do not give instruction to, nor do they speak to them of the traditional lineage, nor of the essential discourses on the Dhamma.
They do not train them. Deprived of those aggregates of Dhamma such as virtue and so forth, and of the seven noble treasures, they thus decline in such qualities.
However, to those who pay them honor and attend upon them, they give instruction such as, "In this way you should approach," and they relate the traditional lineage, which is the very essence.
They train them in the exposition of the Dhamma and instruct them in the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) and the ten bases of discourse (kathāvatthu).
Standing by that instruction, they grow in virtues such as moral discipline (sīla) and so forth, and attain the goal of recluseship (sāmaññattha).
In this way, decline and growth are to be understood here.
"Ponobbhavikā" means that which has renewed existence as its nature; the sense is "that which brings about renewed existence.
[The phrase] "of that *ponobbhavikā*" refers to this. "They will not come under its power":
here, those who, for the sake of the four requisites, wander from village to village following after their attendants, are said to come under its power. Others do not.

In this regard, the decrease and increase [of concentration] are indeed evident. "In forest-dwelling places" means in those located at least five hundred bow-lengths from an inhabited area. "With longing" means with attachment.
For even after entering a jhāna in a lodging within a village boundary, as soon as one has emerged from it, one hears the sounds of men, women, boys, girls, and so forth, by which—
Even one who has attained distinction may indeed fall away. Having slept in a forest lodging, as soon as he awakens, he hears the sounds of lions, tigers, peacocks, and other creatures;
by means of this, having obtained rapture (*pīti*) in the forest and contemplating that very state, he establishes himself in the supreme fruit (*aggaphala*).
Thus, compared to a bhikkhu sitting after entering meditative absorption (*jhāna*) in a village lodging, [the Buddha praised] even one sleeping in the forest.
He praises [this]. Therefore, for that very reason, he said: "They will have regard for forest lodgings.
"They will establish mindfulness within themselves" means they will establish mindfulness within their own internal selves.
"Pesalā" means those of lovely virtue. Here too, the resident monks who do not desire the arrival of their fellow celibates are faithless.
Those who lack faith do not go out to meet the monks arriving at the monastery, nor do they receive their bowls and robes, prepare their seats, or hold the palm-leaf fans, and so forth.
Consequently, a bad reputation arises for them: "The monks residing in such-and-such a monastery are faithless and lacking in confidence;
they do not even perform the proper duties and services for those who have entered the monastery. Hearing this, the renunciants [depart] through the monastery gate.
Even when traveling, they do not enter the monastery. Thus, for those who have not yet arrived, there is simply no arrival.

But for those who have already arrived, if there is no comfortable living, even those who came without knowing [the situation] think, "We came thinking we would stay," but then, seeing that the resident monks behave in such a manner, they ask, "Who will live here? and depart. In this way, that monastery...
For other monks, it becomes a place where they have no residence at all.
Consequently, those resident monks, failing to see the virtuous ones, do not obtain the clearing away of doubts, nor instruction in conduct, nor the hearing of the sweet Dhamma.
Thus, for them there is neither the grasping of the Dhamma not yet grasped, nor the recitation of what has been grasped; in this way, there is only decline for them, not growth.
But those who desire the arrival of their fellow celibates become faithful and confident;
they go out to meet the arriving fellow celibates, prepare lodgings for them, and offer them.
Having accepted these, they enter upon the alms-round, dispel their doubts, and obtain the hearing of the sweet Dhamma. Then their fame rises up.
“In such-and-such a monastery, the bhikkhus are thus endowed with faith, confident, perfected in their duties, and supportive.
Hearing this, bhikkhus come even from afar. The resident bhikkhus perform the duties for them;
having approached, they pay homage to the senior newcomer and sit down, while taking a seat near the junior one and sitting there, [they say]: “In this monastery…”
They ask, "Will you stay, or will you go? When they reply, "We shall go," [the residents] say things such as, "The lodging is suitable;
alms-food is easily obtained," and do not let them depart. If there is one who holds the Vinaya, they recite the Vinaya in his presence.
If there is one who holds the Suttantas and so forth, they recite those various teachings in his presence. Those visiting elders...
By abiding in the instruction, they attain arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
As for visitors, they say, "We came thinking we would stay for one or two days, but because of the ease of living here, we have stayed for ten or twelve years.
In this way, the decline and growth [of the Saṅgha] are to be understood.
4. Commentary on the Second Sattaka Sutta. 24.

In the fourth [verse], "not delighting in work" refers to those who spend the day doing only such tasks as sewing robes, making waist-bands, strainers, Dhamma-wheels, brooms, foot-stones, and so forth;
it is a prohibition directed at them. However, if one performs these very tasks at the time when they ought to be done, [it is not so].
One who takes up the recitation at the time for recitation, studies at the time for study, performs the duties in the shrine courtyard at the time for those duties,
and applies mental attention at the time for mental attention— such a person is not called "one who delights in action.
But he who spends his days and nights merely engaged in conversation and chatter by way of the forms of women, the forms of men, and so forth— [he is one who delights in action].

One who does not set a limit to such talk is said to "delight in talk. However, one who expounds the Dhamma and answers questions throughout the day and night is indeed one who does not indulge in excessive talk and who sets a limit to talk. Why?
Because it has been said: "When you have gathered together, bhikkhus, two things are to be done: either discussion of the Dhamma or noble silence."
One who, whether standing, walking, or sitting, succumbs to sloth and torpor and simply falls asleep, is said to "delight in sleep.
However, when one's mind sinks into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) due to the physical exhaustion of the karmically-born body, this is not delighting in sleep. For this very reason, he said:
"I recall, Aggivessana, that in the last month of summer, after my meal, having returned from my alms round..."
“Having spread out his outer robe folded fourfold, he lies down on his right side, mindful and clearly comprehending.
One who dwells thus in company—thinking, “I am the second for one, the third for two, the fourth for three”—and does not find satisfaction in being alone, is one who delights in society.
But one who remains alone even during the four postures...
He finds gratification; he is not one who delights in social company.
Those possessed by the desire for honor from the unrighteous are called "of evil intent.

Those whose evil friends accompany them in the four postures are "evil companions," and those who, through being inclined toward, leaning toward, and tending toward that [evil], [are established] in evils...
“Completely crooked” means those who are evil friends, evil companions, and completely crooked in their company.
“By a mere trifle” means by something inferior, something insignificant. “In between” means in this interval before reaching Arahatship.
“Satisfaction” means a state of finality, a halting with the thought, “Enough with this much. This is what is meant: as long as...

As long as they do not reach a state of complacency through mere purification of virtue, meditation, insight, or the attainment of stream-entry and so forth, only growth is to be expected for the bhikkhus, not decline. 7.

27. In the seventh [section], the perceptions such as the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*) are perceptions accompanied by the contemplations of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*) and so forth. 28.
In the eighth, they are called "bearers of the burden" (*bhāravāhino*) because they carry the burden by means of accomplishing the duties of the Saṅgha that have arisen.
“They will be known by that”: those elders will be known by that activity corresponding to their own status as elders.
“He applies himself to them” means he engages in the practice; he begins to perform those duties himself.

29. "He neglects the sight of monks" means he neglects going for the purpose of seeing the community of monks (*bhikkhusaṅgha*).
"In regard to higher virtue" refers to the supreme virtue consisting of the five precepts and the ten precepts. "Outside of this" means outside of this teaching (*sāsana*).
"He seeks out those worthy of offerings" means he searches for recipients of gifts. And therein, "he performs acts of priority" means:
Having given to those outside sectarians, he afterwards gives to the monks. The rest is clear throughout.

In the fifth [verse] of the fourth [chapter], "hard to give" (*duddada*) means that which is difficult to relinquish—a precious possession.

"He does what is difficult to do" (*dukkaraṃ karoti*) means he performs an action that is not easy to perform. "He endures what is hard to endure" (*dukkhamaṃ khamati*) means he tolerates what is difficult to bear for the sake of his companion.
He accepts. "He reveals his secrets to him" means he reveals his own secrets to him. "He conceals his secrets from him" means he does not disclose his secrets to others.

he does not harbor self-contempt toward him nor pride toward himself.

In the sixth [verse], *vattā* means one who is skilled in speaking. *Vacanakkhamo* means one who endures speech; that is, he carries out the advice given to him. *Gambhīraṃ* means hidden, secret, or based upon meditative absorption (*jhāna*), insight (*vipassanā*), the path (*magga*), the fruit (*phala*), and Nibbāna.

38. Regarding the seventh [foundation of mindfulness], "this is mental sluggishness in me": when mental sluggishness has arisen, one knows it according to its true nature as "this is my mental sluggishness.
Internally contracted means being accompanied by sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*).

Externally distracted means being distracted among the five strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*). Feeling (*vedanā*) and the following terms are taken here by way of being roots of conceptual proliferation (*papañca*). Feeling...
For craving is the root of suffering because craving arises by way of pleasure; perception is the root of views because views arise regarding an object that has not been clearly discerned;
and applied thought is the root of conceit because the conceit "I am" arises by way of applied thought. "In what is favorable and unfavorable" means in what is beneficial and non-beneficial.
"Sign" means cause. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.

44–45. Regarding the first station of consciousness for the fifth [jhāna], "stations of consciousness" (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*) refers to the bases for rebirth-consciousness (*paṭisandhi-viññāṇa*).
The phrase *seyyathāpi* is a particle used in the sense of illustration; its meaning is "just as among humans.

For indeed, among the immeasurable humans in the immeasurable world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*), there are not even two who are exactly alike in terms of complexion, physical form, and so forth. This is true even for twin brothers born somewhere.

They are similar in terms of color or shape, yet even among them there is indeed a distinction in their looking forward and looking around, their speaking and laughing, their walking, standing, and so forth;
therefore, they are called "those of diverse bodies. However, their rebirth-consciousness may be triple-rooted, double-rooted, or rootless;
therefore, they are called "those of diverse perceptions. And "certain gods" refers to the six classes of sense-sphere gods.
For among them, the bodies of some are blue, while those of others are yellow or other colors. However, their perception is either double-rooted or triple-rooted;

there is none that is rootless. And as for certain beings in the states of deprivation—excluding the four lower realms—there are the yakkhinīs Uttaramātā, Piyaṅkaramātā, Phussamittā, Dhammaguttā, and others such as these, who are spirits wandering in the intermediate realm (vemānika-peta).
For their bodies are diverse by way of yellow, white, black, mottled, and tawny complexions, as well as by being emaciated, stout, short, or tall;
and their perception is likewise twofold, threefold, or rootless, like that of human beings.
However, unlike those gods, they are not of great power; rather, like poor humans, they are of little power, with food and clothing difficult to obtain, and are oppressed by suffering.
They dwell there. Some are afflicted during the dark fortnight and find happiness during the bright fortnight.

Therefore, because they have fallen from a state of great happiness, they are called "those who have fallen" (vinipātika). However, among those here, some who possess three roots (tihetuka) also attain the realization of the Dhamma, as was the case with Piyaṅkaramātā and others.
"The Brahmakāyika devas" refers to the Brahmapārisajja, the Brahmapurohita, and the Mahābrahma devas.
"First produced" means that all of them are produced by the first jhāna. However, the Brahmapārisajjas are produced by the limited (paritta) degree [of the first jhāna];
their lifespan is one-third of an eon (kappa). The Brahmapurohitas are produced by the middling degree; their [lifespan] is half an eon.
Their lifespan and their bodies are more expansive. For the Mahābrahmās, an eon is the measure of their lifespan, and their bodies are even more expansive.
Thus, due to the diversity of their bodies and the unity of their perception by way of the first jhāna, they should be understood as "those with diverse bodies and unified perception."
And just as it is with them, so it is with beings in the four states of misery. For in the hells, the personal body of some is a *gāvuta*, of some half a *yojana*, and of some a *yojana*;
but Devadatta was born with a body one hundred *yojanas* long.
Among animals too, some are small and some are large. In the realm of the hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*) as well, some are sixty cubits tall and some are eighty cubits tall.
Some are beautiful, some are ugly; likewise among the Kālakañjika asuras. Furthermore, there are certain hungry ghosts (petas) called "Long-Backed" who even measure sixty yojanas in length.

However, the perception of all of them is exclusively the unwholesome-resultant rootless perception. Thus, those belonging to the states of deprivation, despite having diverse bodies, are reckoned simply as "those with uniform perception."
They are called *Ābhassara* (Streaming Radiance) because from their bodies radiance streams forth and flashes out, as if breaking off again and again like the flame of a handheld torch;

thus they "stream" (*saranti*) and "flash" (*vissaranti*). Among them, according to the fivefold method, those who have been reborn after developing the second and third jhānas to a limited degree are called *Parittābhā* (Limited Radiance);
their lifespan measure is two eons. Having developed [the jhāna] to a middling degree...
Those reborn there are called the Appamāṇābhas (Immeasurable-Light Devas); their lifespan is four eons.

Having developed [the meditation] to a superior degree, those reborn there are called the Ābhassaras (Radiant Devas); their lifespan is eight eons. Here, however, all of them are included by way of the highest limit.
For the bodies of all of them are of one uniform radiance, while their perception is characterized by the absence of applied thought and the presence of sustained thought alone.
"Or [states] without applied thought and without sustained thought" is the distinction.
"Subhakiṇha" means interspersed or scattered with beauty; the meaning is that they are a single, solid mass due to the radiance and color of their bodies.
For in their case, unlike the Ābhassara devas, the radiance does not go forth by breaking off in fragments. However, in the system of the *Pañcakanaya*...

By means of the fourth jhāna—whether inferior, middling, or superior—they are reborn as the Parittasubhas, Appamāṇasubhas, and Subhakinhās, with lifespans of sixteen, thirty-two, and sixty-four eons respectively.

Thus, it should be understood that all of them possess a single body and, through the perception of the fourth jhāna, possess a single perception. The Vehapphalas likewise [possess] only the fourth station of consciousness.

They partake [of these realms]. Non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*), due to the absence of consciousness, do not fall within this classification; they are included among the abodes of beings (*sattāvāsa*).
The Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsa*) belong to the side of evolution (*vivaṭṭa*); they are not present at all times.

Even for a hundred thousand eons or an incalculable period (*asaṅkheyya*), they do not arise when the world is empty of Buddhas. It is only within the interval of sixteen thousand eons that Buddhas have arisen.
They arise. They are like the locations where the Blessed One established his camp during the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma.
Therefore, they do not belong to the stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*) nor to the abodes of beings (*sattāvāsa*). However, the Elder Mahāsīva said:
"But that dwelling place, Sāriputta, is not easily found which has not been inhabited by me during this long period of time, except for—"
By this sutta, "by the Suddhāvāsa devas," he says that even the Suddhāvāsas belong to the fourth station of consciousness and the fourth abode of beings;
since this cannot be refuted, it is accepted because of the authority of the sutta.
Just as with perception (saññā), the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is not "consciousness" (viññāṇa) because of the subtlety of consciousness as well.

It is not consciousness. Therefore, it is not mentioned among the stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*). In the second [case], "requisites for concentration" (*samādhiparikkhāra*) refers to the equipment for the concentration of the Path (*maggasamādhi*).
3. Commentary on the First Fire Sutta (Paṭhamaaggisutta) 46.

In the third [sutta], all [defilements] beginning with lust (*rāga*) are "fires" in the sense of burning. Regarding the terms "fire worthy of offerings" (*āhuneyyaggi*) and so forth, here "offering" (*āhuna*)...
It is called *sakkāra* (reverence); they are worthy of offerings (*āhuneyya*) because they deserve an offering (*āhuna*). For parents, being of great benefit to their children, deserve an offering;
indeed, children who act wrongly toward them are reborn in the hells and other such realms.
Therefore, although parents do not themselves burn [the child], they are the conditions for burning. Thus, it is precisely in the sense of burning that—
They are called the "fire of those worthy of offerings. A "householder" (*gahapati*), however, is called the master of a house;
he is of great benefit to his wife by providing her with bedding, clothing, ornaments, and so forth. When a woman transgresses against him, she is reborn in the hells and other such realms.

Therefore, for that reason as well—as explained in the previous manner—he is called the "householder-fire" in the sense of burning after death. Regarding the "fire of those worthy of gifts" (*dakkhiṇeyya*): here, "gift" (*dakkhiṇā*) refers to the four [requisites].

The Saṅgha of bhikkhus is worthy of offerings. For it is of great benefit to householders by enjoining them to wholesome qualities such as the three refuges, the five precepts, the ten precepts, the service of mother and father, and the service of righteous recluses and brahmins.
When householders practice wrongly toward him, they revile and disparage the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

They are reborn in the hells and other such realms. Therefore, that too is called the "fire of those worthy of offerings" (dakkhiṇeyyaggi) in the sense of burning [them], according to the same method as before.
Fire produced from wood, being of its ordinary nature, is called "wood-fire" (kaṭṭhaggi).
4. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Fire.
47. "In the fourth [case], 'of one with an exalted body' (uggatasarīra): it is said that this wealthy brahmin was exalted and reached the core both in his personal being and in his wealth;
therefore, he was known specifically as 'one with an exalted body. 'Prepared' (upakkhata) means set forth.

'Brought to the sacrificial post' (thūṇūpanītāni) means brought to the post designated as a sacrificial stake (yūpa). 'For the sake of sacrifice' (yaññatthāya) means for the purpose of sacrificing after having slaughtered [the animal]."
"He approached" means that, having prepared all those requisites for the sacrifice, he thought: "The ascetic Gotama is said to be of great wisdom;
will he speak in praise of my sacrifice or in dispraise? I shall find out by asking him.
For this reason, he approached the Blessed One. "Taking of the fire" refers to [the taking] of new [fire] for the purpose of performing the sacrifice.
"Adopting the fire of auspiciousness. "In every way, entirely" means that he shows how all that has been heard accords with, converges with, and becomes identical to all that has been heard.
"Weapons" (satthāni): they are like weapons in the sense of inflicting injury; thus they are called "weapons.
"He himself first undertakes it" means he begins it earlier than anyone else by himself. "To kill" (hantuṃ) means for the purpose of killing.
"Should be abandoned" means they should be maintained [with care]. "From this indeed" means from mother and father, indeed, this [person].
"Offered" means arrived. "Born" means arisen. "This, O Brahmin, is called the householder’s fire":

because this group consisting of children, wife, and so forth, acts as the master of the house like a householder (*gahapati*) and moves about as a flame (*aggi*), therefore it is called the householder’s fire. "The self..."
The mind. "They tame" means they tame it by the taming of the sense faculties (*indriya*). "They calm" means they calm it by the calming of lust and so forth.
They cause it to attain final Nibbāna by bringing about the final Nibbāna of those very [defilements]. "It should be laid down" means it should be placed so that it does not perish.
"Let it blow away" means let it be blown away. And having spoken thus, the brahmin [offered] the life of all those living beings.
Having given [the gift] and demolished the sacrificial hall, he became like a wellspring for the Teacher’s dispensation.
5–6. Commentary on the Two Suttas on Perception (Saññāsutta). 48–49.
In the fifth [sutta], "plunged into the Deathless" means having Nibbāna as one's foundation; "ending in the Deathless" means having Nibbāna as the final goal. In the sixth...
"Engaging in sexual intercourse" means being endowed with the act of sexual intercourse.
"A piece of sinew" means a fragment of sinew or a scraping of sinew. "Continues" means it proceeds.

"There is no distinction between before and after for me" means there is no distinction for me between the prior time when [the faculties] were undeveloped and the subsequent time when they are developed. "In the variegated worlds" refers to the dwellings within the world-systems of the three realms.
In worldly diversions. "Laziness" means the state of being indolent. "Relaxation" means the state of being lax. "Non-application" means not applying oneself to yoga.
"Free from the notions of 'I' and 'mine' and from conceit" means free from the view of "I," from the craving of "mine," and from the ninefold conceit.
"Transcending the threefold division" means having transcended the three divisions. "Peaceful."
"Peaceful" means [peaceful] from the defilements that are its opposites. "Well-liberated" means well-liberated by means of the five kinds of liberation.

50. "He approached": having finished his morning meal, he approached surrounded by his slaves and laborers. "And you, venerable sir..."
"Does he also claim to be a celibate practitioner?"—he asks this because [the other] claims to dwell in the holy life by declaring, "I am a celibate practitioner.
For it occurred to him thus: "In the tradition of the brahmins, those learning the Veda practice celibacy for forty-eight years;
yet the ascetic Gotama, while living as a householder, indulged in the three types of theatrical pleasures within his three palaces."
"Abhirami, what indeed will he say now?"— it was with reference to this matter that he asked thus.
Then the Blessed One, like one seizing a black snake with a spell, or like one treading upon an enemy’s neck with his foot,

[reflected] even upon a mere thought concerning the six years of ascetic practice during the time of his own defilement, or the bliss of sovereignty, or the splendor of theatrical performances in palaces.
It was with reference to their state of non-arising that he uttered the "lion's roar," saying, "For what reason, O Brahmin," and so forth.
In this context, "the attainment of pairs" means the state of being entered by two [persons] at a time. "From suffering" means from the entire suffering of the round of existence (*saṃsāra*).
"Laughs aloud" means he engages in joking conversation. "Sports" means he plays. "Jests" means he laughs with a loud laugh.
"With his own eye, [he sees] her eye as 'eye'" means that having penetrated her eye with his own eye, he gazes intently upon it.
"Through a wall or through a fence" means through another's wall or another's enclosure. "A god" refers to a certain king of the gods.
"A certain god" refers to a certain son of the gods. "Unsurpassed perfect enlightenment" refers both to Arahantship and to omniscient knowledge.
8. Commentary on the Saṃyoga Sutta 51.

In the eighth [sutta], "bondage and liberation" (*saṃyogavisaṃyoga*) means that which effects bondage and liberation. "A discourse on the Dhamma" (*dhammapariyāya*) means a cause or reason for the Dhamma.

"The female faculty internally" (*ajjhattaṃ itthindriyaṃ*) refers to the state of being female within one's own internal self. "Female gestures" (*itthikuttaṃ*) refers to female behavior. "Female attire" (*itthākappaṃ*)...
"Female attire" refers to what is unbecoming for a woman, such as undergarments, upper robes, and so forth.

"Female manner" means a woman’s way of acting. "Female desire" means a woman’s inclination or intention. "Female voice" means the sound of a woman. "Female ornament" means a woman’s articles of adornment.
The same method applies to the male faculty and the others. "External union" means coming together with a man. "Transgresses" means...
Having reached the Noble Path by means of this powerful insight (vipassanā) described as "non-delight," one transcends it.
In this sutta, the cycle of existence and its cessation (vaṭṭa-vivaṭṭa) are explained.
