52. "In the ninth [verse], *sāpekho* means possessing craving (*sataṇho*). *Paṭibaddhacitto* means having a mind bound to the result of maturation (*vipāka*).
*Sannidhipekho* means being one who looks for a storehouse. *Pecca* means having gone to the other world. *Taṃ kammaṃ khepetvā* means having exhausted that maturation of karma.
*Iddhiṃ* refers to the power of maturation (*vipākiddhi*). *Yasaṃ* refers to the excellence of one's retinue. *Ādhipaccaṃ* refers to the cause of seniority or leadership."

"Āgantā itthattaṃ" means: one who comes back again to this state—namely, these five aggregates; not one who is reborn there [in the higher realms], nor one who is reborn above, but rather one who goes only downward.
This is the meaning. "Sāhu dānaṃ": this gift is indeed good, auspicious, and beautiful. "Tāni mahāyaññāni":
those great sacrifices which have reached completion with ghee, fresh butter, curd, honey, molasses, and so forth.
Great gifts. "An ornament for the mind and an equipment for the mind" means they serve as both an adornment and an accessory for the mind of serenity and insight.
Regarding "companionship with the deities of the Brahma-body": it is not possible to be reborn there by means of giving alone.
However, because that [giving] serves as an ornament for the mind of serenity and insight, one who is adorned with such giving—
Having produced both jhāna and the noble path through the mind, one is reborn there by means of that jhāna.
One becomes an "anāgāmī"—that is, one is called a "jhāna-anāgāmī. "One who does not return to this state" means one will not return again to this present condition;
having been reborn either in the higher realms or right there, one attains final nibbāna in that very place. Thus, among these gifts, the first is the gift of overcoming craving.
The second is the gift of esteem; the third is the gift of moral shame and dread of blame; the fourth is the gift without reserve;
the fifth is the gift to those worthy of offerings; the sixth is the gift accompanied by the mental application of joy; and the seventh is called the gift of ornaments and retinue.
10. Commentary on the Nandamātā Sutta.

53. This tenth [discourse] was taught by way of an occasion for the arising of the matter. It is said that after the Teacher had completed his rains retreat and performed the *pavāraṇā* ceremony, he set out with the intention, “I shall go on a walking tour to Dakkhiṇāgiri,” leaving behind his two chief disciples.
King Pasenadi of Kosala, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, the great female lay follower Visākhā, and many other people were unable to turn the One of Ten Powers back.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍika sat reflecting in private, thinking, "I was unable to turn back the Teacher.
Then a female slave named Puṇṇā saw him and asked, "Master, why are your faculties not as serene as they were before?
He replied, "Yes, Puṇṇā, the Teacher has set out on a journey, and I was unable to turn him back. "Is it not so... [he continued].
"But it is possible to know whether he will return quickly or not; therefore, I am sitting here reflecting. [She asked:
"If I were to turn back the One of Ten Powers, what would you do for me? [He replied: "I would make you a free woman.
She went and, having paid homage to the Teacher, said, "Please turn back, Bhante. "On account of my turning back, you—"
"What will you do? [Puṇṇa replied: "Venerable sir, you know my state of dependence on others;
I am unable to do anything else, but having established myself in the refuges, I shall observe the five precepts. "Excellent, excellent, Puṇṇa!
the Teacher said, turning back at that very word out of reverence for the Dhamma. For it has been said: "Monks, one who reveres the Dhamma..."
“The Tathāgata is one who reveres the Dhamma.
The Teacher turned back and entered the Great Monastery of Jetavana. The great multitude gave Puṇṇā a thousand shouts of “Sādhu!
At that assembly, the Teacher taught the Dhamma, and eighty-four thousand beings drank the drink of the Deathless.
They drank. Having been permitted by the merchant, Puṇṇā went to the nuns’ quarters and went forth.
The Fully Enlightened One addressed Sāriputta and Moggallāna, saying, “I shall not go to the direction toward which I have set out on my journey.
You two, together with your own retinues, go on tour to that direction,” and he dismissed them. In this [matter]...
In the *Atthuppatti* (Origin of the Discourse), it is stated: "At one time, the Venerable Sāriputta...
and so forth. Therein, "Veḷukaṇḍakī" refers to a resident of the city of Veḷukaṇṭaka.

It is said that because bamboos were planted along the perimeter of the city wall for the purpose of guarding the ramparts, the city itself came to be known by the name Veḷukaṇṭaka. "Pārāyana" means...
He speaks with a voice the Dhamma known by the designation *Pārāyana*, so called because it leads to the further shore (*pāra*) termed Nibbāna.
He speaks from the top floor of a seven-storied palace, seated in a well-guarded place;
having spent a portion of the night through the power of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), he emerges from that attainment and reflects: "How shall I spend this remainder of the night?"
Having reflected and made the resolution, "I shall delight in the Dhamma," the noble female disciple, who had attained the three fruits, recited the *Pārāyana Sutta*—
comprising two hundred and fifty verses— in a sweet tone of chanting.
He heard it as he was traveling in a man-borne vehicle along the road that passed above the celestial mansions situated in the sky.
Waiting for the conclusion of the discourse, he stood there and asked, "What sound is this, my man? When it was told to him,

"It is the sound of the laywoman Nandamātā reciting the *sara-bhañña*," he descended and stood in the air at no great distance, observing this conclusion of the teaching as she said, "This is what was spoken."
“Excellent, sister! Excellent, sister! [The Buddha said: “Well-grasped is your teaching of the Dhamma, sister; well-spoken is it.

I see no difference whatsoever between the day the Perfectly Enlightened One spoke to the sixteen Brahmins of the Pārāyana while seated at the Pāsāṇaka Cetiya and today; it is like gold broken into pieces in the middle.”
Having said, "It was spoken exactly as it is," and giving his approval, he spoke thus: "Who indeed is this, O gentle-faced one?
In this place so well-guarded, with such a great sound—who is this, O gentle-faced one, O fortunate one?
Is it a Nāga, a Supaṇṇa, a Deva, Māra, or a Brahmā? Having thus spoken, he opened the window, which was the color of a golden band, and became free from timidity.
Having attained the three fruits [of stream-entry, once-returning, and non-returning], the noble female disciple (ariyasāvikā), while conversing with Vessavaṇa, spoke thus:

"I am your brother, sister. Thinking himself to be her elder because he was himself a stream-enterer (sotāpanna) and she was a noble female disciple who had reached the stage of non-returning (anāgāmī), he addressed her as "sister";
yet, because she was still in her prime, he considered her his junior, whereas he himself was one hundred and ninety thousand years of age.
Thinking him to be somewhat older, he said, "Brother. "Excellent, gentle sir," [the other replied]. "Gentle sir, excellent; it is good, your arrival is welcome;
the meaning is that you have come to a place where it was fitting for you to come. "May this be your hospitality," he said;
"may this very discourse on the Dhamma be your gift for a guest, for there is nothing better than this for you."
His intention was: "I shall see to it that [the gift] is given. Thinking, "In this very way my hospitality will be fulfilled," he thus requested a dedication of his own merit;

then, having filled one hundred and twenty-five storehouses with red rice, saying, "This is your honorarium for preaching the Dhamma," and having made the resolve, "May these not be exhausted as long as this female lay devotee continues her practice," he departed.
As long as the female lay follower remained there, they were unable to see even the bottom floor of the storehouse.
From that time on, the expression "Nandamātā’s storehouse" arose as a common designation.
"One who has not eaten breakfast" means one who has not consumed the morning meal. "Merit" refers to both the prior volition and the volition of relinquishment. "The earth of merit."

"Other volition": "May it be for happiness" means may it be for the sake of happiness and for the sake of welfare. In this way, he gave the merit of his gift to Vessavaṇa. "In the matter" means in the cause.
"Having dragged down and overcome" means having dragged [him] forth and having conquered [him]. "The womb of a yakkha" means the state of being a terrestrial deity.
"He displays himself with that very same former body" means having fashioned a body exactly like his previous form, he appeared fully adorned and prepared.
She showed herself upon the surface of the bed in the inner chamber. "I confessed as a laywoman" means that I declared my status as a laywoman by saying, "I am a laywoman.
"As far as" (yāvad-eva) means just so far. The rest is clear everywhere.
The fifth chapter, the Mahāyañña-vagga.
The Fiftieth Section is finished.
6. The Chapter on the Undeclared (Abyākatavagga). 1. Commentary on the Discourse on the Undeclared (Abyākatasuttavaṇṇanā).

54. Regarding the first section of the sixth chapter, "In the indeterminate bases" (*abyākatavatthūsu*) means in those bases that have not been definitively stated by way of [the four] alternatives and so forth.
"Tathāgata" refers to a sentient being. "This is a mere resort to views" (*diṭṭhigatametam*) means this is merely wrong view;

there is no such thing as a "sentient being grasped by that view. "The path" (*paṭipadam*) refers to the Noble Path. "He does not tremble" (*na chambhati*) means he does not waver because of views. This applies to the remaining phrases as well.
The same method applies here. "Included in craving" refers to craving for views (*diṭṭhitaṇhā*). The same method applies to "included in perception" and so forth.
Here, "perception-included" is simply perception regarding views; "conceitedness" is conceiving based on views or the very act of conceiving views;
"proliferation" is the proliferation of views; "clinging" is clinging to views; and "remorse" is the state of being troubled by the unsuitability of one's resort to views.

It should be understood as "names. And here, by the mention of "views," the sixty-two views are included; by the mention of "the practice leading to the cessation of views," the path of stream-entry is included.
2. Commentary on the Purisagati Sutta (The Discourse on the Destinations of Men)
55. "The second destination for a person" means the destinations of a person's knowledge. "Parinibbāna through non-clinging" means nibbāna without conditions.
"If it had not been" means if the karma that produced this past personal existence had not existed.
"And it would not be for me" means this present personal existence of mine would not exist. "It will not be" refers to the karma that would produce a future personal existence for me at this time.
"Kamma will not be; and it will not be for me" means: "In the future, my personal existence (attabhāva) will not be.
"Whatever exists, whatever has become" refers to the present pentad of aggregates (khandhapañcaka). "I abandon that" means he attains equanimity;
that is, by abandoning desire and lust for that [object], he attains the equanimity of insight (vipassanupekkhā).
“He does not delight in existence” means he does not take pleasure in the past five aggregates through craving and views.

“He does not delight in becoming” means he likewise does not take pleasure in the future. “There is a state beyond that which is peaceful” means there exists a further state of peace called the state of Nibbāna.
“He sees with right wisdom” means he sees that correctly with the wisdom of the Path accompanied by insight.

"Not in every way" means that because some defilements have not been abandoned and because the darkness that conceals the truths has not been entirely dispelled, it is not all-encompassing in every manner. "Being struck" means being seized with tongs and beaten with a mallet.
"One who attains Nibbāna in the interval" refers to one who, from the moment immediately following rebirth, does not exceed the midpoint of the lifespan.
In this interval, he has attained final Nibbāna through the extinction of the defilements (*kilesaparinibbāna*).

By means of these three similes—"without having struck the surface" meaning without striking or exceeding the surface of space, and "without reaching the ground" meaning he would be extinguished in space itself—three types of those who attain final Nibbāna in the interval (*antarāparinibbāyin*) are shown.

One who attains final Nibbāna after having struck (*upahaccaparinibbāyin*) is one who has passed beyond the midpoint of his lifespan but has not yet reached its final limit, and then attains final Nibbāna.

It occurs thus: having struck the surface [of the earth] and gone forth blazing, it would pass beyond the vault of the sky and, striking the surface of the earth, go out as soon as it has fallen upon the ground.
One who extinguishes the defilements without exertion or effort and attains final Nibbāna is an "attainer of Nibbāna without exertion" (asaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī).
One who extinguishes the defilements with exertion and effort and attains final Nibbāna is an "attainer of Nibbāna with exertion" (sasaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī).
They go into the forest without protection; they give [the forest] with protection, having been given for the sake of fearlessness. The rest here is of plain meaning.
In this sutta, only noble persons (ariyapuggala) are spoken of.
3. Commentary on the Tissabrahmā Sutta.
56. "In the third [case], 'bhikkhunīs' refers to the five hundred bhikkhunīs who were the retinue of Mahāpajāpatī.

'Liberated' means liberated by the five kinds of liberation. 'Without residue' (anupādisesa) means liberated by the five kinds of liberation without remainder, having set aside any residue of clinging (upādāna).
Or, regarding 'with residue' (saupādisesa): in a person where there is a residue of clinging, one says 'with residue.'"
"Come! This same method applies to the other [formula] as well. "Tissa" refers to the brahmin who was the elder’s co-resident disciple (*saddhivihārika*).
"Conformable" means conformable to the practice; they are secluded, remote, and situated at the very edge or boundary. "Faculties" refers to the insight-faculties, such as faith and the rest.
"Applying" means establishing them in attention (*samannāhāra*). But why was this [statement], "For indeed, those... introduced? [It is for the sake of the seventh...]
It is for the purpose of showing the individual (puggala). For the seventh type of person, the faith-follower (saddhānusārī), has not yet been shown.

Now, the Blessed One, showing him by way of powerful insight (balavavipassaka), spoke thus. In this context, "all signs" (sabbanimittāni) refers to all signs such as the sign of permanence and so forth;
"signless" (animitta) refers to the concentration of powerful insight (balavavipassanāsamādhi).
4. Commentary on the Sīhasenāpati Sutta 57.
In the fourth [verse], "miserly" (*maccharī*) means one who possesses the fifth kind of miserliness (*macchariya*).

"Avaricious" (*kadariya*) refers to one who is stubbornly miserly and even prevents others from giving. "Delighting in repeated giving" (*anuppadānarata*) means that he finds pleasure only while giving again and again. "Feeling compassion" (*anukampantā*)...
“Who today should be favored by us? Whom should we accept as a recipient of gifts, or to whom should we teach the Dhamma?”—thus they feel compassion with their hearts.
5. Commentary on the Arakkheyya Sutta (The Discourse on What is Not to Be Guarded)
58. In the fifth [case], "sign" (nimitta) refers to both the sign of the Dhamma and the sign of the person.
For this [Buddha], seeing not even a single word among the Dhammas he himself taught as poorly expounded, leading nowhere, or not conducive to liberation, he does not perceive the sign of the Dhamma.
Nor, seeing not even a single person rising up and contending against him by saying, "The Dhamma has been poorly expounded by you, it is not well-expounded," does he perceive the sign of the person.
He does not perceive [it] as "name. The same method applies to the other two [aggregates].
The sixth and seventh [suttas] are self-evident. 8. Commentary on the *Pacalāyamāna-sutta* (61):
Regarding the eighth, "nodding off" (*pacalāyamāno*) refers to one who, while performing the duties of a recluse in a certain grove dependent upon that village...
Because his body was exhausted from the exertion of walking meditation for seven days, he sat dozing at the end of the walkway.
"Are you dozing? means "Are you falling asleep? "Having rubbed" means having massaged thoroughly. "Perception of light" refers to the perception of light used to dispel drowsiness.
"Perception of day" refers to the perception that it is daytime. "As by day, so by night" means as [one perceives] by day...
As you have established the perception of light by day, so should you establish it by night; as by night, so by day.
And as you have established the perception of light by night with radiance for the sake of the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*), so should you establish it by day as well.
"Perceiving what is behind and before" means [perceiving] both in front and behind.
And he was possessed of the perception of bringing [the mind] back. "With the sense-faculties turned inward" means with the five sense-faculties not distracted outward but having entered within.
"The pleasure of sloth" means the pleasure of sleep. By this much, the Blessed One taught the elder the meditation subject for dispelling sloth.
"The snout" means the mental snout. Regarding "duties and tasks": here...
Those duties that must necessarily be performed are *kiccāni*; others are *karaṇīyāni*. "A sense of shame" (*maṅkubhāvo*) means a state of being dispirited or dejected.
By this much, the Teacher has explained the Elder’s duty regarding the practice of alms-gathering.
Now, in order to encourage him to observe moderation in speech, he said, "Therefore, then," and so forth. In that context, "contentious talk" (*viggāhikakathā*)...
“Controversial discussion” refers to discourse proceeding in such a manner as, “You do not understand this Dhamma and Vinaya.
“I am not [your friend], Moggallāna,” and so forth, was said for the purpose of avoiding association with evil friends. “In what way, indeed? means “by how much, indeed?

“One who is liberated through the destruction of craving” means one whose mind is liberated by taking as its object the destruction of craving, which is Nibbāna; thus, one is “liberated through the destruction of craving.”

"In brief, by how much is one called [an arahant]? He asks this to inquire: "Please teach in brief the preliminary practice of a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed—that very practice by which one becomes liberated through the destruction of craving.

"One who has reached the ultimate goal" (*accantaniṭṭha*): it is "ultimate" (*accanta*) because it has transcended the end (*anta*) known as destruction and passing away; one for whom that is the ultimate goal is "one who has reached the ultimate goal," meaning one whose final aim is absolute.
"Ever-cooled" (satata-niṭṭha) is the meaning. "One who has reached ultimate security from bondage" (accanta-yogakkhemī) means one who has reached ultimate security from bondage;

the meaning is "one who is eternally secure from bondage. "One who leads the ultimate holy life" (accanta-brahmacārī) means one who leads the holy life ultimately; the meaning is "one who leads the holy life eternally.

"One whose end is ultimate" (accanta-pariyosāna) means that his end is ultimate, according to the same method as before. "The best among gods and humans" (seṭṭho deva-manussānaṃ) [refers to] among the gods...
He is the best and supreme among human beings. "In what way does such a bhikkhu exist? Please explain his practice in brief," he requested.
Regarding the statement, "All phenomena are not fit for adherence": here, "all phenomena" refers to the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements.
All of these are not fit, nor are they sufficient, for adherence by way of craving and views.

They are not appropriate as ultimate realities. Why? Because they do not persist in the manner in which they are grasped. For although they are grasped as permanent, pleasant, and self, they turn out to be only impermanent, suffering, and non-self. Therefore, they are not fit for dogmatic adherence.

"He directly knows" means he directly knows through the full understanding of the known that they are impermanent, suffering, and non-self. "He fully understands" means he fully understands them in that very same way through the full understanding by scrutinization.
"Whatever feeling whatsoever": he experiences even the slightest feeling, down to that associated with the fivefold sense-consciousness.
By this means, the Blessed One, having turned the Elder's attention away from the perspective of feeling, showed him the discernment of the formless.
"Contemplating impermanence" means contemplating as impermanent. "Contemplating fading away": here, there are two kinds of fading away—fading away through destruction (*khayavirāga*) and...
And there is absolute dispassion (*accantavirāga*). In this context, insight (*vipassanā*) is the seeing of the destruction of formations as destruction;
and the knowledge of the path of seeing, which views Nibbāna—the absolute dispassion—as dispassion, is also "contemplation of dispassion" (*virāgānupassanā*).

A person possessing both of these is called "one who contemplates dispassion. With reference to such a person, it is said: "contemplating dispassion," meaning one who contemplates by way of dispassion. This also applies to "one who contemplates cessation" (*nirodhānupassī*).
The same method applies here. For cessation (*nirodha*) is indeed twofold: cessation by destruction (*khayanirodha*) and absolute cessation (*accantanirodha*).

Regarding the phrase "contemplating relinquishment" (*paṭinissaggānupassī*), "relinquishment" (*paṭinissagga*) here refers to "letting go" (*vossagga*). And that [letting go] is twofold: letting go as abandonment (*pariccāgavossagga*) and letting go as leaping forward (*pakkhandanavossagga*).
Among these, "letting go as abandonment" is insight (*vipassanā*); for it, by way of its specific factor (*tadaṅgavasena*), [abandons] the defilements...
And he relinquishes the aggregates. "Relinquishment by leaping forward" refers to the Path, for it leaps forward toward Nibbāna as its object.

Or rather, for two reasons it is simply relinquishment: because of the relinquishing of both the aggregates and the defilements by way of their total cutting off, and because of the leaping forward into Nibbāna.
Therefore, because it abandons both the defilements and the aggregates, it is "relinquishment by abandoning."
"The mind leaps into the element of Nibbāna for the sake of cessation" is "leaping and relinquishment";

both of these coincide with the Path. A person possessing both of these, by virtue of being endowed with this contemplation of relinquishment (*paṭinissaggānupassanā*), is called a "contemplator of relinquishment. It is with reference to such a person that it was said: "He does not cling to anything in the world."
He does not cling to, grasp, or misapprehend even a single conditioned thing by way of craving.
"Not clinging, he does not tremble" means that, not grasping, he does not tremble through the trembling of craving.

"He attains final nibbāna right here" means that he himself attains final nibbāna through the extinction of the defilements. Furthermore, his reviewing [knowledge] is expressed by the words, "Birth is exhausted," and so forth.
Thus, when asked by the Blessed One for a brief account of the preliminary practice of one whose taints were destroyed, the Blessed One explained it briefly.
Furthermore, this discourse served as both an exhortation and an occasion for insight (vipassanā) for the Elder;
having developed insight through this very discourse, he attained Arahatship.
9. Commentary on the *Mettasutta* 62.
Regarding the ninth [verse], "O monks, do not fear merits": this means that those performing meritorious deeds should not fear them.
"Cultivate a mind of loving-kindness" means having made the mind sublime by associating it with loving-kindness (*mettā*) consisting of the three or four jhānas.
He shows that they will exist. "Indeed, while the world was contracting" means indeed while it was contracting.
"Contracting" means being consumed by fire or falling into ruin. "Righteous" (*dhammika*) means endowed with the ten wholesome qualities (*dasakusala-dhamma*).

"King of Dharma" (*dhammarāja*) is a synonym for that same person; or, he is a "King of Dharma" because his sovereignty was obtained through righteousness. "Of the four quarters" refers to the eastern ocean and so forth.
By virtue of the four oceans, he is the lord of the earth bounded by the four quarters. "Victorious" means one who has won the battle.
"One who has attained stability for his realm" means that the country has reached a state of firmness and steadiness.
"More than a thousand" means exceeding a thousand. "Brave" means fearless. "Heroic-limbed" (*vīraṅgarūpa*): the limb of heroes is the "heroic limb" (*vīraṅga*); this is a term for energy (*vīriya*).
"Name. They possess the form of heroes (*vīraṅgarūpa*); thus they are "those of heroic form.
This means that being born of vigor, having the nature of vigor, and as if consisting of vigor, they do not grow weary even when fighting for a whole day; they do not tire, so it is said.

"As far as the ocean's edge" means bounded by the ocean situated with the Cakkavāḷa mountains as its limit. "Without punishment" means without punishment by wealth, or by execution, mutilation, or instruction.
"Even without the rod of a sword" means even without a weapon for harming others, such as a single-edged blade.

"Having conquered by righteousness" means having conquered the earth in the manner described— by righteousness alone, such as the precept "one must not kill a living being"— and having been received by rival kings with the words, "Come, Great King."
"Sukhesino" means he addresses beings who are seekers of happiness. "Suññabrahmūpago" means one who has approached the empty Brahmā-palace.
"Imaṃ pathaviṃ" means this great earth bounded by the ocean. "Asāhasena" means not by violent action.
"Samena manusāsitaṃ" means I governed by means of impartial action. "Tehi etaṃ sudesitaṃ" means this was well-taught by those [ministers] who were inclusive leaders.
This much has been well-taught and well-expounded by the Buddhas, who possess great compassion. "The earth" (*pathavī*) means the master of the earth (*puthavisāmika*).
10. Commentary on the Bhariyā Sutta:
In the tenth [verse], "I think the fishermen are picking up fish" refers to the place where the fishermen have lowered their fish-trap and are standing.
As soon as a fish is pulled from the water into a net, there is a great clamor among the fishermen; it was with reference to this that it was said.

"Sujātā" was the younger sister of Visākhā. She did not respect her mother-in-law means that there is a certain duty to be performed for a mother-in-law, which she did not do, nor did she even acknowledge her as a mother-in-law.
She did not respect her father-in-law means that she did not accept his word.
Thus, by means of both disregard and non-acceptance, it is said that "he does not take [it]. The same method applies to the remaining cases as well.
In this way, Anāthapiṇḍika, having observed his daughter-in-law’s conduct, sat down before the Teacher.
Sujātā also went to a spot not far away, thinking, "Will this merchant speak of my virtues or my faults in the presence of the One of Ten Powers? and she listened to the sound.
She stood listening. Then the Teacher addressed her, saying, "Come, Sujātā.
"Compassionate toward what is harmful" means not compassionate toward what is beneficial. "Toward others" means toward other men. "She despises" means she despises them by way of contempt and pride.
"One who has been bought with wealth" means one who has been purchased for a price. "Eager for slaughter" means having become intent upon killing.
"Whatever wealth a husband finds for his wife" means whatever wealth the husband obtains for the wife.

"He wishes to take away even a little of that" means he desires to carry off even a small portion; he strives to steal even a little from the rice that must be placed in the mortar set upon the hearth.
"Lazily" means she remains sitting wherever she was sitting, and standing wherever she was standing.
"Harsh" means rough. "One who speaks ill-spoken words" means one who utters what is badly spoken; she speaks only with harsh and savage speech.
"She overcomes those who rise [to work] and conducts herself [toward them]"—here, by the use of the plural "those who rise," the husband endowed with the exertion of energy is meant;
she conducts herself by overcoming that excellence of his exertion and placing it beneath her own. "She takes delight" means...
She was filled with joy and delight. "Of noble birth" means one endowed with a good family. "Faithful" means a wife who is like a deity to her husband.
"Threatened with the punishment of death" means threatened with execution by being seized with a staff; she was told, "I will have you killed.
"Like a slave-girl" means she said, "May the Blessed One consider me a slave-girl fulfilling the duties toward my husband," and thus she established herself in the refuges.
11. Commentary on the Kodhana Sutta 64.
In the eleventh [verse], "dear to enemies" (*sapattakanta*) means dear and beloved to enemies—that is, those who bear enmity—and desired by them.

"Causing enmity" (*sapattakaraṇa*) means performing what is beneficial for enemies, those who bear enmity. "Overcome by anger" (*kodhapareta*) means one who is pursued by anger. "By way of abundance of wealth" (*pacuratthatāya*)...
"For the sake of much benefit and much welfare. "Even what is harmful" (*anattham*) means even non-prosperity (*avuddhim*). "I have grasped what is beneficial" means "I have grasped prosperity.
"Furthermore, having grasped what is beneficial" means furthermore, having grasped prosperity. "He encounters what is harmful" means he perceives, "I have grasped what is harmful.
"Having committed a killing" means having performed the kamma of taking life. "Intoxicated by the madness of anger" means by the intoxication of anger.
"Stolen" means taken, seized, and misappropriated. "Infamy" means the nature of infamy; the meaning is that it becomes a bad reputation.
"Born from within" means arisen internally. "Does not know the goal" means he does not know the goal of prosperity.
"Does not see the Dhamma" means he does not see the Dhamma of serenity and insight. "Blinding darkness" means that which produces blindness.
"Darkness" means very thick darkness. "Overcomes" means it surpasses.
"Wickedness" means the state of being wicked, lack of luster, and a discolored face. "From which it spreads" means when it arises.
"There is no weight to speech" means there is no gravity even in one's words. "There is no light or anything at all" means some...
"Foundation" means there is no support. "Causing torment" means producing distress. "By states" means by the states of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
"Far away" means distant. "The Brahmin" refers to the Brahmin whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*). "By whom she was supported" means by which mother she was nourished and sustained.
"One who gives life, a refuge" means one who is equal to a giver of life. "An angry man slays those of various kinds" means an angry man...
The individual destroys himself by various different means. "Intoxicated by various forms" means being utterly infatuated with various objects.
"Dying bound by a rope" means dying after being tied with a rope. "Even falling into mountain clefts" means dying after falling even into mountain ravines.
"Bhūnahaccāni" means those that have destroyed wisdom. "Itāyaṃ" means this one. "Taṃ damena samucchindeti" means one should cut off that anger by means of self-control.

By what kind of self-control? By means of wisdom and energy—that is, by means of the wisdom of insight (vipassanā-paññā), by means of physical and mental energy associated with insight, and by means of right view of the Path (magga-sammā-diṭṭhi). Likewise regarding phenomena (dhammesu)...
"One should train" means that one should train in the same way as one would cut off unwholesome states, even in the qualities of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
"May there be no stubbornness for us" means aspiring to this purpose: "May there not be a state of stubbornness in us.
"Without distress" means without affliction. "Without striving" means not having undertaken any striving toward anything. The rest is clear everywhere.
The Sixth Chapter on the Undeclared (Abyākatavagga).
7. The Great Chapter (Mahāvagga). 1. Commentary on the Discourse on Moral Shame and Dread (Hiriottappasutta).
65. In the first [section] of the seventh [chapter], "one whose proximate cause has been destroyed" (*hatūpanisa*) means one whose supporting condition (*paccaya*) has been severed.

"Knowledge and vision according to reality" (*yathābhūtañāṇadassana*) refers to nascent insight (*taruṇavipassanā*). "Disenchantment and dispassion" (*nibbidāvirāga*) refers to both powerful insight and the path (*magga*).
"Knowledge and vision of liberation" (*vimuttiñāṇadassana*) refers to the liberation of Arahantship and its subsequent reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇā*).
2. Commentary on the *Sattasūriya-sutta* 66.

In the second [sutta], because this teaching on the seven suns proceeds by way of showing the conflagration (*tejosaṃvaṭṭa*), there are, first of all, three conflagrations, three boundaries of the conflagration, three roots of the conflagration, and three tumults. Thus:

From the very beginning, the introductory discourse of this sutta should be understood; it has already been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga* in the section on the recollection of past lives (*pubbenivāsānussati*).

"He said this" means that, in accordance with the inclination of five hundred bhikkhus who were practitioners of the meditation subject of impermanence, [the Buddha spoke] for the purpose of showing the failure of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), both those clung-to (*upādinnaka*) and those not clung-to (*anupādinnaka*): "Bhikkhus, they are impermanent..."
He spoke the seven Sūriyopama (Sun-like) Suttantas beginning with "Formations" (*saṅkhārā*). Therein: "Impermanent" means impermanent in the sense of non-existence after having existed.
"Formations" refers to conditioned phenomena, both acquired (*upādinnaka*) and unacquired (*anupādinnaka*). "Unstable" means not stable because they do not endure for long in this way.
"Without consolation" means devoid of comfort due to their lack of permanence. "It is indeed enough" means it is indeed appropriate.
"Plunged" means having entered into the water. "Emerging" means having come up from the surface of the water. "The rain does not fall":
first of all, there is what is called the "subsistence-cloud," which rains as a single cloud over a hundred thousand million world-systems;
at that time, the seed that has been sown does not enter back into its husk. From that point on, it is as if it were dried up in a water-vessel.
The water remains, and not even a single drop of rain falls from the sky; this is the measure of the discourse on the nature of the simile.
However, when the world is being destroyed, it first becomes empty starting from the Avīci hell;

then, having emerged from there, beings are reborn in the human world and among the animals. Even those reborn among the animals, having regained loving-kindness (*mettā*) toward their children and brothers...
When their time has come, they are reborn among gods and humans. Deities traveling through the sky announce:
"This place is not eternal, nor is it permanent; cultivate loving-kindness, compassion, gladness, and equanimity.
Having cultivated these qualities such as loving-kindness, when they pass away from there, they are reborn in the Brahma-world.
Regarding "the seed-creepers": here, "seed-creepers" refers to the five kinds of seeds. "The vegetable kingdom" refers to any green plant that has emerged with roots and leaves.
Regarding "herbs, grasses, and trees": here, "herbs" refers to medicinal plants; "grasses" refers to those whose pith is outside, such as palms and coconuts;
"trees" refers to the preeminent trees of the forest. "Small rivers" refers to all flowing streams, excluding the five great rivers.
"Kusobbha" refers to all lakes and such bodies of water, excluding the seven great lakes. Regarding the "second sun" and so forth:
at the time of the second sun, one rises while another sets. At the time of the third, one rises, one sets, and one remains in the middle.
At the time of the fourth, they are like four alms-collecting monks standing in succession at the gates of a village with four walls.
The same method applies even at the time of the fifth dissolution. "They disintegrate" means they fall down, breaking apart again and again.

"Neither ash nor soot is perceived" means that when this much space has been burnt—the world-system (cakkavāḷa), the great earth, Sineru the king of mountains, the Himavat, the Cakkavāḷa mountains, the six heavenly realms of sensual pleasure, and the Brahma-world of the first jhāna—not even a portion as small as a finger-snap remains.
Neither ash nor embers are perceived. Who has the wisdom? Who has the faith?

Who is capable of making others believe in it, or who would believe in it? "Except for those who have seen the Dhamma"—the meaning is: except for the noble disciples who are stream-enterers and have seen the Dhamma, who else would believe?
"Free from lust" means free from lust by way of suppression (*vikkhambhana*). "They understood the teaching" means they understood the instruction;

they set out upon the path for companionship with the Brahma-world. "Of equal destiny" means that in their second existence they have an identical destiny, going to the same destination in every respect.
"They should develop further loving-kindness" means having made it more refined, from the first jhāna up to the third and fourth jhānas.
"I shall cultivate loving-kindness. "One who possesses eyes" means one who possesses eyes by way of the five kinds of vision.
"Parinibbūta" means that at the very seat of enlightenment (bodhipallaṅka), he was parinibbūta through the parinibbāna of the defilements.

Having thus illustrated the characteristic of impermanence, when the Teacher withdrew his discourse, those five hundred bhikkhus who were practicing the meditation subject of impermanence directed their knowledge according to the teaching and remained right in their sitting places.
"They attained arahantship. 3.
Commentary on the Nagaropama Sutta (The Simile of the City). 67.
In the third [verse], "yatā" means when. "Paccantimaṃ" means situated at the edge of the kingdom, at the border of the realm. [It is contrasted with] a city of the Middle Country.
However, there was no need for protection, and therefore that [quality] was not included.

"Well-fortified with city-surrounding defenses" means adorned with city ornaments. "Inviolable" (akaraṇīya) means that which should not be done, that which is unconquerable. "With deep moats" (gambhīranema) means having deep trenches.
"Well-dug" (sunikhātā) means well-settled. Furthermore, they make this pillar-post either of bricks or...
It is made of stone or of heartwood trees such as *khadira* and others.
Those constructing it for the purpose of guarding the city build it outside the city, while those constructing it for the purpose of ornamentation build it inside the city.
When making it of brick, they dig a large pit, pile up a mound of earth, construct an octagonal top, and plaster it with lime. When struck by the tusks of an elephant...
When it does not move, it is said to be "well-fixed. Even stone pillars and the like are eight-sided.
If they are made of the eight precious gems, they enter four *ratana*s into the pit and rise four *ratana*s above ground.
This same principle applies to those measuring sixteen or twenty *ratana*s; for in all cases, half is below and half is above.
Above. Those [walls] are curved like cow-urine; therefore, having placed wooden planks between them, it is possible to perform the work.
Furthermore, those painted decorations remain as if their banners were held aloft.
A moat (*parikhā*) is a trench situated surrounding [the city]. A circumambulatory path (*anupariyāyapatha*) is that which lies inside the wall together with the wall itself.

The "great path" (mahāpatha) is that place where those stationed outside the rampart engage in combat with those stationed inside. "Salāka" refers to projectile weapons such as arrows, spears, and the like.
"Jevanika" refers to weapons with single-edged blades and other similar types.
"Elephant-riders" (hatthāroha) includes all elephant trainers, elephant physicians, elephant-grooms, and so forth. "Horse-riders" (assāroha) includes all [horsemen].
Trainers of horses, horse-physicians, horse-grooms, and so forth. Charioteers refers to all those such as chariot-masters, chariot-warriors, and chariot-guards.
Archers are those skilled in the art of archery. Banner-bearers are those who go at the front of the battle holding the victory-banner.
Standard-bearers are those who arrange the military formations, thinking, "Let this be the king’s position here; let that be the position of such-and-such a high minister. Alms-givers...
They are daring great warriors. It is said that even after entering the enemy army, they cut it up piece by piece as if it were a morsel of food and tear it apart;
the meaning is that they spring up and emerge. Or else, this is the name for those who enter the midst of battle taking the food and drink of the warriors.
"Uggā rājaputtā" means high-born princes who have risen to the highest ranks in the field of battle.
“Pakkhandino” means those who, having said, “Whose head or weapon shall we bring? and being told, “That of so-and-so,” charge into battle and bring back exactly that;
these are called *pakkhandino* because they leap forward (*pakkhandanti*). “Mahānāgā” means like great elephants;
this is a designation for warriors who do not turn back even when elephants and other such creatures come charging toward them. “Sūrā” means brave.

"Single heroes" are those who are able to cross the ocean even when equipped with armor and mail. "Shieldmen" are those who fight having either entered a leather cuirass or taken up a shield for protection against arrows.
"Sons of slave-girls" are household slaves who fight out of strong affection [for their masters].
"Doorkeeper" means a gate-guard. "Endowed with plastering and smearing" means by means of plastering, which covers all cracks and openings.

It was provided with a coating of plaster; or else, it was provided with a plaster coating that was thick and smooth, consisting of a surrounding wall made of wooden pillars, and which displayed rows of full jars and was adorned with banners featuring painted designs.
"Grass, wood, and water" refers to the grass brought and placed in many locations for the sake of fodder for elephants, horses, and so forth, as well as for the covering of houses.
Wood brought and stored for the purpose of building houses, cooking, and so forth; and water introduced by means of machines and placed in lotus ponds.
"It is accumulated" means it has been thoroughly gathered in advance in many locations.
"For the pleasure of those within" means for the sake of the enjoyment of those living inside the city. "For the sake of non-distress" means for the purpose of their not falling into distress.

"Various kinds of rice and barley" means both various types of *sāli* rice and barley. "Sesame, mung beans, beans, and other vegetables" means sesame, mung beans, and beans, as well as other remaining vegetables.

Now, since there is no such thing as "work" for a Tathāgata in the city, [the text] shows that the noble disciple is like a city, the seven qualities are like the requisites of a city, and the four meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) are like the four types of nutriment.
This simile was brought forward with the intention: "I shall conclude the teaching by adding the state of Arahatship to the eleven stages.
Therefore, in order to explain that teaching, the passage beginning with "It is just as if" (*evameva kho*) was commenced.

In this context, *saddhammehi* means "by means of excellent qualities" (*sudhammehi*). *Saddho* refers to one who is endowed with both faith based on conviction (*okappana-saddhā*) and faith based on direct experience (*paccakkha-saddhā*). Regarding these:

Faith that consists in conviction regarding the fruits of giving, virtue, and so forth, and which leads one to perform meritorious deeds such as giving, is called "faith as conviction" (okappana-saddhā). Faith that has arrived via the Path is called "directly perceived faith" (paccakkha-saddhā);
this is also what is meant by "faith as serene confidence" (pasāda-saddhā). Its analysis should be understood through its characteristic and other attributes.
For it is said: "Great King, faith has the characteristic of leaping forward (sampakkhandana) and the characteristic of serene confidence (sampasādana)."
This is called the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) of faith. However, that which is stated in the manner beginning with, “Bhikkhus, one who is faithful and confident is to be known by three grounds.
By which three? He desires to see those possessed of virtue,” is called the sign (*nimitta*) of faith.
Furthermore, regarding its nutriment, it should be said: “What is the nutriment of faith? It is the hearing of the true Dhamma. This, then, is its...
“Food,” it is said. “For a bhikkhu who has gone forth out of faith, bhikkhus, this is the practice in accordance with the Dhamma (*anudhamma*):
that he should dwell abundant in disenchantment toward form. This is what is called his practice in accordance with the Dhamma.
“Faith secures one’s provisions; prosperity is the abode of wealth. “Faith is a person’s second [self]. “Through faith one crosses the flood. “Faith...”
“Seeds are austerity, rain is [the gift of] food. Furthermore, in such suttas as “The Great Elephant has faith for his trunk;
equanimity is his white tusks,” the Blessed One has demonstrated her manifold flavors through similes such as a bowl of cooked rice.
But in this *Nagaropama-sutta*, she is shown as being like a pillar of a city gate because of her immovability and firm foundation.
"Faith as a pillar": by means of this principle—that "the noble disciple abandons the unwholesome having made faith his pillar"—the application should be made for all the following terms.
Furthermore, in this context, restraint through shame and fear is accomplished at the three doors;
that constitutes the fourfold purification of virtue (*cātu-pārisuddhi-sīla*). Thus, in this sutta, having included *arahantship* in eleven instances...
It should be understood that a deception has been employed in the teaching.
4. Commentary on the Dhammaññū Sutta: 68.
In the fourth [sutta], "he knows the proper time" means he knows the time when it is appropriate and fitting. "'This is the time for recitation' means this is the time for the word of the Buddha."
It is the time for learning. "By means of inquiry" means by means of inquiring into what is the meaning and what is not the meaning, and what is the reason and what is not the reason.
"Of yoga" means of applying effort to the practice. "Of seclusion" means of withdrawing, of being alone.
"Practicing the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma" means practicing the preliminary path, which is the Dhamma corresponding to the nine supramundane states. Thus indeed...
"Monks, a monk is one who knows the higher and lower among persons"—thus a monk is called one capable of knowing the higher and lower, the sharpness and dullness, among individuals. 5.
Commentary on the Pāricchattaka Sutta.
69. "With fallen leaves" (*pannapalāsa*) means with leaves that have fallen. "Covered with a network" (*jālakajāta*) means having a network of leaves and flowers produced;
for in this case, both the network of leaves and the network of flowers emerge simultaneously.

"Covered with a web" (*khārakajāta*) means endowed with a distinct, well-arranged network of leaves and a network of flowers that have grown separately. "Covered with buds" (*kuṭumalakajāta*) means having buds produced.
*“Korakajāto”* means endowed with flowers that have not yet blossomed, possessing large bellies and closed mouths.
*“Sabbapāliphullo”* means fully blossomed in every way. *“Dibbe cattāro māse”* means four months by celestial reckoning;
however, by human calculation, these amount to twelve thousand years. *“Paricārentī”* means they move their faculties here and there.
The meaning is that they play and delight.
"It is suffused with radiance" means that much of that place is suffused with light. For those flowers have a radiance like the morning sun;
their petals are the size of a leaf-parasol, and inside there is pollen the size of a large gourd. When they are in bloom...
However, for the *pāricchattaka* tree, there is no need for climbing, nor for bending it by means of a hook,
nor for shaking it with a *caṅgoṭaka* to gather flowers; rather, a wind that cuts arises and strips the flowers from their stalks, a receiving wind catches them,
an entering wind brings them into the Sudhamma assembly hall of the gods, and a sweeping wind removes the withered flowers.
The wind from the spreading fans blows away the fringes and the filaments of the bowl-rim while it spreads out, coloring them.
In the center stands the Dhamma-throne, a jeweled couch measuring one *yojana* in size, with a white parasol held aloft above it measuring three *yojanas*.
Immediately after that, the seat of Sakka, the king of the gods, is spread out, and then the seats for the thirty-three sons of the gods.
Then, for other deities of great influence, a single flower-bud serves as their seat.

Having entered the divine assembly hall, the deities sit down. Then, from those flowers, a cloud of pollen rises and falls, striking against the upper edge of the bud, [revealing] the bodies of the deities measuring three-quarters of a league (tigāvuta), which appear as if prepared by the application of lac-dye.
It makes [the body] appear as if covered in gold dust. Some gods take individual flowers and play by striking one another.

Even at the time of striking, a cloud of pollen the size of large gourds issues forth, making the body—as if with its radiant fragrance—appear like a mass of powdered realgar (manosilā). Thus, that sport [is enjoyed] by the four...
It reaches its conclusion in months. "This is the power" means this is the power to produce a subsequent result.

Now, since the Teacher has no need for the Pāricchattaka tree, but wishes instead to show seven noble disciples by way of comparison with it, he said, "In the same way," and so forth, in order to show them.
In that context, "he intends toward the going-forth" means "I shall go forth."

He reflects: "Like that of the gods" means as if belonging to the gods. "The sound rises up as far as the Brahmā-world" means that from the surface of the earth up to the Brahmā-world, the entire space becomes one single sound through the cry of "Well done!

"This is the majestic power" means this is the pervasive majestic power of the bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed. In this sutta, the fourfold purification of virtue is dependent upon the life of renunciation.
The preliminary work for the kasiṇa is based on the first jhāna; together with insight, the three paths and the three fruits are based on the path of Arahantship.
In a teaching there may be a delimitation from below, from above, or from both sides;
here, however, there is a delimitation from both sides. Therefore this was said. In brief, moreover, herein:
It should be understood that the turning of the wheel and its unwinding have been explained.
6. Commentary on the *Sakkacca-sutta* (Discourse on Respectful Conduct) 70.

Regarding the sixth [verse], "and they will become completely pure": this means they will become even more thoroughly purified and stainless. As for the phrase "gone to the smithy" (*sakammāragato*), here the syllable *sa-* is merely a particle; the meaning is "gone to the smithy," that is, gone to the smith's workshop (*kammāruddhana*).
7. Commentary on the *Bhāvanāsutta* 71.
Regarding the seventh [sutta], "of one who is not devoted" (*ananuyuttassa*) means: of one who dwells without being engaged and applied [to practice].

"Just as, bhikkhus, with the eggs of a hen"—these two similes are stated by way of the dark side (*kaṇhapakkha*) and the bright side (*sukkapakkha*). Of these, the simile of the dark side is as follows:
The meaning should be understood according to the simile of the bright fortnight (sukkapakkhūpamā) alone:
that [the hen] is not one who brings about the success of the purpose, while the other is. *Seyyathā* is a particle used in the sense of a simile. *Api* is used in the sense of esteem.
By both of these, he shows: "Just as if, monks. Regarding the phrase "a hen’s eggs, eight or ten or twelve," although here—regarding the hen—

There may be eggs that are fewer or more than the number described; however, this was stated for the sake of linguistic elegance, for in this way speech is elegant in the world. "Tānassu" means "tāni assu," which signifies "they would be.
"Properly incubated by a hen" means by that mother hen who lies upon them with her wings spread over them.
"Left to steep. "Properly soaked" means that they were well and thoroughly soaked from all sides at the proper times by one who causes them to take on heat;
what is meant is that they were made warm. "Properly fermented" means that they were well and thoroughly fermented from all sides at the proper times;
the meaning is that they were made to take on the smell of a cock.

"Even though that hen"—meaning, even though such a desire might not arise in that hen despite her having practiced diligence by performing these three kinds of actions—"nevertheless, they are indeed capable":
those chicks are indeed capable of breaking out safely in the manner described; for they have been so treated by that hen in these three ways.
As those eggs are being incubated, they do not rot. Whatever moisture they have within them dries up;
the shell becomes thin, the claws on their feet and their beaks become hard, and their own bodies undergo transformation.
Because the shell has become thin, light from the outside is perceived inside; therefore, [he thinks], "For a long time..."
Thinking, "Alas, we have been lying in a cramped space with our hands and feet contracted, yet now this light is seen outside;
here indeed there will be a pleasant dwelling for us," they desire to go out.
They strike the door-panel with their foot and stretch out their necks, whereupon that door-panel splits in two. Then, flapping their wings, they [emerge] at that very moment.
They emerge full of strength; and as they emerge, they wander about, beautifying the village fields.
"In the same way" is the application of the simile. This should be understood by correlating it with the meaning as follows:
for just as that hen performed the threefold action beginning with sitting upon the eggs, so too for this bhikkhu...

It is the time for application to meditation. Just as the non-spoiling of eggs by a hen through the performance of her threefold activity, so too there is no decline of insight-knowledge for a bhikkhu devoted to meditation through his accomplishment of the threefold contemplation.
By performing those three activities, just as the moisture in the eggs is dried up, so too for that bhikkhu, through the accomplishment of the threefold contemplation...
The exhaustion of the affection and attachment that follow the three states of existence is like the thinning of the eggshells;

the thinning of the monk’s eggshell of ignorance is like it; the sharp, harsh, clear, and courageous state of the monk’s insight-knowledge is like the hardness of the claws and beaks of chicklets; and the time for the chicklets’ emergence is like...
The time for the transformation, growth, and conception of a bhikkhu’s insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) is like the time when chicks,
having pierced the eggshell with the tips of their claws or their beaks and fanned out their wings,
emerge safely; it is the time when that bhikkhu, having caused the embryo of insight-knowledge to take hold, proceeds in his development.
It should be understood that when one obtains what is congenial to that [personality], whether it be a favorable climate, suitable food, a compatible person,
or the opportunity to hear the Dhamma, and while sitting on the very same seat increases insight,
one pierces the eggshell of ignorance and bursts open the wings of direct knowledge by means of the path of Arahantship attained through successive stages, reaching Arahantship in safety.
Just as a mother hen, knowing that her chicks have reached maturity, breaks open the shell of the egg, so too the Teacher, knowing the ripening of the knowledge of such a bhikkhu, said:
"Cut off your own attachment, as one would a lily with the hand at the end of autumn;
cultivate only the path to peace, the Nibbāna taught by the Sugata."
In this manner, having pervaded [the world] with light, he strikes the eggshell of ignorance with the verse.
At the conclusion of the verse, having broken the eggshell of ignorance, he attains Arahatship.
From that time forth, just as those chicks roam about beautifying the village fields, so too does this one, whose great taints are destroyed, [roam] with Nibbāna as his object.
Having entered the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), he wanders about, adorning the monastery.
"A carpenter" (*phalagaṇḍa*) means a builder; for he is called a "carpenter" because, having applied the tool known as a plane (*phala*), he removes the swellings (*gaṇḍa*) from the wood.
"In the sheath of the axe" (*vāsijaṭā*) refers to the place where the handle of the axe is held. This much of mine...

"Today the taints have been exhausted": for one who has gone forth, the taints are constantly exhausted through the summary of the going-forth, through recitation, through questioning, through wise attention, and through the performance of duties.

However, as they are thus being exhausted, there is no such knowledge in him as "this much has been exhausted today" or "this much was exhausted yesterday. This is the meaning. By this simile, the benefit of insight (vipassanā) is illustrated.
"By the winter season" means by the time of the cold season. "They subside" means they diminish due to their becoming firm.
"In the same way" refers here to the Teaching (sāsana), which should be regarded as like the great ocean; the practitioner (yogāvacara) as like a ship;
and this bhikkhu’s wandering in the presence of his preceptors and teachers during the period when he has fewer than five years of seniority as like the ship’s sailing upon the great ocean.

Just as the bonds of a ship being devoured by the waters of the great ocean become thin, so too do the fetters of a bhikkhu become thin through the mere summary of the going-forth, by means of recitation, questioning, and so forth;

just as the time when the ship is hauled onto dry land, so is the time when a bhikkhu, released from formal dependence, takes up his meditation subject and dwells in the forest; and just as there is drying up by the wind and heat during the day.
The drying up of the moisture of craving by means of insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) is like the withering [of plants] by the heat of the sun;
the moistening of the mind by means of rapture and gladness (*pīti-pāmojja*) arising in dependence on the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) is like the soaking [of them] by dew-water at night;

and the weakening of the bonds that have been thoroughly dried and scorched day and night by both wind and heat and by dew-water is like [the weakening of the bonds] by means of insight-knowledge and rapture and gladness.
The extreme weakness of the fetters is like a rain-cloud; the knowledge of the path to Arahantship is like the rain from that cloud.

Just as a ship becomes internally rotten through the water of the rain's downpour, so too for one who has begun insight and is increasing it by means of the "sevenfold set of materiality" and so forth, when the meditation subject is being submerged and swept away, on a certain day, due to favorable weather conditions and other factors...
The attainment of the fruit of arahantship by one who has obtained [it] while seated in a single cross-legged posture;
the remaining of a life-span for an arahant whose fetters are exhausted while supporting the great masses of people—like the staying of a ship bound by rotten ropes for a certain time;
and the arrival at the state of non-designation after the ship bound by rotten ropes has gradually broken apart—these are like the case of one whose taints are exhausted.

By this simile—that for one who has attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue through the breaking up of the aggregates subject to clinging, there is the attainment of a state of non-designation—the weakness of the fetters is illustrated.
8. Commentary on the Fire-Heap Simile Sutta.
72. This was spoken in connection with a specific incident (*atthuppatti*). That incident has already been explained in detail below in the commentary on the *Cūḷaccharāsaṅghāta-sutta*.
"Passatha no" means "do you see? "Āliṅgitvā" means having embraced.
"Upanisīdeyya" means would sit down close by, leaning against [him]. "Upanipajjeyya" means would lie down after approaching. "Ārocayāmi" means I declare.
"I declare" means having declared, having made known, I speak. "With a tail-rope" means with a rope twisted from the tails of horses or cows.
"On the chest" means on the middle of the breast. "Foaming up" means having caused foam to rise; the meaning is "having caused it to swell.
"One's own welfare" refers to one's own welfare pertaining to the present life and the future life, both mundane and supramundane. The same applies to the welfare of others and the welfare of both.
This is the method. Whatever else might need to be said here has already been explained in the *Cūḷaccharāsaṅghātasutta* (The Short Discourse on the Gathering of Female Crickets).
After delivering this discourse, the Teacher delivered the *Cūḷaccharāsaṅghātasutta*.
The ninth [discourse] is clear in meaning.
10. Commentary on the Āraka Sutta 74.
In the tenth [verse], *paritta* means small or slight. For it is indeed limited (*paritta*) both by its own nature, by the brevity of its moment, and by the brevity of its duration.
It is "light" because it arises and ceases quickly. It is to be understood through the *manta* (protective chant).
The meaning is: "It is to be understood by means of reflection (*mantāya*), it is to be known by means of wisdom (*paññāya*). "Mountain-born" (*pabbateyyā*) means originating from mountains.
"Carrying away what is to be carried" (*hārahārinī*) means capable of carrying away things to be taken, such as trees, reeds, bamboo, and so forth. The rest is entirely obvious in meaning throughout.
The Seventh Chapter (*Mahāvagga*) is concluded.
8. Vinaya Chapter. 1.
Commentary on the First Discourse on the Bearers of the Vinaya. 75.
In the first [discourse] of the eighth [chapter], "he knows an offense" means he knows an offense as indeed being an offense. The same method applies to the remaining phrases as well.
2. Commentary on the Second Discourse on the Bearers of the Discipline (Dutiyavinayadharasutta) 76.
In the second [discourse], "welcomed" (*svāgatāni*) means well-received or possessing excellent qualities. "Well-analyzed" (*suvibhattāni*) means well-divided according to their constituent parts.
"Well-functioning" (*suppavattīni*) means they function well and possess firm qualities in every instance where they are directed toward the mind. "Well-determined" (*suvinicchitāni*) means...
They are well-determined: by way of the *Sutta* from the *Vibhaṅga*, and by way of the *Anubyañjana* from the *Khandhaka* and *Parivāra*.
3. Commentary on the Third Discourse on the Bearer of the Vinaya (Vinayadhara-sutta) 77.
"But he stands firm in the Vinaya" means he is established in the characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) of the Vinaya. "Irreversible" means it is not possible to make him relinquish what he has grasped.
9. Commentary on the *Satthusāsana Sutta* 83. In the ninth [verse], "one" (*eko*) means without a second.
"Withdrawn" (*vūpakaṭṭho*) means withdrawn from the group by body, and withdrawn from defilements by mind; that is, secluded and distanced.

"Diligent" (*appamatto*) means established in non-forgetfulness of mindfulness. "With heart sent forth" (*pahitatto*) means one whose self is directed [toward the goal]. "For the sake of disenchantment" (*nibbidāya*)...

"For weariness" means for the sake of becoming weary of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*). "For dispassion" means for the sake of the fading away of passion and the other defilements. "For cessation" means for the sake of bringing about non-occurrence.

"For peace" means for the sake of the pacification of the defilements through their non-occurrence. "For direct knowledge" means for the sake of higher realization by applying the three characteristics (*tilakkhaṇa*).
"For full enlightenment" means for the sake of full enlightenment characterized as the Path (*magga*). "For Nibbāna" means for the sake of the realization of Nibbāna.
10. Commentary on the Sutta on the Settlement of Legal Matters (Adhikaraṇasamatha) 84.
In the tenth [sutta], they are called "settlements of legal matters" (*adhikaraṇasamatha*) because they settle and pacify legal matters (*adhikaraṇa*).

"Of those that have arisen repeatedly" means of those that have arisen again and again. "Legal matters" refers to the legal matter of dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*), the legal matter of accusation (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*), and the legal matter of offenses (*āpattādhikaraṇa*).

Regarding "a legal issue arising from business" among these four: "for the sake of settling and pacifying" means for the purpose of settlement (*samatha*) and for the purpose of pacification (*vūpasama*).
The seven methods of settling—*sammukhā-vinaya*, and so forth, up to *tiṇavatthāraka*—are to be applied.
Their detailed exposition should be understood from the *Vinaya-saṃvaṇṇanā*. Furthermore, it has already been explained in detail in the commentary on the *Saṅgīti-sutta* in the *Dīgha Nikāya*.
Likewise, [this is] in the commentary on the Sāmagāma Sutta of the Majjhima Nikāya.
The eighth section, the Vinaya-vagga, is concluded.
The seven suttas following this have their meanings already explained; for there is nothing here that does not follow the method already stated below.
The commentary on the Sattaka-nipāta of the Manorathapūraṇī,
the commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya, is completed.
